For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0` the negative binomial masses sum to one.
For `μ > 0` this is `hasSum_negBinomialPMF` transported along
`negBinomialReal_eq_negBinomialPMF`, so the mean parametrization shares the canonical
law's normalization instead of re-proving it.

articles.title: Normalization
articles.statement:
For a probability measure `ν` concentrated on `[0, ∞)`, the mixed
Poisson masses sum to one.

articles.title: Second moment
articles.statement: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0`, `E N² = μ + μ² / θ + μ²`.

articles.title: Second moment
articles.statement:
For a finite mixing measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with square-integrable rate,
`E N² = E Λ² + E Λ`.

articles.title: Immigration–death stationary law
Net probability flow of the immigration–death chain
articles.statement:
The net probability flow into state `n` of the immigration–death chain on `ℕ`, in which
molecules are made at rate `κ` (`n → n + 1`) and each decays at rate `γ` (`n → n - 1` at rate
`γ n`): `(κ p(n - 1) + γ (n + 1) p(n + 1)) - (κ + γ n) p(n)`, with no inflow from below at
`n = 0`. A law `p` is stationary (global balance) iff this flow vanishes for every `n`.

articles.title: Negative binomial splitting for random variables
articles.statement:
If `X` and `Y` are independent with
`P(X = j) = NB(r₁, p)(j)` and `P(Y = j) = NB(r₂, p)(j)` for all `j`, where `r₁, r₂ > 0` and
`0 < p < 1`, then `P(X = k ∣ X + Y = n) = BB(n; r₁, r₂)(k)` for `k ≤ n`.

articles.title: Negative binomial splitting
articles.statement:
For `r₁, r₂ > 0`, `0 < p < 1` and `k ≤ n`,
`NB(r₁, p)(k) NB(r₂, p)(n - k) / NB(r₁ + r₂, p)(n) = BB(n; r₁, r₂)(k)`; the conditional law of
one component given the total is beta-binomial and does not depend on `p`.

articles.title: Negative binomial mass function with real shape
articles.statement:
Negative binomial mass `P(X = k) = r^{(k)} / k! · p ^ r · (1 - p) ^ k` with real shape `r`
(rising factorial `r^{(k)} = (ascPochhammer ℝ k).eval r`) and success probability `p`, using the
real power `p ^ r`. A probability mass function for `r > 0` and `p ∈ (0, 1]`.

articles.title: Mean parametrization is the canonical `p`-parametrization
articles.statement:
For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0`,
`negBinomialReal θ μ` is `negBinomialPMF θ p` at `p = θ / (θ + μ)`, since
`1 - p = μ / (θ + μ)`. The two APIs are the same law; reuse the splitting and
conditioning results proved for `negBinomialPMF` through this equivalence.

articles.title: Negative binomial law with mean zero is a point mass
articles.statement: With mean `0` the negative binomial law is the point mass at `0`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the negative binomial mass function
articles.statement: The negative binomial mass function is nonnegative on the parameter domain.

articles.title: Zero class of the negative binomial law
articles.statement: The zero class of the negative binomial law is `(θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ`.

articles.title: Negative binomial mass function with size and mean
articles.statement:
The negative binomial mass function with size `θ` and mean `μ`:
`NB(k; θ, μ) = θ⁽ᵏ⁾ / k! · (θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ · (μ / (θ + μ)) ^ k`, with the rising factorial
`θ⁽ᵏ⁾ = Γ(θ + k) / Γ(θ)` and a real power `(θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ`. The parameter domain is `θ > 0`,
`μ ≥ 0`; at `μ = 0` it is the point mass at `0`. Outside the domain the formula is not a
probability mass function.

articles.title: Poisson mixture over a point mass is Poisson
articles.statement: The Poisson mixture over a point mass `δ_m` is the Poisson law with mean `m`.

articles.title: Greenwood–Yule, mean form
articles.statement:
For `θ, μ > 0`, the Poisson mixture over `Gamma(θ, θ / μ)`
(mean `μ`, variance `μ² / θ`) is `NB(θ, μ)`.

articles.title: Greenwood–Yule
articles.statement:
The Poisson mixture over a Gamma rate of shape `a > 0` and rate `b > 0`
is negative binomial with size `a` and mean `a / b`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the mixed Poisson mass function
articles.statement: The mixed Poisson mass function is nonnegative when `ν` is concentrated on `[0, ∞)`.

articles.title: Zero class of a mixed Poisson law
articles.statement: The zero class of a mixed Poisson law is `E e^{-Λ}`.

articles.title: Mixed Poisson mass function
articles.statement:
The mixed Poisson mass function `p(k) = ∫ e^{-λ} λ^k / k! dν(λ)` for a mixing law `ν` of the
rate. It is a probability mass function when `ν` is a probability measure concentrated on
`[0, ∞)`, which the theorems below assume; for such `ν` the integrand lies in `[0, 1]`, so the
integral is never a junk value.

articles.title: Gamma–Poisson conjugacy, posterior predictive
articles.statement:
With prior `Λ ~ Gamma(a, b)`
(`a, b > 0`) and counts `N, N'` that are independent `Po(Λ)` given `Λ`,
`P(N' = j | N = k) = P(N = k, N' = j) / P(N = k) = NB(j; a + k, (a + k) / (b + 1))`.

articles.title: Beta-binomial masses sum to one
articles.statement: The beta-binomial masses sum to one for `α, β > 0`.

articles.title: Mean
articles.statement: For `α, β > 0`, `E M = n α / (α + β) = n π`.

articles.title: Second factorial moment
Convolution of negative binomial laws with a common `p`
articles.statement:
`∑_{k ≤ n} NB(r₁, p)(k) NB(r₂, p)(n - k) = NB(r₁ + r₂, p)(n)` for `p > 0` and all real
shapes.

articles.title: Variance
articles.statement:
**Variance** (Dolzhenko–Smith parametrization). For `α, β > 0`, with `π = α / (α + β)` and
`γ = 1 / (α + β + 1)`, `Var M = E M² - (E M)² = n π (1 - π) (1 + (n - 1) γ)`.

articles.title: Variance
articles.statement:
For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0` the negative binomial law has variance
`μ + μ² / θ`.

articles.title: Variance decomposition
articles.statement:
For a probability measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with square-integrable
rate, `Var N = E N² - (E N)² = E Λ + Var Λ`: Poisson noise plus the variance of the rate.

articles.title: Binomial distribution of a sum of i.i.d. Bernoulli variables
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
probability measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $m \in \mathbb{N}$, let $p$ be a real
number, and let $X_1, \dots, X_m : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ be measurable, mutually independent
random variables, each a Bernoulli random variable with parameter $p$ under $\mu$. Then for
every $j \in \mathbb{N}$ the probability that $X_1 + \dots + X_m = j$ is
$\binom{m}{j} p^j (1 - p)^{m - j}$, where the exponent $m - j$ is taken to be $0$ when $j > m$.

articles.title: Distribution of a sum of independent Bernoulli variables
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability
measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $m \in \mathbb{N}$, and let
$X_1, \dots, X_m : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ be measurable, mutually independent random variables
such that each $X_i$ is a Bernoulli random variable with real parameter $p_i$ under $\mu$.
Then for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$ the probability that $X_1 + \dots + X_m = j$ equals

$$
\sum_{A \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\},\ |A| = j} \ \prod_{i \in A} p_i \prod_{i \notin A} (1 - p_i).
$$

This is the Poisson binomial distribution.

articles.title: Binomial upper tail is monotone in the success probability
articles.statement: The upper tail `Bin(n, p)([k, ∞))` of Mathlib's binomial law is monotone in `p`.

articles.title: Binomial tail monotonicity
Law of a Bernoulli random variable
articles.statement:
If $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ is a Bernoulli random
variable with parameter $p$ under a measure $\mu$, then $X$ is $\mu$-almost everywhere
measurable and its law under $\mu$, the pushforward of $\mu$ along $X$, is the Bernoulli
distribution $p\,\delta_1 + (1 - p)\,\delta_0$ on $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Bernoulli random variable
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, let
$X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ and let $p$ be a real number. Then $X$ is a Bernoulli random
variable with parameter $p$ under $\mu$ when $0 \le p \le 1$, $X$ is $\mu$-almost everywhere
measurable, and the pushforward of $\mu$ along $X$ is the Bernoulli distribution
$p\,\delta_1 + (1 - p)\,\delta_0$ on $\mathbb{N}$, which gives mass $p$ to $1$, mass $1 - p$
to $0$ and no mass elsewhere.

articles.title: Bernoulli parameters are at most one
articles.statement:
If $X$ is a Bernoulli random variable with
parameter $p$ under a measure $\mu$, then $p \le 1$.

articles.title: Tail of a sum of independent Bernoulli variables is Poisson-binomial
articles.statement:
For independent Bernoulli variables `X i` with parameters `p i`, the one-sided burden
p-value `P(∑ X i ≥ k)` is the Poisson-binomial tail.

articles.title: Probability that a Bernoulli variable equals one
articles.statement:
If $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ is a
Bernoulli random variable with parameter $p$ under a measure $\mu$, then
$\mu(\{\omega : X(\omega) = 1\}) = p$, as an extended nonnegative real.

articles.title: Probability that a Bernoulli variable equals zero
articles.statement:
If $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ is a
Bernoulli random variable with parameter $p$ under a measure $\mu$, then
$\mu(\{\omega : X(\omega) = 0\}) = 1 - p$, as an extended nonnegative real.

articles.title: Bernoulli parameters are nonnegative
articles.statement:
If $X$ is a Bernoulli random variable with
parameter $p$ under a measure $\mu$, then $0 \le p$.

articles.title: First-step recurrence for the Poisson-binomial mass function
articles.statement:
Adding a trial with probability `a`: first-step decomposition of the mass function,
`P(S' = j + 1) = a P(S = j) + (1 - a) P(S = j + 1)`.

articles.title: Poisson-binomial mass at zero after adding a trial
articles.statement: Adding a trial with probability `a`: no successes requires a failure of the new trial.

articles.title: Poisson-binomial law with equal probabilities is binomial
articles.statement: With equal probabilities the Poisson-binomial law is the binomial law.

articles.title: Poisson-binomial mass vanishes above the number of trials
articles.statement: The Poisson-binomial mass function vanishes above the number of trials.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the Poisson-binomial mass function
articles.statement: The Poisson-binomial mass function is nonnegative for probabilities in `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Poisson-binomial mass function
articles.statement:
Poisson-binomial mass function of the number of successes among independent trials with
success probabilities `p : Fin m → ℝ`:
`∑_{A ⊆ [m], |A| = j} ∏_{i ∈ A} p i ∏_{i ∉ A} (1 - p i)`. A probability mass function when
every `p i ∈ [0, 1]`; the algebraic identities below hold for all real `p`.

articles.title: Poisson-binomial tail after adding a trial
articles.statement:
Adding a trial with probability `a` raises the upper tail by exactly `a P(S = k)`:
`P(S' ≥ k + 1) = P(S ≥ k + 1) + a P(S = k)`. So the tail is affine in each trial's probability,
with nonnegative slope a point mass of the remaining trials.

articles.title: Peeling off the lowest term of the Poisson-binomial tail
articles.statement: Peeling off the lowest term of the tail: `P(S ≥ k) = P(S = k) + P(S ≥ k + 1)`.

articles.title: The burden-test p-value is monotone in every background rate
articles.statement:
If `p i ≤ q i` for all
`i`, with all probabilities in `[0, 1]`, then `P_p(S ≥ k) ≤ P_q(S ≥ k)`.

articles.title: Upper tail of the Poisson-binomial law
articles.statement:
Upper tail `P(S ≥ k) = ∑_{k ≤ j ≤ m} P(S = j)` of the Poisson-binomial law (the mass
function vanishes above `m`).

articles.title: Poisson-binomial masses sum to one
articles.statement:
The Poisson-binomial masses sum to one (an identity for all real `p`; it is the expansion
of `∏ ((1 - p i) + p i) = 1`).

articles.title: Le Cam's inequality, finite truncations
articles.statement:
For probabilities `p i ∈ [0, 1]` and
`λ = ∑ p i`, every partial sum of `∑_j |P(S = j) - e^{-λ} λ^j / j!|` is at most `2 ∑ (p i)²`.

articles.title: Le Cam's inequality
articles.statement:
**Le Cam's inequality** (Le Cam 1960): the series `∑_j |P(S = j) - e^{-λ} λ^j / j!|` is
summable and its sum is at most `2 ∑ (p i)²`, where `λ = ∑ p i`.

articles.title: Continuity points of the cdf have null boundary
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F(y) = \mu((-\infty, y])$. If $F$ is
continuous at a point $x \in \mathbb{R}$, then the boundary of the half-line $(-\infty, x]$,
which is $\{x\}$, has $\mu$-measure zero.

articles.title: No atom at a continuity point of the cdf
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F(y) = \mu((-\infty, y])$. If $F$ is
continuous at a point $x \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\mu(\{x\}) = 0$.

articles.title: The cdf is continuous exactly at the non-atoms
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F(y) = \mu((-\infty, y])$. For every
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F$ is continuous at $x$ if and only if $\mu(\{x\}) = 0$.

articles.title: The continuity points of the cdf are dense
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F(y) = \mu((-\infty, y])$. The set of
points $x \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous is dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

This follows from the fact that a monotone function has only countably many discontinuities.

articles.title: Mass of a half-open interval via the cdf
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F(y) = \mu((-\infty, y])$. For all
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, the measure $\mu((a, b])$ equals $\max(F(b) - F(a), 0)$, as an extended
nonnegative real.

articles.title: Atoms are the jumps of the cdf
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with
cumulative distribution function $F(y) = \mu((-\infty, y])$, and for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ let
$F(x^-) = \lim_{y \to x^-} F(y)$ be its left limit at $x$. Then $\mu(\{x\})$ equals the jump
$F(x) - F(x^-)$, which is a nonnegative real number since $F$ is nondecreasing.

articles.title: Joint law of two random variables on a rectangle
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a measure on a measurable
space $\Omega$, and let $X : \Omega \to \mathcal{X}$ and $Y : \Omega \to \mathcal{Y}$ be
$P$-almost everywhere measurable maps into measurable spaces. For measurable sets
$s \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ and $t \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$, the pushforward of $P$ under
$\omega \mapsto (X(\omega), Y(\omega))$ gives $s \times t$ the measure
$P(\{\omega : X(\omega) \in s \text{ and } Y(\omega) \in t\})$.

When $P$ is a probability measure this pushforward is the joint law of $X$ and $Y$, and the value
is the probability that both events occur.

articles.title: Absolute deviations are integrable exactly when the mean exists
articles.statement:
Let $
u$ be a finite
measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $	heta \mapsto |	heta - c|$ is
$
u$-integrable if and only if $	heta \mapsto 	heta$ is $
u$-integrable.

articles.title: A median minimizes the expected absolute loss
articles.statement:
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ and let $m$ be a median of $\nu$. Then for every $y \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$
\int |\theta - m| \, d\nu(\theta) \le \int |\theta - y| \, d\nu(\theta).
$$

When $\nu$ has no first moment, neither integrand is integrable and both integrals are $0$ by
the convention for non-integrable functions.

articles.title: Median of a measure on the real line
articles.statement:
Let $
u$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$, typically a
probability measure. A real number $m$ is a median of $
u$ when $
u((-\infty, m]) \ge 1/2$
and $
u([m, \infty)) \ge 1/2$, where a set of infinite measure counts as having measure $0$.

articles.title: The quantile function as a generalized inverse of the cdf
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative distribution function $F_\mu$ and quantile function $Q_\mu$. For
every $u \in (0, 1)$ and every real $x$, $Q_\mu(u) \le x$ if and only if $u \le F_\mu(x)$.

articles.title: The cdf at the quantile is at least the level
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with
cumulative distribution function $F_\mu$ and quantile function $Q_\mu$. For every $u \in (0, 1)$,
$u \le F_\mu(Q_\mu(u))$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the quantile function
articles.statement:
For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the quantile
function $Q_\mu$ is monotone on $(0, 1)$: if $0 < u \le v < 1$, then $Q_\mu(u) \le Q_\mu(v)$.

articles.title: Quantile function of a real measure
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with cumulative
distribution function $F_\mu$ (for a probability measure, $F_\mu(x) = \mu((-\infty, x])$). The
quantile function of $\mu$, the generalized inverse of $F_\mu$, is the function
$Q_\mu : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by
$Q_\mu(u) = \inf \lbrace x \in \mathbb{R} : u \le F_\mu(x) \rbrace$ for $u \in (0, 1)$ and
$Q_\mu(u) = 0$ for $u \notin (0, 1)$.

articles.title: Inverse transform sampling
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with quantile
function $Q_\mu$. The pushforward under $Q_\mu$ of Lebesgue measure restricted to $[0, 1]$ is
$\mu$.

articles.title: Measurability of the quantile function
articles.statement:
For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the
quantile function $Q_\mu : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is measurable.

articles.title: The regression function is the Bayes-optimal regressor
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure
on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $X : \Omega \to \mathcal{X}$ be a measurable map into a
measurable space $\mathcal{X}$, and let $Y : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be square-integrable with
respect to $\mu$. Write $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]$ for the conditional expectation of $Y$ with
respect to $\mu$ given the σ-algebra generated by $X$. Then for every measurable
$h : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $h \circ X$ is square-integrable with respect to $\mu$,
$\int (Y - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X])^2 \, d\mu \le \int (Y - h \circ X)^2 \, d\mu$.

articles.title: The conditional mean minimizes the expected squared error
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure
on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, let $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ be a
sub-σ-algebra, and let $Y : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be square-integrable with respect to $\mu$.
Write $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}]$ for the conditional expectation of $Y$ with respect to
$\mu$ given $\mathcal{G}$. Then for every strongly $\mathcal{G}$-measurable
$g : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ that is square-integrable with respect to $\mu$,
$\int (Y - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}])^2 \, d\mu \le \int (Y - g)^2 \, d\mu$.

articles.title: Pythagorean identity for the conditional mean
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on a
measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, let $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ be a
sub-σ-algebra, and let $Y : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be square-integrable with respect to $\mu$.
Write $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}]$ for the conditional expectation of $Y$ with respect to
$\mu$ given $\mathcal{G}$. Then for every strongly $\mathcal{G}$-measurable
$g : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ that is square-integrable with respect to $\mu$,
$\int (Y - g)^2 \, d\mu = \int (Y - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}])^2 \, d\mu +
\int (\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}] - g)^2 \, d\mu$.

articles.title: Orthogonality of the conditional-expectation residual
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure
on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, let $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ be a
sub-σ-algebra, and let $Y : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be square-integrable with respect to $\mu$.
Write $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}]$ for the conditional expectation of $Y$ with respect to
$\mu$ given $\mathcal{G}$. Then for every strongly $\mathcal{G}$-measurable
$h : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ that is square-integrable with respect to $\mu$, the residual
$Y - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}]$ is orthogonal to $h$:
$\int (Y - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{G}]) \, h \, d\mu = 0$.

articles.title: De Finetti's theorem for binary sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on the space
$\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of binary sequences $\omega = (\omega_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, with $0$ and
$1$ standing for false and true. Suppose $\mu$ is exchangeable: for every permutation $\pi$ of
$\mathbb{N}$ that moves only finitely many points, the image of $\mu$ under the map
$\omega \mapsto \omega \circ \pi$ is $\mu$. Then there is a probability measure $\nu$ on $[0, 1]$
such that for all disjoint finite sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$,

$$\mu\{\omega : \omega_i = 1 \text{ for all } i \in A \text{ and } \omega_i = 0 \text{ for all }
i \in B\} = \int_{[0, 1]} p^{|A|} (1 - p)^{|B|} \, d\nu(p).$$

## Sources

- B. de Finetti, Funzione caratteristica di un fenomeno aleatorio, Atti Accad. Naz. Lincei 4 (1931) and La prévision: ses lois logiques (1937); textbook in Kallenberg, Probabilistic Symmetries and Invariance Principles; also Durrett, Probability Theory and Examples

articles.title: Hewitt–Savage zero–one law for i.i.d. sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
a measurable space $\Omega$, let $S$ be a measurable space, and let
$X_0, X_1, X_2, \ldots : \Omega \to S$ be measurable maps that are independent under $\mu$ and
each have the same distribution under $\mu$ as $X_0$. If an event $E \subseteq \Omega$ is
exchangeable with respect to $(X_n)$, then $\mu(E) = 0$ or $\mu(E) = 1$.

articles.title: Hewitt–Savage zero–one law
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on a measurable space $S$,
and let $E \subseteq S^{\mathbb{N}}$ be a set that is measurable for the product σ-algebra and
invariant under every finitely supported permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$, that is,
$\{\omega : \omega \circ \sigma \in E\} = E$ whenever $\sigma$ moves only finitely many points.
Then $E$ has measure $0$ or $1$ under the product measure $\mu^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$.

No topological assumption on $S$ is needed.

articles.title: Hewitt–Savage zero–one law on a Polish space
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a Polish space with its Borel
σ-algebra, let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $S$, and let $E \subseteq S^{\mathbb{N}}$ be a set
that is measurable for the product σ-algebra and invariant under every finitely supported
permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$, that is, $\{\omega : \omega \circ \sigma \in E\} = E$
whenever $\sigma$ moves only finitely many points. Then $E$ has measure $0$ or $1$ under the
product measure $\mu^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$.

The Polish and Borel assumptions are not used in the proof: the same conclusion holds for a
probability measure on any measurable space.

## Sources

- E. Hewitt and L. J. Savage, Symmetric measures on Cartesian products, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 80 (1955) 470–501; textbook in Kallenberg, Probabilistic Symmetries and Invariance Principles; general holds for product of identical Borel probabilities.

articles.title: Event exchangeable with respect to a sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ and $S$ be measurable spaces
and let $X_0, X_1, \ldots : \Omega \to S$ be a sequence of maps. An event $E \subseteq \Omega$ is
exchangeable with respect to $(X_n)$ if there is an exchangeable event $A \subseteq S^{\mathbb{N}}$
such that $E = \{\omega \in \Omega : (X_n(\omega))_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \in A\}$.

Equivalently, $E$ belongs to the σ-field of exchangeable events generated by $(X_n)$.

articles.title: Exchangeable event
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a measurable space. A set $A \subseteq S^{\mathbb{N}}$ is an
exchangeable (or permutable) event if it is measurable for the product σ-algebra and
$\{x : x \circ \sigma \in A\} = A$ for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$ that moves only
finitely many indices.

articles.title: Exchangeable events of a measurable sequence are measurable
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ and $S$ be
measurable spaces and let $X_0, X_1, \ldots : \Omega \to S$ be measurable maps. If
$E \subseteq \Omega$ is exchangeable with respect to $(X_n)$, then $E$ is measurable.

articles.title: Kolmogorov extension theorem
articles.statement:
Let $(\alpha_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of Polish spaces, each
with its Borel σ-algebra, indexed by an arbitrary type $\iota$. For each finite set
$J \subseteq \iota$ let $P_J$ be a probability measure on $\prod_{j \in J} \alpha_j$, and suppose
the family is projective: whenever $J \subseteq I$ are finite, the image of $P_I$ under the
restriction map $\prod_{i \in I} \alpha_i \to \prod_{j \in J} \alpha_j$ is $P_J$. Then there is a
measure $\mu$ on $\prod_{i \in \iota} \alpha_i$ whose image under the restriction map to
$\prod_{j \in J} \alpha_j$ is $P_J$ for every finite $J \subseteq \iota$.

## Sources

- A. N. Kolmogorov, Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, 1933; P. J. Daniell 1918 precursor; textbook in Kallenberg, Foundations of Modern Probability, 3rd ed. (Kolmogorov extension) and Tao, Introduction to Measure Theory Lean Polish Borel projective-limit version; full general version handles standard Borel factors.

articles.title: Construction of measures on ℝ, as unique existence
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a Stieltjes function, that is, non-decreasing and
right-continuous, with $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to -\infty$ and $f(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \infty$.
Then there is exactly one measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ that is a probability measure and
satisfies $\mu((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all real $a \le b$.

articles.title: Construction of measures on ℝ
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a Stieltjes
function, that is, non-decreasing and right-continuous, with $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to -\infty$
and $f(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \infty$, and let $\mu_f$ be its Stieltjes measure on $\mathbb{R}$.
Then $\mu_f$ is a probability measure, $\mu_f((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all real $a \le b$,
and every finite measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\nu((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all real
$a \le b$ equals $\mu_f$.

articles.title: The conditional distribution kernel is a regular conditional distribution
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$
be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\alpha$, and $X : \alpha \to \beta$,
$Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ measurable maps. Then the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under
$\mu$, the kernel from $\beta$ to $\Omega$ obtained by disintegrating the joint law of $(X, Y)$
under $\mu$, is a regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$.

articles.title: Existence of measure-valued regular conditional distributions given a sub-σ-algebra
articles.statement:
Let
$\Omega$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on a measurable space
$(\alpha, \mathcal{F})$, $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ a sub-σ-algebra, and
$Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ an $\mathcal{F}$-measurable map. Then some family of measures on $\Omega$
indexed by $\alpha$ is a measure-valued regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given
$\mathcal{G}$ under $\mu$.

The witness is the conditional distribution of $Y$ given the identity map from
$(\alpha, \mathcal{F})$ to $(\alpha, \mathcal{G})$.

articles.title: Existence of measure-valued regular conditional distributions given a random variable
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\alpha$, and
$X : \alpha \to \beta$, $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ measurable maps. Then some family of measures on
$\Omega$ indexed by $\alpha$ is a measure-valued regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given
the σ-algebra $\sigma(X)$ on $\alpha$ generated by $X$, under $\mu$.

articles.title: Existence of regular conditional distributions (kernel form)
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty
standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\alpha$, and $X : \alpha \to \beta$,
$Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ measurable maps. Then there exists a kernel $\kappa$ from $\beta$ to
$\Omega$ that is a regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$; in particular
$\kappa$ is a Markov kernel.

articles.title: Regular conditional distribution (kernel form)
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\alpha$ and let
$X : \alpha \to \beta$ and $Y : \alpha \to \Omega$ be maps. A kernel $\kappa$ from $\beta$ to
$\Omega$ is a regular conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ under $\mu$ if $X$ and $Y$ are
measurable, $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, and for every measurable set $s \subseteq \Omega$ the
real-valued function $a \mapsto \kappa(X(a))(s)$ is $\mu$-almost everywhere equal to the
conditional expectation $\mu[\mathbf{1}_{Y^{-1}(s)} \mid \sigma(X)]$, where $\sigma(X)$ is the
σ-algebra on $\alpha$ generated by $X$.

articles.title: Regular conditional distribution (measure-valued family)
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a measure on a
measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, let $S$ be a measurable space, $X : \Omega \to S$ a
map, $\mathcal{G}$ a σ-algebra on $\Omega$, and $\rho$ a family assigning a measure $\rho_\omega$
on $S$ to each $\omega \in \Omega$. Then $\rho$ is a regular conditional distribution of $X$
given $\mathcal{G}$ under $P$ if $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$; $X$ is
$\mathcal{F}$-measurable; for every measurable $A \subseteq S$ the map
$\omega \mapsto \rho_\omega(A)$ is $\mathcal{G}$-measurable; $\rho_\omega(S) \le 1$ for every
$\omega$; for every measurable $A \subseteq S$ the real number $\rho_\omega(A)$ agrees, for
$P$-almost every $\omega$, with the conditional expectation
$P[\mathbf{1}_{X^{-1}(A)} \mid \mathcal{G}](\omega)$; and $\rho_\omega$ is a probability measure
for $P$-almost every $\omega$.

Because each $\rho_\omega$ is a measure, countable additivity holds at every sample point,
including null ones; this is stricter than the raw set-function definition of Lecture 26, whose
set functions need to form probability measures only almost everywhere.

articles.title: Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant
articles.statement:
The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant is the
BHH constant of the uniform law on the closed unit square $[0,1]^2$ (Lebesgue measure restricted
to $[0,1]^2$): the infimum of the set of real numbers $\beta$ such that i.i.d. samples with this
law exist and, for every such sample $X_1, X_2, \dots$, the length of the shortest closed tour
through $X_1, \dots, X_n$ divided by $\sqrt{n}$ tends to $\beta$ almost surely. The infimum of a
set of reals that is empty or not bounded below is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley lower bound
articles.statement:
The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$
for uniform points in the unit square satisfies $\beta_2 \ge 5/8 = 0.625$.

## Sources

- Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley (1959), catalogue lower-bound row.

articles.title: Statement of the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley lower bound
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ for uniform points in the unit square satisfies
$\beta_2 \ge 5/8 = 0.625$, the lower bound reported by Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley (1959).

articles.title: Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley upper bound
articles.statement:
The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$
for uniform points in the unit square satisfies $\beta_2 \le 0.92117$.

## Sources

- Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley (1959), catalogue upper-bound row.

articles.title: Statement of the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley upper bound
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ for uniform points in the unit square satisfies
$\beta_2 \le 0.92117$, the upper bound reported by Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley (1959).

articles.title: The BHH constant equals the unique BHH limit
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on the plane and
$\beta$ a real number. If, for every real $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is a BHH limit for $\mu$ if and only
if $\gamma = \beta$, then the BHH constant of $\mu$ (the infimum of its BHH limits) equals $\beta$.

The hypothesis excludes the case with no BHH limit, where the infimum is $0$ by convention.

articles.title: BHH constant of a sampling law
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on the plane, the BHH constant of $\mu$
is the infimum of the set of real numbers $\beta$ that are BHH limits for $\mu$. The infimum of a
set of reals that is empty or not bounded below is taken to be $0$.

No existence theorem is assumed: the definition does not presuppose that a BHH limit exists.

articles.title: BHH limit values of a sampling law
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on the plane, the BHH limit values
of $\mu$ form the set of real numbers $\beta$ that are BHH limits for $\mu$.

articles.title: Notation C₁₂ for the BHH constant
articles.statement:
The constant $C_{12}$ is defined to be the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ for uniform points in the unit square; $C_{12}$ is
the name the source uses for it.

articles.title: Cyclic successor
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and an index $i$ with $0 \le i < n$, the cyclic
successor of $i$ is $(i + 1) \bmod n$; in particular the successor of $n - 1$ is $0$. For $n = 0$
there are no indices.

articles.title: Gaudio–Jaillet lower bound for the BHH constant
articles.statement:
The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley
constant $\beta_2$ of the unit square satisfies $0.6277 \le \beta_2$.

## Sources

- Gaudio and Jaillet, An improved lower bound for the Traveling Salesman constant.

articles.title: Statement of the Gaudio–Jaillet lower bound
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ of the unit square is at least $0.6277$, that is,
$0.6277 \le \beta_2$.

articles.title: Almost-sure BHH limit
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a measurable space with a measure $\mu$, let
$X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be functions into the plane, and let $\beta$
be a real number. The sequence has BHH limit $\beta$ when, for $\mu$-almost every
$\omega \in \Omega$, the normalized tour length $L_n(\omega)/\sqrt{n}$ tends to $\beta$ as
$n \to \infty$, where $L_n(\omega)$ is the length of a shortest closed tour through
$X_0(\omega), \dots, X_{n-1}(\omega)$.

articles.title: Unique BHH constant of a law
articles.statement:
A measure $\nu$ on the plane has a unique BHH constant when
there is exactly one real number $\beta$ that is a BHH constant for $\nu$.

articles.title: I.i.d. realization
articles.statement:
For a measure $\nu$ on the plane, an i.i.d. realization with law $\nu$
consists of a measurable space $\Omega$ with a measure $\mathbb{P}$, together with a sequence
$X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2$ of points that is i.i.d. with common law
$\nu$ under $\mathbb{P}$.

articles.title: BHH constant of a law
articles.statement:
For a measure $\nu$ on the plane and a real number $\beta$, $\beta$
is a BHH constant for $\nu$ when an i.i.d. realization with law $\nu$ exists and every i.i.d.
realization with law $\nu$ has almost-sure BHH limit $\beta$: almost surely,
$L_n/\sqrt{n} \to \beta$, where $L_n$ is the length of a shortest closed tour through the first
$n$ points.

Requiring a realization to exist keeps the condition from holding vacuously.

articles.title: I.i.d. points with a given law
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a measurable space with a measure
$\mathbb{P}$, let $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be functions and let $\nu$
be a measure on the Borel sets of the plane. The $X_i$ are i.i.d. with law $\nu$ when
$\mathbb{P}$ and $\nu$ are probability measures, every $X_i$ is measurable, the $X_i$ are mutually
independent under $\mathbb{P}$, and the distribution of each $X_i$ under $\mathbb{P}$ is $\nu$.

articles.title: Membership in the set of BHH limit values
articles.statement:
For a measure $
u$ on the plane and a real
number $ eta$, $ eta$ belongs to the set of BHH limit values of $
u$ if and only if $ eta$ is a
BHH constant for $
u$.

articles.title: Normalized tour length
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a set and let
$X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be functions. For an outcome
$\omega \in \Omega$ and $n \ge 1$, the normalized tour length is $L_n(\omega)/\sqrt{n}$, where
$L_n(\omega)$ is the length of a shortest closed tour through $X_0(\omega), \dots, X_{n-1}(\omega)$.
For $n = 0$ it is defined to be $0$.

The value at $n = 0$ does not affect limits as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Points of the Euclidean plane
articles.statement:
A planar point is a point of the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$: a pair $(x, y)$ of real numbers, with the Euclidean norm
$\lVert (x, y) \rVert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.

articles.title: Shortest tour length
articles.statement:
For points $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in the Euclidean plane, $L_n$ is
the minimum, over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, of the length of the closed
tour that visits $x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}$ in this order and returns to its start.

articles.title: Gaudio–Jaillet corrected lower bound for the BHH constant
articles.statement:
The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley
constant $\beta_2$ satisfies $\frac{5}{8} + \frac{19}{10368} \le \beta_2$.

## Sources

- Gaudio and Jaillet (2020), correction of Steinerberger's lower coefficient.

articles.title: Statement of the corrected Steinerberger lower bound
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ satisfies
$\frac{5}{8} + \frac{19}{10368} \le \beta_2$.

The bound is the exact rational $\frac{5}{8} + \frac{19}{10368}$, not a decimal approximation of it.

articles.title: Steinerberger's upper bound for the BHH constant
articles.statement:
The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant
$\beta_2$ satisfies $\beta_2 \le 0.92117 - \frac{9}{16} \cdot 10^{-6}$.

## Sources

- Steinerberger, New Bounds for the Traveling Salesman Constant (2015).

articles.title: Statement of Steinerberger's upper bound
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ satisfies
$\beta_2 \le 0.92117 - \frac{9}{16} \cdot 10^{-6}$.

articles.title: Length of a closed tour
articles.statement:
For points $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in the Euclidean plane and a
permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the tour length is
$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \lVert x_{\sigma(i)} - x_{\sigma(i+1 \bmod n)} \rVert$, the length of the closed
tour that visits $x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}$ in this order and returns to its start.

articles.title: Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\beta_2$ be the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley
constant and, for points $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of the plane, let $L_n$ be the length of the shortest
closed tour through $X_0, \dots, X_{n-1}$. Then a sequence of independent random points
$X_0, X_1, \dots$, each uniformly distributed on the closed unit square $[0,1]^2$, exists on some
probability space; for every such sequence, almost surely $L_n / \sqrt{n} \to \beta_2$ as
$n \to \infty$; and $\beta_2$ is the only real number $\beta$ such that every such sequence almost
surely satisfies $L_n / \sqrt{n} \to \beta$.

## Sources

- Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley (1959), quoted in Steinerberger (2015).

articles.title: Statement of the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley theorem
articles.statement:
The proposition that the
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ is a BHH constant for the uniform law on the closed
unit square $[0,1]^2$, and that every real number $\beta$ that is a BHH constant for this law equals
$\beta_2$. Here a real number $\beta$ is a BHH constant for a law $\mu$ on the plane when a
sequence $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of independent random points with common law $\mu$ exists on some
probability space, and for every such sequence, almost surely $L_n / \sqrt{n} \to \beta$ as
$n \to \infty$, where $L_n$ is the length of the shortest closed tour through $X_0, \dots, X_{n-1}$.

articles.title: Uniform law on the unit square
articles.statement:
Lebesgue measure on the Euclidean plane restricted to the
closed unit square $[0,1]^2$.

articles.title: Unit square
articles.statement:
The closed unit square $[0,1]^2$: the set of points of the Euclidean plane
both of whose coordinates lie in the interval $[0,1]$.

articles.title: The notation $\beta_2$
articles.statement:
We write $\beta_2$ for the real-valued Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley
constant of the unit square.

articles.title: Yu–Carlsson upper bound on the BHH constant
articles.statement:
The real-valued Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley
constant $\beta_2$ of the unit square satisfies $\beta_2 < 0.90304$.

## Sources

- Yu and Carlsson (2023), strict upper-bound row in the catalogue.

articles.title: Statement of the Yu–Carlsson upper bound
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that the real-valued
Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ of the unit square satisfies $\beta_2 < 0.90304$.

## Sources

- [YC2023], strict computer-aided upper bound.

articles.title: Entropy of the uniform density of a convex body
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body with Lebesgue measure
$\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ and uniform density $f_K$, equal to $1/\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ on $K$ and to $0$
outside $K$. Then the differential entropy $-\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_K(x) \log f_K(x) \, dx$ of
$f_K$ equals $\log \mathrm{Vol}(K)$.

articles.title: Uniform density of a convex body
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a
full-dimensional convex body, so that its Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ is finite and
positive. The uniform density of $K$ is the function $f_K \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ equal
to $1/\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ on $K$ and to $0$ outside $K$.

articles.title: The uniform law on a convex body as an intrinsic log-concave law
articles.statement:
For a full-dimensional
convex body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, this is the intrinsic log-concave law on $\mathbb{R}^n$
of intrinsic dimension $n$ whose chart is the identity map of $\mathbb{R}^n$, whose law is the
uniform probability law on $K$, and whose coordinate law is that uniform law viewed as a
log-concave law with density $\mathbf{1}_K / \operatorname{vol}(K)$.

articles.title: Isotropic constant of a convex body
articles.statement:
For a full-dimensional convex body $K$ in
$\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\operatorname{Cov}(K)$ be the covariance matrix of the uniform probability
law on $K$ and let $\operatorname{vol}(K)$ be the Lebesgue volume of $K$. The isotropic constant
of $K$ is the real number
$L_K = \left(\det \operatorname{Cov}(K) / \operatorname{vol}(K)^2\right)^{1/(2n)}$.

articles.title: The uniform law on a convex body spans the whole space
articles.statement:
For a full-dimensional convex
body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (a convex body with nonempty interior, $n > 0$), the affine span
of the support of the uniform probability law on $K$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Uniform distribution on a convex body
articles.statement:
For a full-dimensional convex body $K$ in
$\mathbb{R}^n$, the uniform law on $K$ is the probability measure obtained by restricting
Lebesgue measure to $K$ and dividing by the volume of $K$; it gives a set $A$ the mass
$\operatorname{vol}(A \cap K) / \operatorname{vol}(K)$.

articles.title: The entropy and volume isotropic constants of a convex body agree
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body of Lebesgue measure
$\mathrm{Vol}(K)$, with uniform probability measure $\lambda_K$, uniform density $f_K$, and
covariance matrix $C_K$ of the coordinates under $\lambda_K$. Then the entropy isotropic constant
of the uniform law of $K$ equals the isotropic constant of $K$, that is,
$\exp\big(\frac{1}{n} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_K(x) \log f_K(x) \, dx\big) (\det C_K)^{1/(2n)} =
\big(\det C_K / \mathrm{Vol}(K)^2\big)^{1/(2n)}$.

articles.title: Uniform law of a convex body
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a
full-dimensional convex body of Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$. The uniform law of $K$ is the
log-concave law on $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose probability measure is Lebesgue measure restricted to $K$
and divided by $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$, and whose density is the uniform density of $K$.

articles.title: Supremum of isotropic constants of convex bodies
articles.statement:
This is the value
$\sup_{n \ge 1} \sup_K L_K \in [0, \infty]$, where for each dimension $n \ge 1$ the inner
supremum runs over all full-dimensional convex bodies $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $L_K$ is the
isotropic constant of $K$.

## Sources

- `constants/20b.md`, the sharp-value body constant.

articles.title: Supremum of isotropic constants of symmetric convex bodies
articles.statement:
This is the value
$\sup_{n \ge 1} \sup_K L_K \in [0, \infty]$, where for each dimension $n \ge 1$ the inner
supremum runs over the full-dimensional convex bodies $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are centrally
symmetric, that is $K = -K$, and $L_K$ is the isotropic constant of $K$.

articles.title: Conditioning on a set is the normalized indicator density
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a
measurable space $\alpha$ and let $K \subseteq \alpha$ be a measurable set with $\mu(K) \neq 0$.
Then the conditional measure $\mu(\cdot \mid K)$, that is $\mu(K)^{-1}$ times the restriction of
$\mu$ to $K$, equals the measure with density $x \mapsto \mu(K)^{-1} \mathbf{1}_K(x)$ with respect
to $\mu$. Here $\mu(K)^{-1}$ is taken in $[0, \infty]$, so it is $0$ when $\mu(K) = \infty$.

## Sources

- `constants/20b.md`, normalized Lebesgue law on a convex body.

articles.title: Isotropic log-concave laws have identity covariance
articles.statement:
If $\mu$ is an isotropic log-concave
probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, then the covariance matrix of $\mu$ is the $n \times n$
identity matrix.

articles.title: Covariance matrices of log-concave laws are positive semidefinite
articles.statement:
For every log-concave
law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the covariance matrix of $\mu$ is positive semidefinite.

The proof writes the quadratic form of the covariance matrix as the integral of the square of a
centered linear form.

articles.title: Covariance matrix
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the covariance matrix of $\mu$ is
the $n \times n$ real matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is
$\int (x_i - m_i)(x_j - m_j) \, d\mu(x)$, where $m_i = \int x_i \, d\mu(x)$ is the mean of the
$i$-th coordinate.

## Sources

- `constants/20b.md`, covariance definition.

articles.title: Differential entropy
articles.statement:
For a function $f \colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, usually the
Lebesgue density of a probability law, the differential entropy of $f$ is
$-\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x) \log f(x) \, dx$, with the natural logarithm and $0 \log 0 = 0$.

## Sources

- `constants/20b.md`, Ent(μ)=-∫f log f.

articles.title: Body isotropic constants are bounded by the law supremum
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
the supremum of the isotropic constants of full-dimensional convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is at
most the supremum of the entropy isotropic constants of probability laws on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a
log-concave Lebesgue density $f$ such that every coordinate $x_i$ and every product $x_i x_j$ is
integrable under the law and $f \log f$ is Lebesgue integrable, both suprema taken in
$[0, \infty]$. Both families are defined only for $n \ge 1$, so for $n = 0$ they are empty and
both suprema are $0$.

articles.title: Supremum of isotropic constants in a fixed dimension
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, this is
$\sup_K L_K \in [0, \infty]$, the supremum of the isotropic constants $L_K$ over all
full-dimensional convex bodies $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Full-dimensional convex bodies are taken
only in dimension $n \ge 1$, so for $n = 0$ the supremum is over the empty family and is $0$.

articles.title: Supremum of intrinsic isotropic constants in a fixed ambient dimension
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $N$, this is the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the isotropic constants $L_\mu$ over all
intrinsic log-concave laws $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^N$.

The family includes laws whose support spans a proper affine subspace of positive dimension.

articles.title: Supremum of entropic isotropic constants in a fixed dimension
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, this
is $\sup_\mu L_\mu \in [0, \infty]$, the supremum of the isotropic constants
$L_\mu = e^{-\operatorname{Ent}(f)/n} (\det \operatorname{Cov}(\mu))^{1/(2n)}$ over all
log-concave laws $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $f$ is the log-concave Lebesgue density of $\mu$,
$\operatorname{Ent}(f)$ its differential entropy and $\operatorname{Cov}(\mu)$ its covariance
matrix. Here a log-concave law is a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \ge 1$, with
finite second moments and with $f \log f$ integrable, so for $n = 0$ the supremum is over the
empty family and is $0$.

articles.title: The entropy isotropic constant is at most the full-dimensional supremum
articles.statement:
The entropy
isotropic constant, the supremum of the isotropic constants of intrinsic log-concave laws over
all ambient dimensions $N > 0$, is at most the supremum in $[0, \infty]$, over all dimensions
$n > 0$ and all log-concave laws $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, of the entropy isotropic constant
$L_\nu = e^{-h(f)/n} \det(\operatorname{Cov} \nu)^{1/(2n)}$, where $f$ is the density of $\nu$
and $h(f) = -\int f \log f$.

Each intrinsic law contributes the isotropic constant of its coordinate law, which is a
full-dimensional log-concave law.

articles.title: Entropy-convention isotropic constant
articles.statement:
This is the supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, over all
dimensions $N > 0$ of the supremum of the isotropic constants $L_\mu$ over all intrinsic
log-concave laws $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^N$. A law supported on a proper affine subspace thus
contributes the isotropic constant computed in orthonormal coordinates on its affine span.

## Sources

- C20b, with the entropy convention and actual intrinsic-span laws.

articles.title: Full-dimensional convex body
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a full-dimensional convex body in
dimension $n$ is a nonempty compact convex set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose
interior is nonempty, where $n$ is required to be positive.

## Sources

- `constants/20b.md`, convex-body domain.

articles.title: Supremum of the isotropic constant over full-dimensional log-concave laws
articles.statement:
This is the
supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, of the isotropic constant
$L_\mu = e^{-h(f)/n} (\det \mathrm{Cov}(\mu))^{1/(2n)}$ over all positive integers $n$ and all
log-concave laws $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Lebesgue density $f$, where
$h(f) = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f \log f$ is the differential entropy of $f$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(\mu)$
is the covariance matrix of the coordinates under $\mu$.

Each such law has a density on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$, so laws supported on a proper affine
subspace are not included here.

articles.title: Symmetric interval as a convex body
articles.statement:
For a real number $a > 0$, this is the closed
interval $[-a, a]$ in the one-dimensional Euclidean space, regarded as a full-dimensional convex
body.

articles.title: Isotropic constant of an intrinsic log-concave law
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be an intrinsic log-concave
law on $\mathbb{R}^N$, given by a log-concave law $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with density $f$ and an
affine isometric embedding of $\mathbb{R}^d$ onto the affine span of the support of $\mu$. The
isotropic constant of $\mu$ is the entropy isotropic constant of $\nu$,

$$L_\mu = e^{-h(f)/d} \, \det(\operatorname{Cov} \nu)^{1/(2d)},$$

where $h(f) = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \log f$ is the differential entropy of $f$ and
$\operatorname{Cov} \nu$ is the covariance matrix of the coordinates under $\nu$.

Entropy and covariance are thus computed relative to the intrinsic affine span.

articles.title: Log-concave law in intrinsic coordinates
articles.statement:
Fix an ambient dimension $N$. An intrinsic
log-concave law on $\mathbb{R}^N$ consists of a dimension $d$, a log-concave law $\nu$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$ (that is, $d > 0$ and $\nu$ is a probability measure with a log-concave Lebesgue
density $f$, integrable coordinates and coordinate products, and integrable $f \log f$), an
affine isometric embedding $\varphi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^N$ of Euclidean spaces, and a
measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^N$, such that $\mu$ is the pushforward $\varphi_* \nu$ and the image
of $\varphi$ equals the affine span of the support of $\mu$.

The pushforward identity ties the ambient law $\mu$ to the density and entropy of $\nu$, which
are computed in the intrinsic coordinates.

articles.title: Cube lower bound for the supremal isotropic constant
articles.statement:
The supremum, over all positive
integers $n$ and all full-dimensional convex bodies $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, of the isotropic
constant $L_K = \left(\det \mathrm{Cov}(K) / \mathrm{Vol}(K)^2\right)^{1/(2n)}$, where
$\mathrm{Cov}(K)$ is the covariance matrix of the uniform distribution on $K$, is at least
$1/\sqrt{12}$.

The interval $[-1/2, 1/2]$ in dimension one already attains $L_K = 1/\sqrt{12}$.

articles.title: Centrally symmetric convex body
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a full-dimensional convex
body $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is centrally symmetric when $K = -K$, that is, for every
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \in K$ if and only if $-x \in K$.

## Sources

- arXiv:2412.15044v1, Introduction after Theorem 1.2.

articles.title: Constant densities on convex sets are log-concave
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a
measurable convex set and let $c > 0$. Then the function equal to $c$ on $K$ and to $0$ outside
$K$ is a log-concave density.

## Sources

- the uniform convex-body example in `constants/20b.md`.

articles.title: Isotropic constant of a log-concave law
articles.statement:
For a log-concave law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with
Lebesgue density $f$, the isotropic constant of $\mu$ is
$L_\mu = e^{-h(f)/n} (\det \mathrm{Cov}(\mu))^{1/(2n)}$, where
$h(f) = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f \log f$ is the differential entropy of $f$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(\mu)$
is the covariance matrix of the coordinates under $\mu$.

articles.title: Identification of the line with one-dimensional Euclidean space
articles.statement:
The linear isometric
isomorphism from $\mathbb{R}$ onto one-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^1$ that sends a
real number $x$ to the vector whose only coordinate is $x$.

articles.title: Log-concave law
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$, a log-concave law on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a
probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ together with a Lebesgue density $f$ of $\mu$ that is
log-concave: $f$ is measurable and nonnegative, and $f((1-t)x + ty) \ge f(x)^{1-t} f(y)^t$ for all
$x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0 < t < 1$. Moreover every coordinate $x_i$ and every product
$x_i x_j$ is $\mu$-integrable, and $f \log f$ is Lebesgue integrable.

## Sources

- `constants/20b.md`; finite moments and entropy integrability ensure the displayed real integrals do not use the non-integrable default value.

articles.title: Squared-radius thin-shell width
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the squared-radius thin-shell
width in dimension $n$ is the supremum, in $[0, \infty]$, of
$\left(\int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x) / n\right)^{1/2}$ (with $0/0 = 0$) over all isotropic
log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, those with a log-concave
Lebesgue density, mean zero and identity covariance.

It measures the fluctuation of the squared radius $|x|^2$, not of the radius $|x|$.

articles.title: Symmetric interval in one-dimensional Euclidean space
articles.statement:
For a real number $a$, the set of
points of one-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^1$ whose only coordinate lies in the closed
interval $[-a, a]$. It is empty when $a < 0$.

articles.title: The uniform law on (−1, 1) is not isotropic log-concave
articles.statement:
The uniform distribution on the
symmetric interval $[-1, 1]$ of one-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^1$ is not an isotropic
log-concave probability measure.

Its second moment is $1/3$ rather than $1$.

articles.title: Radius fluctuation of the uniform law on (−√3, √3)
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be the uniform distribution
on the symmetric interval $[-\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}]$ of one-dimensional Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^1$. Then $\int (\|x\| - \sqrt{1})^2 \, d\mu(x)$, the mean squared deviation of the
Euclidean norm from $\sqrt{1} = 1$, is at most the thin-shell variance constant.

articles.title: The uniform law on (−√3, √3) is isotropic log-concave
articles.statement:
The uniform distribution on the
symmetric interval $[-\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}]$ of one-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^1$ is
an isotropic log-concave probability measure: it has a log-concave density with respect to
Lebesgue measure, mean zero and identity covariance.

## Sources

- the one-dimensional isotropic cube, uniform on [-√3, √3].

articles.title: Thin-shell variance bound for the uniform law on (−√3, √3)
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be the uniform
distribution on the symmetric interval $[-\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}]$ of one-dimensional Euclidean
space $\mathbb{R}^1$. Its normalized radius variance $\int (\|x\|^2 - 1)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ is at most
the thin-shell variance constant, the supremum of the normalized radius variance over all
isotropic log-concave probability measures in all positive dimensions.

articles.title: Uniform distribution on a symmetric interval
articles.statement:
For a real number $a$, the measure on
one-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^1$ obtained by conditioning Lebesgue measure on the
set $\{x : -a \le x_1 \le a\}$ of points whose only coordinate $x_1$ lies in $[-a, a]$, that is,
Lebesgue measure restricted to this set and divided by its measure. For $a > 0$ this is the
uniform probability distribution with density $1/(2a)$ on the interval; for $a \le 0$ the set has
measure zero and the conditioned measure is the zero measure.

It is conditioned Lebesgue measure, not a discrete uniform measure.

articles.title: Membership in the unit interval body
articles.statement:
A point $x$ of the one-dimensional Euclidean space
lies in the unit interval body if and only if its single coordinate $x_1$ satisfies
$-1/2 \le x_1 \le 1/2$.

articles.title: Unit interval body
articles.statement:
The unit interval body is the closed interval $[-1/2, 1/2]$, of length
one and centred at the origin, in the one-dimensional Euclidean space, regarded as a
full-dimensional convex body.

articles.title: Johnstone's Tracy–Widom limit
articles.statement:
Let `q` be the Hastings–McLeod solution of Painlevé II
(`q'' = s q + 2 q³` with `q(s) · 2 √π s^{1/4} e^{(2/3) s^{3/2}} → 1` as `s → ∞`). Let
`n k, p k → ∞` with `n k / p k → γ ≥ 1`, and let `X` have independent standard Gaussian entries
(`Measure.pi` of `gaussianReal 0 1` over `Fin (n k) × Fin (p k)`). The largest eigenvalue of
`Xᵀ X` is `ℓ₁ = sup_{‖v‖ = 1} ‖X v‖²`. Then for every `s`, the function
`x ↦ q x + (x - s) q x ²` is integrable on `(s, ∞)` and
`P((ℓ₁ - μ_k) / σ_k ≤ s) → F₁(s) = exp (-(1/2) ∫ₛ^∞ (q x + (x - s) q x ²) dx)` with Johnstone's
`μ_k = (√(n - 1) + √p)²` and `σ_k = (√(n - 1) + √p) (1/√(n - 1) + 1/√p)^{1/3}`.

## Sources

- I. M. Johnstone, Ann. Statist. 29 (2001), 295–327, Theorem 1.1; Tracy–Widom (1996) for `F₁`; Hastings–McLeod (1980) for `q`.

articles.title: Lower Poincaré–Cheeger comparison with coefficient 1/π
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\mu$ be an
isotropic log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with inverse Cheeger constant
$\psi(\mu) \in [0, \infty]$ and smooth Poincaré constant $C_P(\mu) \in [0, \infty]$. Then
$\frac{1}{\pi} \psi(\mu)^2 \le C_P(\mu)$.

## Sources

- optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, Poincare comparison display. Klartag arXiv:2303.14938v1 states the weaker lower coefficient `1/9`, not `1/pi`.

articles.title: The Cheeger coefficient is at most the half-space Cheeger coefficient
articles.statement:
For every measure
$\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric, the Cheeger coefficient of $\mu$ is at most
its half-space Cheeger coefficient.

articles.title: Cheeger coefficient of the zero measure
articles.statement:
On every pseudometric space $E$ equipped with a
σ-algebra, the zero measure has Cheeger coefficient $\infty$.

No set has measure strictly between $0$ and $1$ under the zero measure, so the infimum is taken
over the empty family.

articles.title: Cheeger coefficient
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on a pseudometric space $E$ equipped with a
σ-algebra, the Cheeger coefficient of $\mu$ is the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of
$\mu^+(A) / \min(\mu(A), 1 - \mu(A))$ over all measurable sets $A \subseteq E$ with
$0 < \mu(A) < 1$, where
$\mu^+(A) = \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} (\mu(A_\varepsilon) - \mu(A)) / \varepsilon$ is the
outer Minkowski boundary measure of $A$ and $A_\varepsilon$ is the closed
$\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $A$. The infimum of the empty family is $\infty$; the measure
$\mu$ is not required to be a probability measure.

articles.title: Chen's subpolynomial bound on the KLS constant, weaker form
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and
an integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every $n \ge N$ the dimensional KLS constant
$\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\psi_n \le \exp\bigl(C \sqrt{\log n} \, \log \log n\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Chen, GAFA 31 (2021), 34--61; optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`. Jambulapati--Lee--Vempala v1 quotes the stronger exponent `sqrt(log n * log(log n))`.

articles.title: Dimensional KLS constants are bounded by the KLS constant
articles.statement:
For every positive integer
$n$, the dimensional KLS constant in dimension $n$ is at most the KLS constant.

articles.title: Dimensional KLS constant
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the dimensional KLS constant in
dimension $n$ is the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the inverse Cheeger constants of all isotropic
log-concave probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric.

articles.title: Half-space Cheeger coefficient
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean
metric, the half-space Cheeger coefficient of $\mu$ is the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of
$\mu^+(H) / \min(\mu(H), 1 - \mu(H))$ over all closed half-spaces
$H = \{x : \langle v, x \rangle \le a\}$ with $v \ne 0$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$0 < \mu(H) < 1$, where $\mu^+(H)$ is the outer Minkowski boundary measure of $H$. The infimum
of the empty family is $\infty$.

articles.title: Inverse Cheeger constant bounded by the KLS constant
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$ and
every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean
metric, the inverse Cheeger constant of $\mu$ is at most the KLS constant.

articles.title: Inverse Cheeger constant bounded by the dimensional KLS constant
articles.statement:
For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$
with the Euclidean metric, the inverse Cheeger constant of $\mu$ is at most the dimensional KLS
constant in dimension $n$.

articles.title: Inverse Cheeger constant of the zero measure
articles.statement:
On every pseudometric space $E$ equipped
with a σ-algebra, the zero measure has inverse Cheeger constant $0$.

articles.title: Inverse Cheeger constant
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on a pseudometric space $E$ equipped with a
σ-algebra, the inverse Cheeger constant of $\mu$ is $1 / h(\mu) \in [0, \infty]$, where $h(\mu)$
is the Cheeger coefficient of $\mu$, with the conventions $1 / 0 = \infty$ and
$1 / \infty = 0$.

articles.title: Inverse half-space Cheeger constant
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the inverse
half-space Cheeger constant of $\mu$ is $h^{-1}$, where $h \in [0, \infty]$ is the half-space
Cheeger coefficient of $\mu$ and the inverse is taken in $[0, \infty]$, so that
$0^{-1} = \infty$ and $\infty^{-1} = 0$.

articles.title: Half-spaces
articles.statement:
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a half-space if there are a nonzero
vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and a real number $a$ such that
$A = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle v, x \rangle \le a\}$.

articles.title: Smooth Poincaré bounds
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let
$C \in [0, \infty]$. For a differentiable $g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ write
$\|\nabla g(x)\|$ for the Euclidean norm of the gradient of $g$ at $x$ (equivalently, the
operator norm of the derivative of $g$ at $x$). Then $C$ is a smooth Poincaré bound for $\mu$
if for every infinitely differentiable function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
$f$, $f^2$ and $\|\nabla f\|^2$ are $\mu$-integrable,

$$\int \Big(f(x) - \int f \, d\mu\Big)^2 \, d\mu(x) \le C \int \|\nabla f(x)\|^2 \, d\mu(x),$$

where the outer integral on the left and the integral on the right are computed in
$[0, \infty]$ with $0 \cdot \infty = 0$, and the inner integral $\int f \, d\mu$ is the usual
real integral. The measure $\mu$ need not be a probability measure.

articles.title: Jambulapati–Lee–Vempala polylogarithmic bound on the KLS constant
articles.statement:
Let
$\alpha = 1 + \bigl(1 + 7\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{53 - 4\sqrt{2}}\bigr)/8$. There are a real $C > 0$ and an
integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every $n \ge N$ the dimensional KLS constant
$\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\psi_n \le C (\log n)^{\alpha}$.

The exponent is kept in exact algebraic form rather than as a rounded decimal.

## Sources

- arXiv:2208.11644v1, Theorem 22 and the preceding KLS/thin-shell comparison.

articles.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits bound on the KLS constant
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and an
integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every $n \ge N$ the dimensional KLS constant
$\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\psi_n \le C \sqrt{n}$.

## Sources

- Kannan, Lovasz and Simonovits, DCG 13 (1995), 541--560; optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, KLS1995 row.

articles.title: Klartag's square-root-logarithmic bound on the KLS constant
articles.statement:
There is a real $C > 0$ such
that for every integer $n \ge 2$ the dimensional KLS constant $\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies
$\psi_n \le C \sqrt{\log n}$.

## Sources

- Klartag, arXiv:2303.14938v1, Theorem 1.2.

articles.title: Lower Poincaré–Cheeger comparison with coefficient 1/9
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\mu$ be an
isotropic log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with inverse Cheeger constant
$\psi(\mu) \in [0, \infty]$ and smooth Poincaré constant $C_P(\mu) \in [0, \infty]$. Then
$\frac{1}{9} \psi(\mu)^2 \le C_P(\mu)$.

## Sources

- Klartag, arXiv:2303.14938v1, equation comparing `psi` and `C_P`. The locally Lipschitz-to-smooth approximation remains part of the requested proof.

articles.title: Klartag–Lehec polylogarithmic bound on the KLS constant
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and an
integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every $n \ge N$ the dimensional KLS constant
$\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\psi_n \le C (\log n)^5$.

## Sources

- Klartag and Lehec, GAFA 32 (2022), 1134--1159; optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, KL2022 row.

articles.title: Bounding the KLS constant measure by measure
articles.statement:
For every $C \in [0, \infty]$, the KLS
constant is at most $C$ if and only if, for every positive integer $n$ and every isotropic
log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the inverse Cheeger constant of $\mu$ is
at most $C$.

articles.title: Bounding the KLS constant dimension by dimension
articles.statement:
For every $C \in [0, \infty]$, the KLS
constant is at most $C$ if and only if, for every positive integer $n$, the dimensional KLS
constant in dimension $n$ is at most $C$.

articles.title: Finiteness of the KLS constant
articles.statement:
The KLS constant is finite if and only if there is a real
number $C$ such that, for every positive integer $n$ and every isotropic log-concave probability
measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the inverse Cheeger constant of $\mu$ is at most $\max(C, 0)$.

The right-hand side is the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture.

articles.title: KLS constant
articles.statement:
The KLS constant is the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the dimensional KLS
constants in dimension $n$, taken over all positive integers $n$.

articles.title: Dimensional KLS constant versus thin-shell variance, up to a squared logarithm
articles.statement:
Let
$\Sigma \in [0, \infty]$ be the thin-shell variance constant: the supremum, over all dimensions
$m \ge 1$ and all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^m$, of
$\frac{1}{m} \int (\lVert x \rVert^2 - m)^2 \, d\mu(x)$. There is a real $C > 0$ such that for
every integer $n \ge 3$ the dimensional KLS constant $\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies
$\psi_n^2 \le C (\log n)^2 \, \Sigma$.

## Sources

- Jambulapati--Lee--Vempala, arXiv:2208.11644v1, KLS/thin-shell comparison.

articles.title: Lee–Vempala bound on the KLS constant
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$
such that for every $n \ge N$ the dimensional KLS constant $\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies
$\psi_n \le C n^{1/4}$.

## Sources

- Lee and Vempala, Ann. of Math. 199 (2024), 1--104; optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, LV2024 row.

articles.title: Lehec's reported polylogarithmic bound on the KLS constant, weakened
articles.statement:
There are a real
$C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every $n \ge N$ the dimensional KLS constant
$\psi_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\psi_n \le C (\log n)^{3.083}$.

The exponent $3.083$ lies just above Lehec's reported exponent $3.082\ldots$, which the primary
gives only to this decimal precision; $3.083$ is not claimed to be the exact exponent.

## Sources

- Klartag, arXiv:2303.14938v1, Introduction, personal-communication paragraph.

articles.title: Smooth Poincaré bounds are upward closed
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let
$C \le D$ in $[0, \infty]$. If $C$ is a smooth Poincaré bound for $\mu$, then so is $D$.

articles.title: The empty set has zero outer Minkowski boundary
articles.statement:
For every measure $\mu$ on a
pseudometric space $E$, the outer Minkowski boundary measure of the empty set with respect to
$\mu$ is $0$.

articles.title: Outer Minkowski boundary measure
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a pseudometric space $E$ and
let $A \subseteq E$. For $\varepsilon > 0$ let
$A_\varepsilon = \{x \in E : \inf_{a \in A} d(x, a) \le \varepsilon\}$ be the closed
$\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $A$, with $\inf \emptyset = \infty$. The outer Minkowski boundary
measure of $A$ with respect to $\mu$ is

$$\mu^+(A) = \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{\mu(A_\varepsilon) - \mu(A)}{\varepsilon},$$

where the difference and the quotient are computed in $[0, \infty]$, with $\infty - \infty = 0$.

articles.title: Cheeger's inequality for isotropic log-concave measures
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $\mu$ be an
isotropic log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $\psi_\mu \in [0, \infty]$ be
the inverse Cheeger constant of $\mu$. Then the smooth Poincaré constant of $\mu$ is at most
$4 \psi_\mu^2$.

## Sources

- optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, comparison display, and Klartag, arXiv:2303.14938v1, Introduction.

articles.title: The smooth Poincaré constant is at most every smooth Poincaré bound
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $C \in [0, \infty]$. If $C$ is a smooth Poincaré bound for
$\mu$, then the smooth Poincaré constant of $\mu$ is at most $C$.

articles.title: Smooth Poincaré constant
articles.statement:
The smooth Poincaré constant of a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$
is the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of all $C \in [0, \infty]$ that are smooth Poincaré bounds for
$\mu$; it is $\infty$ when $\mu$ has no smooth Poincaré bound.

articles.title: A lower bound for the KLS constant
articles.statement:
The KLS constant is at least $\sqrt{\pi/2}$.

The bound comes from the standard Gaussian measure in any dimension $n \ge 1$, whose inverse Cheeger
constant is $\sqrt{\pi/2}$.

## Sources

- optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, classical Gaussian lower-bound row.

articles.title: Inverse Cheeger constant of the standard Gaussian
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$, the standard
Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ has inverse Cheeger constant exactly $\sqrt{\pi/2}$.

## Sources

- optimizationproblems `constants/20c.md`, classical Gaussian row; the Gaussian isoperimetric theorem supplies the minimizing half-space claim.

articles.title: Singularity probability of Bernoulli matrices
articles.statement:
Let $0 < p \le 1/2$. For each $n$, let $B_n$ be
a random $n \times n$ real matrix on a probability space $(\Omega_n, P_n)$ whose $n^2$ entries are
mutually independent and each equal to $1$ with probability $p$ and to $0$ with probability $1 - p$.
Then there is a function $o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $o(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ such
that $P_n(\det B_n = 0) = (1 - p + o(n))^n$ for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- K. Tikhomirov, `Singularity of random Bernoulli matrices`, Annals of Math, 191 (2) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_random_bernoulli_matrices` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Singularity probability of Rademacher matrices
articles.statement:
For each $n$, let $M_n$ be a random
$n \times n$ real matrix on a probability space $(\Omega_n, P_n)$ whose $n^2$ entries are mutually
independent and each have the Rademacher law, with mass $1/2$ at each of $1$ and $-1$. Then there
is a function $o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $o(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ such that
$P_n(\det M_n = 0) = (1/2 + o(n))^n$ for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- K. Tikhomirov, `Singularity of random Bernoulli matrices`, Annals of Math, 191 (2) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_random_bernoulli_matrices` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Smallest singular value of a matrix
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and
let $M$ be a matrix over $\mathbb{K}$ whose rows and columns are indexed by finite sets $n$ and $m$.
Its smallest singular value is the real number
$\sigma_{\min}(M) = \inf_{x \in \mathbb{K}^m,\ \lVert x \rVert_2 = 1} \lVert Mx \rVert_2$, where
$\lVert \cdot \rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm. When $m$ is empty there are no unit vectors, and
$\sigma_{\min}(M) = 0$.

articles.title: Rademacher measure on the real line
articles.statement:
The Rademacher measure is the probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ that assigns mass $1/2$ to $1$ and mass $1/2$ to $-1$.

articles.title: Tikhomirov's Theorem A: smallest singular value of shifted Bernoulli matrices
articles.statement:
Let
$0 < p \le 1/2$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, and write $\sigma_{\min}(A)$ for the smallest singular value
of a real square matrix $A$. There exist a natural number $N > 0$ and a real number $C > 0$ such
that for every $n \ge N$ the following holds. Let $B$ be a random $n \times n$ real matrix on a
probability space $(\Omega, P)$ whose $n^2$ entries are mutually independent and each equal to $1$
with probability $p$ and to $0$ with probability $1 - p$, and let $J$ be the $n \times n$ matrix
all of whose entries are $1$. Then for every $s \in [-1, 0]$ and every real $t > 0$,

$$P\bigl(\sigma_{\min}(B + sJ) \le t / \sqrt{n}\bigr) \le (1 - p + \varepsilon)^n + C t.$$

## Sources

- K. Tikhomirov, `Singularity of random Bernoulli matrices`, Annals of Math, 191 (2) 2020. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_random_bernoulli_matrices` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Binomial random subset
articles.statement:
For a type $X$ and $p \in [0, 1]$, the binomial random subset
distribution on $X$ with parameter $p$ is the probability measure on the subsets of $X$ under
which each element of $X$ belongs to the random subset independently with probability $p$. A
random subset with this law is denoted $X_p$.

articles.title: $p$-small families of sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite type and $p \in [0, 1]$. A family
$\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $X$ is $p$-small when there is a family $\mathcal{G}$ of subsets of
$X$ such that every member of $\mathcal{F}$ contains some member of $\mathcal{G}$ and
$\sum_{S \in \mathcal{G}} p^{|S|} \le 1/2$.

articles.title: Park–Pham theorem on selector processes (Talagrand's selector process conjecture)
articles.statement:
There is
a real number $L > 0$ with the following property. Let $0 < p < 1$, let $X$ be a finite type,
let $\Lambda$ be a set of functions from $X$ to $[0, \infty)$, and let $X_p$ be a binomial random
subset of $X$ with parameter $p$. Write
$E = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\sup_{f \in \Lambda} \sum_{i \in X_p} f(i)\bigr]$, computed in
$[0, \infty]$. If $0 < E < \infty$, then the family of subsets $s \subseteq X$ with
$\sup_{f \in \Lambda} \sum_{i \in s} f(i) \ge L E$ is $p$-small.

The hypothesis $0 < E < \infty$ is not stated explicitly in the paper's theorem, but it is used
in the last step of the proof, which derives a contradiction from an inequality $E \ge c E$
with a constant $c > 1$.

## Sources

- J. Park and H. T. Pham, `On a conjecture of Talagrand on selector processes and a consequence on positive empirical processes`, Annals of Math, 199 (3) 2024. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_supremum_of_selector_processes` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Park–Pham theorem on positive empirical processes
articles.statement:
There is a real number $L > 0$ with the
following property. Let $N > 0$, let $\mathbb{T}$ be a Polish space with its Borel
$\sigma$-algebra and a probability measure $\nu$, and let $Y_1, \dots, Y_N$ be independent random
variables on a measure space $(\Omega, P)$ with values in $\mathbb{T}$, each with law $\nu$. For
$f : \mathbb{T} \to [0, \infty)$ let $Z_f = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(Y_i)$. Let
$\mathcal{F}$ be a finite set of measurable functions from $\mathbb{T}$ to $[0, \infty)$ that are
essentially bounded with respect to $\nu$, and write
$E = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} Z_f\bigr]$, computed in $[0, \infty]$. If
$0 < E < \infty$, then there is a finite collection $\mathcal{C}$ of pairs $(g, t)$, where
$g : \mathbb{T} \to [0, \infty)$ is measurable and $t > 0$ is real, such that every $\omega$
with $\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} Z_f(\omega) \ge L E$ satisfies $Z_g(\omega) \ge t$ for some
$(g, t) \in \mathcal{C}$, and $\sum_{(g, t) \in \mathcal{C}} P(Z_g \ge t) \le 1/2$.

The paper does not state explicitly that $\mathcal{C}$ is finite. It must at least be countable
for the sum to make sense, and the collections produced by the proof are finite.

## Sources

- J. Park and H. T. Pham, `On a conjecture of Talagrand on selector processes and a consequence on positive empirical processes`, Annals of Math, 199 (3) 2024. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_supremum_of_selector_processes` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Empirical averages
articles.statement:
Given random variables $Y_1, \dots, Y_N$ on $\Omega$ with values in
$\mathbb{T}$ and a function $f : \mathbb{T} \to [0, \infty)$, $Z_N(f)$ is the random variable
$Z_N(f)(\omega) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(Y_i(\omega))$, which is $0$ when $N = 0$.

When $Y_1, \dots, Y_N$ are i.i.d., $Z_N(f)$ is called an empirical process.

articles.title: Chen's thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number
$N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width
$\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies
