$\sigma_n \le \exp\big((\log n)^{1/2 + \varepsilon}\big)$.

There is no constant multiplier inside the exponential.

## Sources

- Chen, GAFA 31 (2021), 34--61; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Fleury's thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such
that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of
dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{3/8}$.

## Sources

- Fleury, J. Funct. Anal. 259 (2010), 832--841; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Cube lower bound for the thin-shell variance constant
articles.statement:
The thin-shell variance constant,
an element of $[0, \infty]$, is at least $4/5$.

The value $4/5$ is the exact normalized radius variance of the uniform law on a cube scaled to
identity covariance.

## Sources

- Klartag and Lehec, arXiv:2507.15495v1, Introduction.

articles.title: Guan's thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$ such
that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of
dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C \log \log n$.

## Sources

- Guan, arXiv:2412.09075; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Guédon–Milman thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number $N \ge 3$
such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of
dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{1/3}$.

## Sources

- Guedon and Milman, GAFA 21 (2011), 1043--1068; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Isotropic log-concave probability measures
articles.statement:
A measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is
isotropic log-concave when it is a probability measure, it has density $f$ with respect to
Lebesgue measure for some log-concave density $f$, and for all coordinates $i, j$ the
functions $x \mapsto x_i$ and $x \mapsto x_i x_j$ are $\mu$-integrable with
$\int x_i \, d\mu(x) = 0$ and $\int x_i x_j \, d\mu(x) = \delta_{ij}$, that is, $1$ if $i = j$
and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Log-concave densities
articles.statement:
A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a log-concave
density when it is measurable, $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x$, and
$f(x)^{1-t} f(y)^t \le f((1-t)x + ty)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and every real $t$
with $0 < t < 1$.

No integrability or normalization of $f$ is required.

articles.title: Jambulapati–Lee–Vempala thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
Let
$\alpha = \big(1 + 7\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{53 - 4\sqrt{2}}\big)/8$. There are a real $C > 0$ and a
natural number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width
$\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C (\log n)^{\alpha}$.

The exponent $\alpha$ is algebraic, not rational; the paper bounds it by $2.2226$. The paper
proves this bound for the square root of the normalized variance of the squared radius, which
bounds the thin-shell width from above.

## Sources

- Jambulapati, Lee and Vempala, arXiv:2208.11644v1, Theorem 22.

articles.title: Klartag's first thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural number
$N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width
$\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C \sqrt{n / \log n}$.

This is Klartag's first bound in the weaker form tabulated by the optimization catalogue.

## Sources

- Klartag, Invent. Math. 168 (2007), 91--131; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Klartag's power-law thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant
$C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every dimension $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width
$\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C n^{2/5 + \varepsilon}$. Here $\sigma_n$ is
the square root of the supremum of $\mathbb{E}\,(|X| - \sqrt{n})^2$ over isotropic log-concave
random vectors $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Sources

- Klartag, J. Funct. Anal. 245 (2007), 284--310; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Klartag's square-root-logarithmic thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a constant $C > 0$ and an
integer $N \ge 3$ such that for every dimension $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width
$\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C \sqrt{\log n}$. Here $\sigma_n$ is the square
root of the supremum of $\mathbb{E}\,(|X| - \sqrt{n})^2$ over isotropic log-concave random
vectors $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Sources

- Klartag, Ars Inveniendi Analytica (2023), Paper 4; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Klartag–Lehec polylogarithmic thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a real $C > 0$ and a natural
number $N \ge 3$ such that for every natural number $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width
$\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$ satisfies $\sigma_n \le C (\log n)^4$.

## Sources

- Klartag and Lehec, GAFA 32 (2022), 1134--1159; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: Klartag–Lehec thin-shell variance bound
articles.statement:
There is a real $C > 0$ such that for every
natural number $n \ge 1$ and every isotropic log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the
normalized radius variance $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ is at most $C$.

## Sources

- arXiv:2507.15495v1, Theorem 1.1. The constant is not optimized or made explicit.

articles.title: Klartag–Lehec bounded thin-shell width
articles.statement:
There is a real $C > 0$ such that for every
natural number $n \ge 1$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ of dimension $n$
satisfies $\sigma_n \le C$.

## Sources

- Klartag and Lehec, arXiv:2507.15495v1, Introduction and Theorem 1.1.

articles.title: Lee–Vempala thin-shell bound
articles.statement:
There are a constant $C > 0$ and an integer $N \ge 3$
such that for every dimension $n \ge N$ the thin-shell width $\sigma_n \in [0, \infty]$ satisfies
$\sigma_n \le C n^{1/4}$. Here $\sigma_n$ is the square root of the supremum of
$\mathbb{E}\,(|X| - \sqrt{n})^2$ over isotropic log-concave random vectors $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Sources

- Lee and Vempala, FOCS 2017, 998--1007; catalogue `constants/20a.md`.

articles.title: The thin-shell variance constant bounds the normalized radius variance of isotropic log-concave measures
articles.statement:
**The thin-shell variance constant bounds the normalized radius variance of isotropic
log-concave measures.** For every $n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is at most the thin-shell
variance constant.

articles.title: Normalized radius variance
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the normalized radius
variance of $\mu$ is $\frac{1}{n} \int (\|x\|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$, computed in $[0, \infty]$,
where $\|x\|$ is the Euclidean norm (for $n = 0$ the integral is $0$ and so is the value).

When $\mu$ is a probability measure with $\int \|x\|^2 \, d\mu(x) = n$, as for an isotropic
one, this is the variance of $\|x\|^2$ divided by $n$.

articles.title: Elementary radius deviation bound
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $r \ge 0$ and $d > 0$,
$(r - \sqrt{d})^2 \le (r^2 - d)^2 / d$.

articles.title: The thin-shell variance constant bounds the radius fluctuation
articles.statement:
For every $n > 0$ and
every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the integral
$\int (\|x\| - \sqrt{n})^2 \, d\mu(x)$, taken in $[0, \infty]$ with $\|x\|$ the Euclidean
norm, is at most the thin-shell variance constant.

articles.title: Radius fluctuation is bounded by the normalized radius variance
articles.statement:
For every $n > 0$ and
every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the integral $\int (\|x\| - \sqrt{n})^2 \, d\mu(x)$,
taken in $[0, \infty]$ with $\|x\|$ the Euclidean norm, is at most the normalized radius
variance of $\mu$.

The bound holds even when the moments are infinite.

articles.title: The standard Gaussian has normalized radius variance 2
articles.statement:
For every dimension $n \ge 1$,
the standard Gaussian measure $\gamma_n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is isotropic log-concave (a probability
measure with a log-concave Lebesgue density, mean $0$ and identity covariance), and its normalized
radius variance $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\gamma_n(x)$ equals $2$.

## Sources

- Klartag--Lehec, arXiv:2507.15495v1, Introduction.

articles.title: Characterization of bounds on the thin-shell variance constant
articles.statement:
For every
$C \in [0, \infty]$, the thin-shell variance constant is at most $C$ if and only if, for every
$n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the
normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is at most $C$.

articles.title: A uniform variance bound makes the thin-shell variance constant finite
articles.statement:
If $C$ is a real
number such that for every $n > 0$ and every isotropic log-concave probability measure $\mu$
on $\mathbb{R}^n$ the normalized radius variance of $\mu$ is at most $\max(C, 0)$, then the
thin-shell variance constant is finite.

articles.title: The thin-shell variance constant is finite
articles.statement:
The thin-shell variance constant, the
supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the normalized radius variances
$\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all dimensions $n \ge 1$ and all isotropic
log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, is finite.

## Sources

- Klartag and Lehec, arXiv:2507.15495v1, Theorem 1.1.

articles.title: The thin-shell variance constant is nonnegative
articles.statement:
The thin-shell variance constant, a
value in $[0, \infty]$, is at least $0$.

articles.title: Thin-shell variance constant
articles.statement:
Write $|x|$ for the Euclidean norm. The thin-shell
variance constant is the supremum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the normalized radius variance
$\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all dimensions $n \ge 1$ and all isotropic
log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: Thin-shell width is at most the square root of the variance constant
articles.statement:
For every
dimension $n \ge 1$, the thin-shell width in dimension $n$ is at most the square root of the
thin-shell variance constant, computed in $[0, \infty]$ with $\sqrt{\infty} = \infty$.

articles.title: Thin-shell width
articles.statement:
Write $|x|$ for the Euclidean norm. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
thin-shell width in dimension $n$ is the square root of the supremum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of
$\int (|x| - \sqrt{n})^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all isotropic log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on
$\mathbb{R}^n$, with $\sqrt{\infty} = \infty$.

articles.title: The thin-shell variance constant is at least 2
articles.statement:
The thin-shell variance constant, the
supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the normalized radius variances
$\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$ over all dimensions $n \ge 1$ and all isotropic
log-concave probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, is at least $2$.

The lower bound comes from the standard Gaussian, whose normalized radius variance is $2$ in
every dimension.

## Sources

- Klartag and Lehec, arXiv:2507.15495v1, Introduction.

articles.title: The isotropic cube has normalized radius variance 4/5
articles.statement:
For every dimension $n \ge 1$, let
$\mu$ be the uniform probability measure on the cube $[-\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}]^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue measure restricted to the cube and divided by its volume). Then $\mu$ is isotropic
log-concave (a probability measure with a log-concave Lebesgue density, mean $0$ and identity
covariance), and its normalized radius variance $\frac{1}{n} \int (|x|^2 - n)^2 \, d\mu(x)$
equals $4/5$.

The cube is scaled to covariance identity, so this is the unit-variance convention.

## Sources

- Klartag--Lehec, arXiv:2507.15495v1, Introduction.

articles.title: Empirical spectral measure of a Hermitian matrix
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a Hermitian $n \times n$
complex matrix with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$, listed with multiplicity. The
empirical spectral measure of $W$ is the measure $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \delta_{\lambda_j}$
on $\mathbb{R}$, where $\delta_\lambda$ is the Dirac measure at $\lambda$; for $n = 0$ it is the
zero measure.

articles.title: Semicircle distribution
articles.statement:
The semicircle distribution is the measure $\sigma$ on
$\mathbb{R}$ given by $\sigma(A) = \int_{A \cap [-2, 2]} \frac{\sqrt{4 - x^2}}{2\pi} \, dx$ for
every measurable set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.

Since $\int_{-2}^{2} \sqrt{4 - x^2} \, dx = 2\pi$, it is a probability measure.

articles.title: Wigner matrices are Hermitian
articles.statement:
For every family of real functions
$X_{ij} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, on a set $\Omega$, every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
and every $\omega \in \Omega$, the Wigner matrix $W_n(\omega)$ is Hermitian.

The matrix is in fact real symmetric: its entry at $(i, j)$ is the real number
$X_{\min(i, j)\, \max(i, j)}(\omega)$, and $\min$ and $\max$ are symmetric in their arguments.

articles.title: Wigner matrix
articles.statement:
Let $X_{ij} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, for $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, be real
functions on a set $\Omega$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, the Wigner matrix
$W_n(\omega)$ is the $n \times n$ complex matrix, with rows and columns indexed by
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, whose entry at $(i, j)$ is the real number
$X_{\min(i, j)\, \max(i, j)}(\omega)$. Only the $X_{ij}$ with $i \le j$ are used, and the matrix
is real symmetric.

articles.title: Wigner's semicircle law
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mu)$ be a probability space and let
$X_{ij} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, for $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, be measurable functions. Suppose that
the family $(X_{ij})_{i \le j}$ is mutually independent, that all $X_{ij}$ with $i \le j$ have the
same distribution, and that for $i \le j$ both $X_{ij}$ and $X_{ij}^2$ are integrable with
$\mathbb{E}[X_{ij}] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[X_{ij}^2] = 1$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$\omega \in \Omega$, let $W_n(\omega)$ be the Wigner matrix of $X$ and let $L_n(\omega)$ be the
image of its empirical spectral measure under $x \mapsto x / \sqrt{n}$ (for $n \ge 1$, the
empirical spectral measure of $W_n(\omega) / \sqrt{n}$). Then for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$,
every bounded continuous function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies

$$\int f \, dL_n(\omega) \to \int f \, d\sigma \quad (n \to \infty),$$

where $\sigma$ is the semicircle distribution.

## Sources

- E. Wigner, 'Characteristic vectors of bordered matrices with infinite dimensions', Ann. of Math. (2) 62 (1955) 548–564 (Gaussian case). Pastur's universality extending to all variances with finite second moments: L. Pastur, 'On the spectrum of random matrices', Teor. Mat. Fiz. 10 (1972) 102–112. Listed as §102 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `wigner_semicircle` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Benjamini–Hochberg index satisfies the step-up condition
articles.statement: At the BH step-up index `k`, at least `k` p-values are at most `q k / m`.

articles.title: Benjamini–Hochberg index is at most the number of hypotheses
articles.statement: The BH step-up index is at most `m`.

articles.title: Benjamini–Hochberg step-up index
articles.statement:
The Benjamini–Hochberg step-up index: the largest `k ∈ {0, …, m}` such that at least `k`
p-values are at most `q k / m` (`k = 0` always qualifies).

articles.title: Benjamini–Hochberg rejection set
articles.statement:
The hypotheses rejected by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at level `q`: those whose
p-value is at most `q * bhIndex q p / m`.

articles.title: Number of Benjamini–Hochberg rejections
articles.statement: The BH procedure at level `q ≥ 0` rejects exactly `bhIndex q p` hypotheses.

articles.title: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control
articles.statement:
If the p-values are independent and every true-null
p-value is uniformly distributed on `[0, 1]`, the BH procedure at level `q ∈ [0, 1]` has false
discovery rate at most `q |H0| / m`. Nothing is assumed about the false-null p-values beyond
measurability and independence. (For `m = 0` both sides are `0`.)

## Sources

- Benjamini & Hochberg (1995), Theorem 1.

articles.title: Maximality of the Benjamini–Hochberg index
articles.statement: The BH step-up index is the largest `k ≤ m` with at least `k` p-values at most `q k / m`.

articles.title: Bonferroni rejection set
articles.statement:
The hypotheses rejected by the Bonferroni procedure at level `α`: those whose p-value is
at most `α / m`.

articles.title: The Bonferroni procedure controls the FWER
articles.statement:
If every true-null p-value is valid, the
probability that the Bonferroni procedure at level `α ∈ [0, 1]` rejects at least one true null
is at most `α`.

articles.title: Bonferroni inequality
articles.statement:
If every true-null p-value is valid, the probability that some
true null has p-value at most `α / m` is at most `α |H0| / m`, for `α ∈ [0, 1]`. No
independence is assumed. (For `m = 0` there is no hypothesis and both sides are `0`.)

## Sources

- Bonferroni (1936); Dunn (1961).

articles.title: Union bound for valid p-values
articles.statement:
If every true-null p-value is valid and
`c ∈ [0, 1]`, the probability that some true null has p-value at most `c` is at most
`|H0| c`. No independence is assumed.

articles.title: Bonferroni local test of an intersection hypothesis
articles.statement:
The Bonferroni local test of the intersection hypothesis `H_J` at level `α`: reject when
some `j ∈ J` has `p j ≤ α / |J|`. (It never rejects `H_∅`.)

articles.title: Closed testing procedure
articles.statement:
The closed testing procedure: given the decisions `φ J` of local tests of the intersection
hypotheses `H_J`, reject `Hᵢ` exactly when `φ J` holds for every `J` containing `i`.

articles.title: Holm's procedure is a closed test
articles.statement:
For `α ≥ 0`, the hypotheses rejected by Holm's
step-down procedure are exactly those rejected by the closed testing procedure built on the
Bonferroni local tests.

## Sources

- Holm (1979) introduces the procedure; the closure is that of Marcus, Peritz and Gabriel (1976).

articles.title: Closed testing rejection implies the intersection test rejects
articles.statement:
If the closed procedure rejects a hypothesis in `H0`, then the local test of the
intersection hypothesis `H_{H0}` rejects.

articles.title: Level of the Bonferroni local test
articles.statement:
The Bonferroni local test of `H_{H0}` has level `α ∈ [0, 1]` when the p-values in `H0`
are valid.

articles.title: The closed testing principle
articles.statement:
If `H0` is the set of true nulls and the local test of
`H_{H0}` rejects with probability at most `α`, then the closed procedure rejects some true
null with probability at most `α`. Applied to every possible `H0`, local level-`α` tests give
strong control of the family-wise error rate. No assumption on the dependence between local
tests is made.

## Sources

- Marcus, Peritz and Gabriel (1976).

articles.title: Membership in the closed rejection set
articles.statement: Membership in the closed rejection set.

articles.title: Levene's formula is the conditional law under random union of gametes
articles.statement:
Among the
`C(2N, nA)` equally likely placements of the `nA` copies of `A` in the `2N` gamete slots, the
fraction with exactly `h` heterozygous individuals is `leveneProb N nA h`.

No hypothesis `nA ≤ 2N` is needed: for `nA > 2N` there is no placement and `C(2N, nA) = 0`, so
the left side is `0 / 0 = 0`, matching `leveneProb N nA h = 0`; the statement is meaningful for
`nA ≤ 2N`. The uniform law on placements is taken as the model; deriving it from independent
gametes conditioned on `nA` is not part of this file.

## Sources

- Levene (1949); Wigginton, Cutler and Abecasis (2005).

articles.title: Number of heterozygous individuals
articles.statement:
The number of heterozygous individuals when the `A` gametes occupy the slots `s`:
individuals `j` carrying exactly one of the slots `(j, 0)`, `(j, 1)`.

articles.title: Levene's exact Hardy–Weinberg probability
articles.statement:
Levene's conditional probability of `h` heterozygotes among `N` diploid individuals given
`nA` copies of allele `A` (and `nB = 2N - nA` of `B`) under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium:
`N! nA! nB! 2^h / (nAA! h! nBB! (2N)!)` with `nAA = (nA - h) / 2`, `nBB = (nB - h) / 2`, when
`h ≤ nA`, `h ≤ nB` and `nA - h` is even, and `0` otherwise. The parameter domain is
`nA ≤ 2N`; for `nA > 2N` the value is `0`.

articles.title: Normalization of Levene's distribution
articles.statement:
For `nA ≤ 2N` the probabilities
`leveneProb N nA h` over the admissible heterozygote counts `h` sum to one.

## Sources

- Levene (1949); Wigginton, Cutler and Abecasis (2005).

articles.title: Fisher's exact conditional law
articles.statement:
Let `X ~ Bin(n₁, p)` and `Y ~ Bin(n₂, p)` be independent
with a common `p ∈ (0, 1)`. Given the margin `X + Y = t` with `t ≤ n₁ + n₂`, the cell `X` is
hypergeometric: `P(X = k | X + Y = t) = C(n₁, k) C(n₂, t - k) / C(n₁ + n₂, t)`, whatever `p`.

## Sources

- Fisher (1934, §21.02; 1935); Lehmann–Romano (2005), §4.5.

articles.title: Sum of independent binomials
articles.statement:
If `X ~ Bin(n₁, p)` and `Y ~ Bin(n₂, p)` are independent,
then `X + Y ~ Bin(n₁ + n₂, p)`: `P(X + Y = t) = C(n₁ + n₂, t) p^t (1 - p)^(n₁ + n₂ - t)`.

articles.title: Number of hypotheses rejected by Holm's procedure
articles.statement: Holm's procedure at level `α ≥ 0` rejects exactly `holmIndex α p` hypotheses.

articles.title: Holm rejection bound for a set of hypotheses
articles.statement:
If Holm rejects a hypothesis in `J`, then some `j ∈ J` has p-value at most `α / |J|`:
the first hypothesis of `J` in sorted order sits at a position `k ≤ m - |J| + 1`. This
is the shared Holm rejection bound, used both for Holm's FWER control below and for
identifying Holm's procedure with the closure of the Bonferroni local tests.

articles.title: Holm's step-down count is at most the number of tests
articles.statement: Holm's step-down count is at most `m`.

articles.title: Holm's step-down count
articles.statement:
Holm's step-down count at level `α`: the largest `r ∈ {0, …, m}` such that for every
`k ∈ {1, …, r}` the `k`-th smallest p-value is at most `α / (m - k + 1)`, i.e. at least `k`
p-values are at most `α / (m - k + 1)`. (`r = 0` always qualifies.)

articles.title: Hypotheses rejected by Holm's step-down procedure
articles.statement:
The hypotheses rejected by Holm's step-down procedure at level `α`: those whose p-value is
at most `α / (m - r + 1)` with `r = holmIndex α p`; these are the hypotheses with the `r`
smallest p-values.

articles.title: Holm's count is the largest index where every step succeeds
articles.statement: Holm's count is the largest index up to which every step succeeds.

articles.title: Every step up to Holm's count succeeds
articles.statement:
Every step up to Holm's count succeeds: for `1 ≤ k ≤ holmIndex α p`, at least `k`
p-values are at most `α / (m - k + 1)`.

articles.title: Holm's procedure controls the FWER
articles.statement:
If every true-null p-value is valid, the
probability that Holm's step-down procedure at level `α ∈ [0, 1]` rejects at least one true
null is at most `α`. No independence is assumed.

## Sources

- Holm (1979).

articles.title: Holm's rejection set is closed under smaller p-values
articles.statement: The rejection set is closed under smaller p-values.

articles.title: Reweighting an infinite product measure by a product density
articles.statement:
If `μ.withDensity r` is a
probability measure, then reweighting the product measure `μ^ℕ` by `∏_{i<n} r (xᵢ)` and
projecting onto the first `n` coordinates gives the product measure `(μ.withDensity r)^n`.

articles.title: Local power of the likelihood-ratio test
articles.statement:
Let row `n` of the triangular array
`X n 0, X n 1, …` be i.i.d. with law `p θₙ ν`, `θₙ = θ₀ + h / √n`, under the Cramér conditions
at `θ₀` of `LikelihoodRatioTests.tendstoInDistribution_two_mul_logLikelihood_sub` (all moment
and envelope conditions are under the null law `p θ₀ ν`). If `θ̂ₙ` solves the likelihood
equation for row `n` with probability tending to one and `θ̂ₙ → θ₀` in probability, then
`2 (ℓₙ(θ̂ₙ) - ℓₙ(θ₀))` converges in distribution to the law of `(Z + h √I(θ₀))²`,
`Z ~ N(0, 1)` (noncentral `χ²₁` with noncentrality `h² I(θ₀)`). For `h = 0` this is Wilks'
theorem for a triangular array.

The row `n = 0` is irrelevant for the limit; with Lean's `h / √0 = 0` its law is `p θ₀ ν`, which
makes `p θ₀ ν` a probability measure. No normalization `∫ p θ dν = 1` is assumed otherwise:
the laws `p θₙ ν` are probability measures because they are laws of random variables.

## Sources

- van der Vaart (1998), ch. 16 (local power), via local asymptotic normality (ch. 7) and Le Cam's first and third lemmas (ch. 6).

articles.title: Wilks' expansion for a triangular array
articles.statement:
Let `X n i` be random variables (row `n` is the
sample of size `n`) and `θ̂ₙ` estimators that solve the likelihood equation
`∑_{i<n} ∂_θ log p θ (X n i) = 0` with probability tending to one and converge to `θ₀` in
probability. Suppose that on the ball of radius `δ > 0` about `θ₀` the log-likelihood is
differentiable in `θ`, the score is twice differentiable, and `|∂³_θ log p θ x| ≤ M x`. Assume
the laws of large numbers `-(n⁻¹ ∑_{i<n} ∂²_θ log p θ₀ (X n i)) → I` with `I > 0` and
`n⁻¹ ∑_{i<n} M (X n i) → c` in probability, and that the normalized score
`n^{-1/2} ∑_{i<n} ∂_θ log p θ₀ (X n i)` converges in distribution to `Y`. Then
`2 (ℓₙ(θ̂ₙ) - ℓₙ(θ₀)) → Y² / I` in distribution, where `ℓₙ θ = ∑_{i<n} log p θ (X n i)`.

No independence or distributional assumption on the rows is made: they enter only through the
three limit hypotheses. The positivity of `p` is not used either: the expansion holds for any
criterion `log p θ x` with these derivatives. For i.i.d. rows with law `p θ₀ ν` this is Wilks'
theorem; under local alternatives it gives the local power
(`tendstoInDistribution_two_mul_logLikelihood_sub_local`).

## Sources

- Wilks (1938); van der Vaart (1998), Theorem 5.41 and ch. 16.

articles.title: Local asymptotic normality of the log-likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
Suppose that on the ball of
radius `δ > 0` about `θ₀` the log-likelihood `log p θ x` is differentiable in `θ`, the score
`∂_θ log p θ x` is twice differentiable in `θ`, and `|∂³_θ log p θ x| ≤ M x`. Let `Y 0, Y 1, …`
be random variables such that `-(n⁻¹ ∑_{i<n} ∂²_θ log p θ₀ (Y i)) → I` and
`n⁻¹ ∑_{i<n} M (Y i) → c` in probability (laws of large numbers). Then, for the local
parameters `θₙ = θ₀ + h / √n`,
`∑_{i<n} (log p θₙ (Y i) - log p θ₀ (Y i)) - h n^{-1/2} ∑_{i<n} ∂_θ log p θ₀ (Y i)`
converges to `-h² I / 2` in probability.

## Sources

- van der Vaart (1998), Theorem 7.2 (local asymptotic normality), here under Cramér's third-derivative envelope instead of differentiability in quadratic mean.

articles.title: Empirical AUC = Mann–Whitney with ties
articles.statement:
**Empirical AUC = Mann–Whitney with ties** (Bamber 1975): the trapezoidal area under the
empirical ROC curve equals `U / (m n)`, for nonempty samples.

articles.title: Empirical area under the ROC curve
articles.statement:
Trapezoidal area under the empirical ROC curve of positive scores `x` and negative scores
`y`: the sum over the distinct observed scores `t` of the trapezoid from the point
`(rocRateAbove y t, rocRateAbove x t)` to `(rocRate y t, rocRate x t)`.

articles.title: Mann–Whitney U statistic
articles.statement:
Mann–Whitney count `U = ∑ᵢ ∑ⱼ (1[y j < x i] + ½ 1[y j = x i])` of (positive, negative)
pairs ranked correctly, with ties counted one half.

articles.title: Strict ROC rate equals the rate at the next score
articles.statement:
If no score lies strictly between `t < t'`, the strict rate at `t` is the rate at `t'`: the
left end of the trapezoid at `t` is the ROC point of the next larger distinct score.

articles.title: Strict ROC rate vanishes above the largest score
articles.statement: Above the largest score the strict rate is zero: the first trapezoid starts at `(0, 0)`.

articles.title: Empirical ROC rate strictly above a threshold
articles.statement:
Empirical rate `#{i | t < z i} / k` of scores strictly above `t`: the ROC coordinate at the
next larger distinct score.

articles.title: Empirical ROC rate at or above a threshold
articles.statement:
Empirical rate `#{i | t ≤ z i} / k` of scores at or above the threshold `t` (the true- or
false-positive rate when `z` are the positive or negative scores).

articles.title: Cochran's Q as a squared projection norm
articles.statement:
Algebraic core of Cochran's theorem for `Q`: if `Xᵢ = θ + √vᵢ zᵢ` with `vᵢ > 0`, then `Q` is
the squared distance from `z` to the line spanned by `a = (vᵢ^{-1/2})ᵢ`, i.e. the squared norm
of the projection of `z` onto the orthogonal complement of that line.

articles.title: Cochran's heterogeneity statistic Q
articles.statement:
Cochran's heterogeneity statistic `Q = ∑ᵢ vᵢ⁻¹ (Xᵢ - ∑ⱼ wⱼ Xⱼ)²` of the estimates `X` with
variances `v`, where `w = inverseVarianceWeights v`.

articles.title: Fisher's combined statistic
articles.statement: Fisher's combined statistic `-2 ∑ log pᵢ` of `k` p-values.

articles.title: Cochran (1954)
articles.statement:
For `k ≥ 2` independent Gaussian estimates `Xᵢ ~ N(θ, vᵢ)` with
positive known variances, Cochran's `Q` has the chi-square law with `k - 1` degrees of
freedom.

articles.title: Fisher's method for combining p-values
articles.statement:
Fisher (1932), §21.1: for `k ≥ 1` independent p-values, each uniform on `[0, 1]`, Fisher's
statistic `-2 ∑ log pᵢ` is chi-square with `2k` degrees of freedom.

articles.title: Minus twice the log of a uniform variable is chi-square
articles.statement:
`-2 log U` has the exponential law of rate `1/2`, i.e. chi-square with two degrees of
freedom, when `U` is uniform on `[0, 1]`.

articles.title: Stouffer's method
articles.statement:
Stouffer's method (Stouffer et al. 1949; Liptak 1958): for independent standard normal
z-scores and a nonzero weight vector, the weighted z statistic is standard normal.

articles.title: Optimality of inverse-variance weights
articles.statement:
Optimality of inverse-variance weighting: for positive variances `v` and weights `c` summing
to one, `∑ cᵢ² vᵢ ≥ (∑ vᵢ⁻¹)⁻¹`. The gap is `∑ vᵢ (cᵢ - wᵢ)²` for the inverse-variance
weights `w`.

articles.title: Inverse-variance weights
articles.statement: The inverse-variance (fixed-effect) weights `vᵢ⁻¹ / ∑ⱼ vⱼ⁻¹` for study variances `v`.

articles.title: Stouffer's weighted z statistic
articles.statement: Stouffer's weighted z statistic `∑ wᵢ zᵢ / √(∑ wᵢ²)` of the study z-scores `zᵢ`.

articles.title: Inverse-variance weights sum to one
articles.statement: The inverse-variance weights sum to one.

articles.title: Variance of the inverse-variance-weighted average
articles.statement: The variance `∑ wᵢ² vᵢ` of the inverse-variance-weighted average is `(∑ vᵢ⁻¹)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Cochran's minimum-variance theorem for weighted averages
articles.statement:
Cochran (1954): for pairwise independent square-integrable estimates `X i` with positive
variances, the inverse-variance-weighted average has variance `(∑ Var[Xᵢ]⁻¹)⁻¹`, the smallest
variance among all weighted averages `∑ cᵢ Xᵢ` with `∑ cᵢ = 1`.

articles.title: Binomial family has monotone likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
A binomial family whose success probability lies in `[0, 1]` and is monotone on `S` has a
monotone likelihood ratio on `S`.

articles.title: Binomial likelihood
articles.statement:
Binomial likelihood with `N` trials and parameter-dependent success probability `p θ`:
`L n θ = C(N, n) p θ ^ n (1 - p θ) ^ (N - n)` (zero for `n > N`, since `C(N, n) = 0`).

articles.title: Antitone likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
The likelihood family has an **antitone likelihood ratio** on `S`: `L` is nonnegative
on `S`, and for `n ≤ m` and `θ ≤ θ'` in `S`, `L n θ * L m θ' ≤ L m θ * L n θ'`.
For positive likelihoods this says `θ ↦ L m θ / L n θ` is nonincreasing (larger counts
favor smaller parameters).

articles.title: Monotone likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
The likelihood family `L : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ` (observation, parameter) has a **monotone
likelihood ratio** on the parameter set `S`: `L` is nonnegative on `S`, and for
observations `n ≤ m` and parameters `θ ≤ θ'` in `S`,
`L m θ * L n θ' ≤ L n θ * L m θ'` (total positivity of order two). For positive
likelihoods this is monotonicity of `θ ↦ L m θ / L n θ`. The nonnegativity is part of
the predicate: without it the downstream `posteriorTail` would not be a posterior
probability (a signed `L` can give `posteriorTail > 1`).

articles.title: Poisson family with antitone mean has antitone likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
A Poisson family whose mean is nonnegative and antitone on `S` has an antitone likelihood
ratio on `S`.

articles.title: Poisson family with monotone mean has monotone likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
A Poisson family whose mean is nonnegative and monotone on `S` has a monotone likelihood
ratio on `S`.

articles.title: Poisson likelihood
articles.statement:
Poisson likelihood with parameter-dependent mean `λ θ`:
`L n θ = e^{-λ θ} λ θ ^ n / (n !)`.

articles.title: The posterior is stochastically nonincreasing in the observation
articles.statement:
**The posterior is stochastically nonincreasing in the observation** for a family with an
antitone likelihood ratio and every prior: if `n ≤ m` and both marginal likelihoods are
positive, then `P(θ > t ∣ m) ≤ P(θ > t ∣ n)` for every `t`.

articles.title: The posterior is stochastically nondecreasing in the observation
articles.statement:
**The posterior is stochastically nondecreasing in the observation** for an MLR family and
every prior (Milgrom 1981, Prop. 2): if `n ≤ m` and both marginal likelihoods are positive, then
`P(θ > t ∣ n) ≤ P(θ > t ∣ m)` for every `t`.

articles.title: Posterior tail probability
articles.statement:
Posterior probability of `{θ > t}` after observing `n`, by Bayes' formula for the prior
`μ` and likelihood `L`: `(∫_{θ > t} L n θ dμ) / ∫ L n θ dμ`. Meaningful when the marginal
likelihood `∫ L n dμ` is positive (otherwise the division returns the junk value `0`), and a
genuine posterior probability only when `L` is nonnegative (as in the MLR predicates:
a signed `L` can give a value outside `[0, 1]`).

articles.title: Posterior stochastic ordering for an antitone likelihood ratio, cross-multiplied form
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of `setIntegral_Ioi_mul_integral_le_of_hasMLR` with the reversed ratio
condition, for `n ≤ m`:
`(∫_{θ > t} L m dμ) (∫ L n dμ) ≤ (∫_{θ > t} L n dμ) (∫ L m dμ)`.

articles.title: Posterior stochastic ordering, cross-multiplied form
articles.statement:
**Posterior stochastic ordering, cross-multiplied form** (Milgrom 1981, Prop. 1). If the
family `L` has a monotone likelihood ratio on a set `S` carrying the prior `μ`
(`μ Sᶜ = 0`), and every `L n` is `μ`-integrable, then for `n ≤ m` and every threshold `t`,
`(∫_{θ > t} L n dμ) (∫ L m dμ) ≤ (∫_{θ > t} L m dμ) (∫ L n dμ)`.

articles.title: Neyman–Pearson lemma
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, and let
$p, q : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be measurable, nonnegative and $\mu$-integrable. Let $k \ge 0$ be a
real number and let $\varphi^\star : \Omega \to [0, 1]$ be measurable with $\varphi^\star(x) = 1$
whenever $q(x) > k\,p(x)$ and $\varphi^\star(x) = 0$ whenever $q(x) < k\,p(x)$. Then every
measurable test $\varphi : \Omega \to [0, 1]$ satisfying
$\int \varphi\, p \, d\mu \le \int \varphi^\star p \, d\mu$ also satisfies
$\int \varphi\, q \, d\mu \le \int \varphi^\star q \, d\mu$.

No normalization of $p$ or $q$ and no condition on $\varphi^\star$ on the set where $q = k\,p$ are
assumed.

## Sources

- J. Neyman and E. S. Pearson, "On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses", Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 231 (1933), 289–337, DOI `10.1098/rsta.1933.0009`.

articles.title: Counting lemma for rank counts
articles.statement:
Counting lemma: for any family of reals `t` indexed by `G` and any `k`, at most `k`
elements `h` have rank count `#{g | t h ≤ t g}` at most `k`.

articles.title: Validity of Monte Carlo permutation p-values
articles.statement:
Phipson and Smyth (2010); Hemerik and Goeman (2018): if the null law `μ` is invariant under
a finite group `G` and `g₁, …, g_B` are drawn independently and uniformly from `G`,
independently of the data, then `(1 + #{b | T(g_b • ω) ≥ T(ω)}) / (B + 1)` is a valid p-value
under the joint law.

articles.title: Validity of permutation p-values
articles.statement:
Lehmann and Romano (2005), §15.2; Hemerik and Goeman (2018): if the law `μ` is invariant
under the action of a finite group `G`, the permutation p-value of any measurable statistic is
valid.

articles.title: Monte Carlo permutation p-value
articles.statement:
The Monte Carlo permutation p-value `(1 + #{b | T(g_b • ω) ≥ T(ω)}) / (B + 1)` of the
statistic `T` at the data `ω` with the `B` drawn group elements `g`.

articles.title: Permutation p-value
articles.statement:
The permutation (group-invariance) p-value of the statistic `T` at `ω`: the fraction of
group elements `g` with `T (g • ω) ≥ T ω`.

articles.title: Law of the positive part squared of a standard normal variable
articles.statement:
`max(Z, 0)²` has the
mixture law `½ δ₀ + ½ χ²₁` (chi-bar-square with weights `½, ½`).

articles.title: Squared normalized Gaussian is chi-square with one degree of freedom
articles.statement: If `Y ~ N(0, v)` with `v ≠ 0`, then `Y² / v ~ χ²₁`.

articles.title: Rao's score test with an estimated information
articles.statement:
As
`tendstoInDistribution_scoreStatistic`, with `I(θ₀)` replaced by any estimators `Î n`
converging to `I(θ₀)` in probability. Where `Î n ω = 0` the statistic takes Lean's value
`x / 0 = 0`; this event has probability tending to `0` because `0 < I(θ₀)`.

articles.title: Rao's score test, known information
articles.statement:
Under the conditions of
`tendstoInDistribution_score` and `0 < I(θ₀)`, the score statistic
`(n^{-1/2} ∑_{i<n} score p θ₀ (X i))² / I(θ₀)` converges in distribution to `χ²₁`.

## Sources

- Rao (1948), one-parameter case; the central limit theorem for the score as in Lehmann & Casella (1998), §6.3.

articles.title: Wilks' theorem, supremum form
articles.statement:
If moreover `θ̂ₙ ω` maximizes the log-likelihood
`ℓₙ θ = ∑_{i<n} log p θ (X i ω)` over all `θ` for every `n` and `ω`, then the
likelihood-ratio statistic `2 (sup_θ ℓₙ θ - ℓₙ θ₀)` converges in distribution to `χ²₁`.

articles.title: Likelihood ratio on the boundary
articles.statement:
**Likelihood ratio on the boundary** (one-sided parameter space `θ ∈ [0, ∞)`, true value
`θ₀ = 0`). Let the model be defined and regular on a ball about `0` as in
`tendstoInDistribution_two_mul_logLikelihood_sub` (so `0` is interior to the domain of the
family, though not to the parameter space), and let `θ̂ₙ` be a consistent root of the
likelihood equation. The statistic `2 (ℓₙ(max θ̂ₙ 0) - ℓₙ(0))` of the estimator projected onto
`[0, ∞)` converges in distribution to the mixture `½ δ₀ + ½ χ²₁`. The projection `max θ̂ₙ 0`
is the restricted maximizer when, for example, `ℓₙ` is concave; that is not assumed here.

## Sources

- Chernoff (1954); van der Vaart (1998), ch. 16.

articles.title: Wilks' theorem (simple null)
articles.statement:
Under the conditions of `tendstoInDistribution_waldStatistic`
and joint measurability of `(θ, x) ↦ p θ x`, the log-likelihood-ratio statistic
`2 (ℓₙ(θ̂ₙ) - ℓₙ(θ₀))`, `ℓₙ θ = ∑_{i<n} log p θ (X i)`, of a consistent root `θ̂ₙ` of the
likelihood equation converges in distribution to `χ²₁`.

## Sources

- Wilks (1938), case of a one-dimensional parameter and a simple null hypothesis; van der Vaart (1998), ch. 16.

articles.title: Wald's test with an estimated information
articles.statement:
As `tendstoInDistribution_waldStatistic`,
with `I(θ₀)` replaced by any estimators `Î n → I(θ₀)` in probability (for example the observed
information of `tendstoInMeasure_observedInformation`; `I(θ̂ₙ)` also qualifies when
`θ ↦ I(θ)` is continuous at `θ₀`, by the continuous mapping theorem).

articles.title: Wald's test
articles.statement:
Under the conditions of
`tendstoInDistribution_sqrt_mul_sub_of_likelihoodEquation` (without the normalization
`∫ p θ dν = 1`, which that proof does not use), the Wald statistic `n (θ̂ₙ - θ₀)² I(θ₀)` of a
consistent root `θ̂ₙ` of the likelihood equation converges in distribution to `χ²₁`.

## Sources

- Wald (1943), one-parameter case; the asymptotic normality of `θ̂ₙ` as in Lehmann & Casella (1998), §6.3.

articles.title: Consistency of the observed information
articles.statement:
For i.i.d. observations with law `p θ₀ ν`,
if `∂_θ score p θ₀` is measurable and integrable with `E ∂_θ score p θ₀ = -I(θ₀)` (the
information identity), then `-(1/n) ∑_{i<n} ∂_θ score p θ₀ (X i) → I(θ₀)` in probability.

articles.title: Quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood ratio
articles.statement:
Let `θ̂ₙ` be `√n`-consistent
(`√n (θ̂ₙ - θ₀)` converges in distribution) and solve the likelihood equation with probability
tending to one. If on the ball of radius `δ > 0` about `θ₀` the log-likelihood is twice
differentiable in `θ` with `|∂³_θ log p θ x| ≤ M x` for an integrable `M`, and
`∂²_θ log p θ₀` is integrable with mean `-I(θ₀)`, then
`2 (ℓₙ(θ̂ₙ) - ℓₙ(θ₀)) - n (θ̂ₙ - θ₀)² I(θ₀) → 0` in probability, where
`ℓₙ θ = ∑_{i<n} log p θ (X i)`.

The positivity of `p` is not used: the expansion holds for any criterion `log p θ x` with these
derivatives, and the theorems below assume `0 < p θ x`.

## Sources

- the second-order expansion of Wilks (1938); van der Vaart (1998), ch. 16.

articles.title: Non-null law as the integral of the non-null density
articles.statement: `P₁(A) = ∫_A f₁`.

articles.title: Law of a non-null z-value
articles.statement: The law `P₁` of a non-null z-value.

articles.title: Local fdr is the posterior null probability
articles.statement:
Efron et al. (2001): `fdr(Z) = P(H = 0 | Z)` almost surely, as a conditional expectation
of the null indicator given the z-value.

articles.title: Tail-area fdr is the posterior null probability given a region
articles.statement:
`P(H = 0 | Z ∈ Γ) = Fdr(Γ)`: the tail-area false discovery rate is the posterior null
probability given `Z ∈ Γ` (Storey 2002, Theorem 1; Efron 2010, ch. 2). Both sides are `0` when
`P(Z ∈ Γ) = 0`.

articles.title: Mixture density is integrable
articles.statement: The mixture density is integrable.

articles.title: Joint probability of a non-null case in a set
Null probability as an integral of the local fdr
articles.statement:
Efron et al. (2001): `P(H = 0, Z ∈ A) = ∫_A fdr(z) dP_Z(z)` for every measurable `A`, so
`fdr(Z)` is a version of the posterior null probability `P(H = 0 | Z)`.

articles.title: Joint probability of a null case in a set
articles.statement: `P(H = 0, Z ∈ A) = π₀ P₀(A)`.

articles.title: z-value has the mixture law
articles.statement: The z-value has the mixture law: `P(Z ∈ A) = ∫_A f`.

articles.title: Joint law of null indicator and z-value
articles.statement: Joint law of (null indicator, z-value) on `Bool × ℝ`; `true` means the case is null.

articles.title: Conservative bias of Storey's null proportion estimator
articles.statement:
Conservative bias of Storey's (2002) estimator for a fixed set `H0` of true nulls: if their
p-values are valid, then `E[π̂₀(t)] ≥ m₀ / m` for every `t ∈ [0, 1)`. No independence is
assumed; the non-null p-values are arbitrary measurable functions.

articles.title: Local false discovery rate is at most one
articles.statement: The local false discovery rate is at most one.

articles.title: Local fdr times mixture density equals the null part
articles.statement:
The basic identity `fdr(z) f(z) = π₀ f₀(z)`, for every `z` (where `f(z) = 0` both sides
vanish because `π₀ f₀ ≤ f`).

articles.title: Local false discovery rate is nonnegative
articles.statement: The local false discovery rate is nonnegative.

articles.title: Local false discovery rate
articles.statement: Efron's local false discovery rate `fdr(z) = π₀ f₀(z) / f(z)` (zero where `f(z) = 0`).

articles.title: Marginal z-value law of the joint law is the mixture
articles.statement: The law of the z-value under the joint law is the mixture `f · Lebesgue`.

articles.title: Local false discovery rate is measurable
articles.statement: The local false discovery rate is measurable.

articles.title: Mixture density is measurable
articles.statement: The mixture density is measurable.

articles.title: Mixture density is nonnegative
articles.statement: The mixture density is nonnegative.

articles.title: Mixture density of the two-groups model
articles.statement: The mixture density `f = π₀ f₀ + (1 - π₀) f₁` of the z-values.

articles.title: q-value is monotone in the statistic
articles.statement: The q-value is monotone in the statistic.

articles.title: Null part of the mixture is dominated by the mixture
articles.statement: The null part of the mixture is dominated by the mixture: `π₀ f₀ ≤ f`.

articles.title: Null law as the integral of the null density
articles.statement: `P₀(A) = ∫_A f₀`.

articles.title: Law of a null z-value
articles.statement: The law `P₀` of a null z-value.

articles.title: True-null set of a test outcome vector
articles.statement:
The true-null set of an outcome vector `x : Fin m → Bool × Bool`, where `(x i).1` records
that hypothesis `i` is null and `(x i).2` that it is rejected.

articles.title: Probability of a test outcome vector
articles.statement:
The probability `∏ᵢ q(xᵢ)` of an outcome vector when the `m` (null, rejected) pairs are
i.i.d. with law `q`.

articles.title: Law of a test's null and rejection pair
articles.statement:
The law of one test's (null, rejected) pair in the two-groups model when the test rejects
iff its z-value lies in `Γ`.

articles.title: Storey's theorem: pFDR is a posterior null probability
articles.statement:
Storey (2002), Theorem 1: for `m ≥ 1` i.i.d. tests, `pFDR = P(H = 0 | T ∈ Γ)`, where
`q (true, true) = P(H = 0, T ∈ Γ)` and `q (false, true) = P(H = 1, T ∈ Γ)`. The identity is
homogeneous in `q`, so only `q ≥ 0` is assumed; when `P(T ∈ Γ) = 0` both sides are `0`.

articles.title: Storey's theorem in the two-groups model
articles.statement:
Storey (2002), Theorem 1, in the two-groups model: for `m ≥ 1` i.i.d. tests rejecting on
`Γ`, `pFDR(Γ) = π₀ P₀(Γ) / P(Γ) = Fdr(Γ)`.

articles.title: Storey's positive false discovery rate
articles.statement:
Storey's positive false discovery rate `pFDR = E[V / R | R > 0]` for `m` tests whose
(null, rejected) indicator pairs are i.i.d. with law `q`: `V / R` is the false discovery
proportion.

articles.title: q-value equals the pFDR when the pFDR is monotone
articles.statement: When the pFDR is nondecreasing along the nested regions, the q-value is the pFDR.

articles.title: q-value is at most the pFDR of the smallest region
articles.statement: The q-value is at most the pFDR of the smallest region containing the statistic.

articles.title: Storey's q-value
articles.statement:
Storey's (2003) q-value for a nested family of rejection regions `Γ_s = {T ≤ s}` with
`pFDR(Γ_s) = pfdr s`: `q(t) = inf_{s ≥ t} pfdr s`, the smallest pFDR over the regions that
contain the observed statistic `t`.

articles.title: Rejection set of a test outcome vector
articles.statement: The rejection set of an outcome vector.

articles.title: Storey's estimator of the null proportion
articles.statement:
Storey's estimator `π̂₀(t) = #{i | pᵢ > t} / (m (1 - t))` of the proportion of true nulls,
for a tuning parameter `t ∈ [0, 1)`.

articles.title: Tail-area fdr is the average local fdr over the region
articles.statement:
`E[fdr(Z) | Z ∈ Γ] = Fdr(Γ)`, written with densities: the tail-area false discovery rate is
the `f`-weighted average of the local false discovery rate over `Γ` (Efron 2010, ch. 5).

articles.title: Tail-area false discovery rate
articles.statement:
The tail-area false discovery rate of a region `Γ`: `Fdr(Γ) = π₀ P₀(Γ) / P(Γ)`, written with
the densities. Efron's `Fdr(z)` is `tailFdr (Set.Iic z)`. It is `0` when `P(Γ) = 0`.

articles.title: Two-groups model
articles.statement:
The two-groups model of Efron et al. (2001): prior null probability `π₀ ∈ [0, 1]`, null
density `f₀` and non-null density `f₁` of the z-value (probability densities on `ℝ`).

articles.title: False discovery proportion is at most one
articles.statement: The false discovery proportion is at most one.

articles.title: False discovery proportion is nonnegative
articles.statement: The false discovery proportion is nonnegative.

articles.title: False discovery proportion
articles.statement:
The false discovery proportion of a rejection set `R` when `H0` is the set of true nulls:
`|R ∩ H0| / max |R| 1` (zero when nothing is rejected).

articles.title: Uniform p-values are valid
articles.statement: A p-value distributed uniformly on `[0, 1]` is valid.

articles.title: Valid p-value
articles.statement:
A real random variable `X` is a *valid* (super-uniform) p-value under `μ` if
`μ {X ≤ t} ≤ t` for every level `t ∈ [0, 1]`. Uniform p-values are the equality case.

articles.title: Number of p-values below a threshold is at most the total
articles.statement: At most `m` p-values lie below any threshold.

articles.title: Number of p-values below a threshold is monotone
articles.statement: `numBelow p` is monotone in the threshold.

articles.title: Number of p-values below a threshold
articles.statement: The number of p-values that are at most `t`.

articles.title: Interchange law for convolution
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra for which addition $M \times M \to M$ is measurable. For all s-finite measures
$a, b, c, d$ on $M$ we have $(a * b) * (c * d) = (a * c) * (b * d)$, where $*$ denotes
convolution of measures.

articles.title: Convolution powers add exponents
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra for which addition $M 	imes M 	o M$ is measurable, and let $
u$ be an s-finite
measure on $M$. Writing $*$ for convolution of measures and $
u^{*n}$ for the $n$-th
convolution power of $
u$, for all natural numbers $m$ and $n$ we have
$
u^{*(m+n)} = 
u^{*m} * 
u^{*n}$.

articles.title: Convolution power of a convolution
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra for which addition $M \times M \to M$ is measurable, and let $\nu$ and $\rho$ be
s-finite measures on $M$. Writing $*$ for convolution of measures and $\mu^{*n}$ for the $n$-th
convolution power of a measure $\mu$, for every natural number $n$ we have
$(\nu * \rho)^{*n} = \nu^{*n} * \rho^{*n}$.

articles.title: Convolution powers of a Dirac measure
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra for which addition $M \times M \to M$ is measurable. For every point $x \in M$ and
every natural number $n$, the $n$-th convolution power of the Dirac measure $\delta_x$ is
$\delta_{nx}$, where $nx$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $x$ (so $0x = 0$).

articles.title: The first convolution power
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra for which addition $M 	imes M 	o M$ is measurable, and let $
u$ be an s-finite
measure on $M$. Then the first convolution power of $
u$ is $
u$ itself.

articles.title: Convolution powers as iterated left convolution
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative
monoid with a σ-algebra for which addition $M \times M \to M$ is measurable, and let $\nu$ be an
s-finite measure on $M$. For every natural number $n$, the $(n+1)$-st convolution power of
$\nu$ equals the measure obtained from $\nu$ by applying the map $\mu \mapsto \nu * \mu$
exactly $n$ times, where $*$ denotes convolution of measures.

articles.title: Convolution powers of a Poisson measure
articles.statement:
For every real rate $r \ge 0$ and every natural
number $n$, the $(n+1)$-st convolution power of the Poisson measure on $\mathbb{N}$ with rate
$r$ is the Poisson measure on $\mathbb{N}$ with rate $(n+1)r$.

articles.title: Recursion for convolution powers
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra and let $
u$ be a measure on $M$. For every natural number $n$, the $(n+1)$-st
convolution power of $
u$ is the convolution of the $n$-th convolution power of $
u$
with $
u$.

articles.title: The zeroth convolution power
articles.statement:
For every measure $\nu$ on an additive commutative monoid
$M$ with a σ-algebra, the zeroth convolution power of $\nu$ is the Dirac measure $\delta_0$ at
the identity element $0$ of $M$.

articles.title: Convolution power of a measure
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
σ-algebra and let $
u$ be a measure on $M$. The $n$-th convolution power $
u^{*n}$ of $
u$ is
defined by recursion on $n$: $
u^{*0} = \delta_0$, the Dirac measure at the identity $0$ of
$M$, and $
u^{*(n+1)} = 
u^{*n} * 
u$, where $*$ denotes convolution of measures.

When addition on $M$ is jointly measurable and $
u$ is the law of a random variable $Y$,
$
u^{*n}$ is the law of the sum of $n$ independent copies of $Y$.

articles.title: Infinite divisibility is closed under convolution
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative
monoid with a measurable structure in which addition is jointly measurable. If $\mu$ and $\eta$
are infinitely divisible measures on $M$, then their convolution $\mu * \eta$ is infinitely
divisible.

For each $n \ge 1$, convolving an $n$-th convolution root of $\mu$ with one of $\eta$ gives an
$n$-th convolution root of $\mu * \eta$.

articles.title: Dirac measures on the real line are infinitely divisible
articles.statement:
For every real number $a$, the
Dirac measure $\delta_a$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is infinitely divisible: for every $n \ge 1$, $\delta_a$
is the $n$-fold convolution power of $\delta_{a/n}$.

articles.title: Infinite divisibility through iterated convolution
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative
monoid with a measurable structure in which addition is jointly measurable. A measure $\mu$ on
$M$ is infinitely divisible if and only if for every natural number $n 
e 0$ there is a
probability measure $
u$ on $M$ such that $\mu = 
u * (
u * (\cdots * (
u * 
u)))$ with $n$
factors $
u$, that is, $\mu$ is obtained from $
u$ by convolving on the left with $
u$ exactly
$n - 1$ times.

articles.title: Poisson distributions are infinitely divisible
articles.statement:
For every real $r \ge 0$, the Poisson
distribution with parameter $r$, as a measure on $\mathbb{N}$, is infinitely divisible: for
every $n \ge 1$ it is the $n$-fold convolution power of the Poisson distribution with parameter
$r/n$.

articles.title: Infinitely divisible measures
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive commutative monoid with a measurable
structure in which addition is jointly measurable. A measure $\mu$ on $M$ is
**infinitely divisible** if for every natural number $n \ge 1$ there is a probability measure
$\nu$ on $M$ whose $n$-fold convolution power $\nu^{*n}$ equals $\mu$.

Equivalently, a random variable $X$ with law $\mu$ can, for every $n \ge 1$, be written in law as
the sum of $n$ i.i.d. copies of some random variable $Y$.

articles.title: Convolution powers of a probability measure are probability measures
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an
additive commutative monoid with a measurable structure. If $\nu$ is a probability measure on
$M$, then for every natural number $n$ its $n$-fold convolution power $\nu^{*n}$ is a probability
measure.

articles.title: Infinitely divisible measures are probability measures
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a measurable structure in which addition is jointly measurable. Every
infinitely divisible measure on $M$ is a probability measure.

The convolution root of order one is the measure itself, and it is a probability measure by
definition.

articles.title: Convolution powers of an s-finite measure are s-finite
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a measurable structure. If $\nu$ is an s-finite measure on $M$, then for
every natural number $n$ its $n$-fold convolution power $\nu^{*n}$ is s-finite.

articles.title: Lévy–Khintchin representation on the real line
articles.statement:
A probability measure $\mu$ on
$\mathbb{R}$ is infinitely divisible, meaning that for every integer $n \ge 1$ there is a
probability measure $\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}$ whose $n$-fold convolution power $\rho^{\ast n}$
equals $\mu$, if and only if there are real numbers $\gamma$ and $\sigma \ge 0$ and a measure
$\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\nu(\{0\}) = 0$ and
$\int \min(1, x^2)\, d\nu(x) < \infty$ such that the characteristic function $\hat\mu$ of $\mu$
satisfies, for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$
\hat\mu(t) = \exp\Big(i \gamma t - \frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2} +
\int_{\mathbb{R}} \big(e^{itx} - 1 - itx \, \mathbf{1}_{\{|x| \le 1\}}(x)\big) \, d\nu(x)\Big).
$$

Proof: The reverse implication uses compound Poisson approximation plus Lévy continuity; the
forward implication uses a distinguished logarithm, canonical measures, and Prokhorov compactness.
For the equivalence, see William Feller, *An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its
Applications*, vol. II, Theorem XVII.2.1.

## Sources

- Ken-iti Sato, *Lévy Processes and Infinitely Divisible Distributions*, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 68, Cambridge University Press (1999), Theorem 8.1, pp. 37–38, ISBN 978-0-521-55302-5. <https://books.google.com/books?vid=ISBN9780521553025&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=Theorem+8.1> Scope: restricts Sato Theorem 8.1 (stated for `ℝ^d`) to `ℝ`, and formalizes only the existence direction (i), omitting uniqueness of the generating triplet (ii). The jump integrand uses the hard truncation `x * 1_{|x| ≤ 1}`, which is an equivalent convention to Sato's `x / (1 + |x|^2)` after reparameterizing the drift `γ`.

articles.title: The combined tail is antitone
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and write
$T(x) = \mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$ for its combined tail at a real number $x$. Then
$T$ is antitone: $T(b) \le T(a)$ whenever $a \le b$.

articles.title: The combined tail of a probability measure is at most two
articles.statement:
For every probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every real number $x$, the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$ satisfies
$\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x)) \le 2$.

articles.title: Combined tail of a measure
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and a real number $x$,
the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is the real number $\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$,
where each of the two measures is converted from $[0, \infty]$ to a real number, an infinite
value becoming $0$.

For a finite measure and $x \ge 0$ this equals $\mu(\{y : |y| > x\})$. At negative thresholds
the two intervals can overlap, so the combined tail is not the mass of the absolute tail.

articles.title: Positive multiples of regularly varying functions
articles.statement:
If $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is
regularly varying with index $\rho$ and $c > 0$, then $x \mapsto c f(x)$ is regularly varying
with index $\rho$.

articles.title: Positive multiples of slowly varying functions
articles.statement:
If $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is slowly
varying and $c > 0$, then $x \mapsto c L(x)$ is slowly varying.

articles.title: Regularly varying functions are eventually positive
articles.statement:
If $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is
regularly varying with some index $\rho$, then $f(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$.

articles.title: Tail balance zero from a vanishing right tail
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on
$\mathbb{R}$. If $\mu((x, \infty)) = 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and the combined tail
$\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$ is positive for all sufficiently large $x$, then $\mu$ has
tail balance $0$.

articles.title: Tail balance
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and $p$ a real number. Write
$R(x) = \mu((x, \infty))$ for the right tail and $T(x) = \mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$
for the combined tail of $\mu$. The measure $\mu$ has tail balance $p$ when $0 \le p \le 1$,
$T(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$, and $R(x) / T(x) \to p$ as $x \to \infty$.

For the law of a random variable $X$ this says $P(X > x) / P(|X| > x) \to p$. Eventual
positivity of $T$ rules out an eventual $0 / 0$.

articles.title: Positive multiples of powers are regularly varying
articles.statement:
For real numbers $c > 0$ and $\rho$, the
function $x \mapsto c x^\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.

articles.title: Powers are regularly varying
articles.statement:
For every real number $\rho$, the function $x \mapsto x^\rho$
on $\mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.

The slowly varying factor can be taken to be the constant function $1$.

articles.title: Regularly varying function
articles.statement:
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying
with index $\rho \in \mathbb{R}$ if there is a slowly varying function
$L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x) = x^{\rho} L(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.

articles.title: Positive constants are slowly varying
articles.statement:
For every real $c > 0$, the constant function
$x \mapsto c$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying.

articles.title: The function $1 + (1 + x)^{-1}$ is slowly varying
articles.statement:
The function
$x \mapsto 1 + (1 + x)^{-1}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying; it tends to the positive limit $1$
at infinity.

articles.title: The constant function one is slowly varying
articles.statement:
The constant function $x \mapsto 1$ on
$\mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying.

articles.title: Slowly varying function
articles.statement:
A function $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is slowly varying (at
infinity) if $L(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and, for every real $c > 0$,
$L(cx) / L(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \infty$.

articles.title: Karamata's integral theorem
articles.statement:
**Karamata's integral theorem** for antitone functions with a ratio limit.
If `W` is antitone, nonnegative, bounded, eventually positive and
`W (c * x) / W x → c ^ ρ` for every `c > 0`, then for `β ≥ 0` and
`β + 1 + ρ > 0`,
`(∫ t in (0)..x, t ^ β * W t) / (x ^ (β + 1) * W x) → 1 / (β + 1 + ρ)`.
The proof substitutes `t = x * u` and applies dominated convergence with
Potter's bound as the dominator.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the left tail
articles.statement:
For every finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the left tail
of $\mu$ is antitone in the threshold: if $a \le b$, then
$\mu((-\infty, -b)) \le \mu((-\infty, -a))$.

articles.title: The left tail is at most the combined tail
articles.statement:
For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and
every real $x$, the left tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$.

articles.title: The left tail of a probability measure is at most one
articles.statement:
For every probability measure $\mu$
on $\mathbb{R}$ and every real $x$, the left tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most $1$.

articles.title: Left tail of a measure
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and a real $x$, the left tail of
$\mu$ at $x$ is the real number $\mu((-\infty, -x))$, where an infinite value is sent to $0$.

For a finite measure it is the mass of the strict left tail $(-\infty, -x)$.

articles.title: Products of regularly varying functions
articles.statement:
If $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly
varying with index $\rho$ and $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is regularly varying with index
$\sigma$, then the pointwise product $fg$ is regularly varying with index $\rho + \sigma$.

articles.title: Products of slowly varying functions
articles.statement:
If $L_1, L_2 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are
slowly varying, then so is their pointwise product $x \mapsto L_1(x) L_2(x)$.

articles.title: Dirac masses have no tail balance
articles.statement:
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and every
$p \in \mathbb{R}$, the Dirac measure $\delta_a$ at $a$ does not have tail balance $p$.

The combined tail of $\delta_a$ vanishes at every threshold $x \ge |a|$, so the eventual
positivity required by tail balance fails.

articles.title: Eventually vanishing combined tail rules out tail balance
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure
on $\mathbb{R}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{R}$. If the combined tail of $\mu$ at $x$ equals $0$ for
all sufficiently large $x$, then $\mu$ does not have tail balance $p$.

articles.title: Regular variation is preserved by eventual equality
articles.statement:
Let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$
and $\rho \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$ and $f(x) = g(x)$ for
all sufficiently large $x$, then $g$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.

articles.title: Slow variation is preserved by eventual equality
articles.statement:
Let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$.
If $f$ is slowly varying and $f(x) = g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$, then $g$ is slowly
varying.

articles.title: Functions with a positive limit are slowly varying
articles.statement:
Let $L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and
$a > 0$. If $L(x) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and $L(x) \to a$ as $x \to \infty$, then
$L$ is slowly varying.

Indeed, for every $c > 0$ the ratio $L(cx) / L(x)$ tends to $a / a = 1$.

articles.title: Potter's bound
articles.statement:
**Potter's bound** for antitone functions with a ratio limit. If `W` is
antitone, bounded, eventually positive and `W (c * x) / W x → c ^ ρ` for
every `c > 0`, then for every `δ > 0` there are `C > 0` and `Y` such that
`W (x * u) / W x ≤ C * u ^ (ρ - δ)` for all `x ≥ Y` and `u ∈ (0, 1]`.
The proof chains the ratio limit at the dyadic scales `1/2` and `2`.

articles.title: Ratio limit of a regularly varying function
articles.statement: A regularly varying function has the expected ratio limit.

articles.title: Generalized inverse of a regularly varying function
articles.statement:
For a regularly
varying function `f` of index `-α` with `α > 0` that is eventually
non-increasing, there exists a sequence `a : ℕ → ℝ` of positive reals such
that `n · f (a n) → 1` as `n → ∞`.

articles.title: The right tail of a finite measure is antitone
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on
$\mathbb{R}$. If $x \le y$, then the right tail of $\mu$ at $y$ is at most the right tail of
$\mu$ at $x$.

articles.title: The right tail is at most the combined tail
articles.statement:
For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and
every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most the combined tail of $\mu$
at $x$.

articles.title: The right tail of a probability measure is at most one
articles.statement:
For every probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is at most
$1$.

articles.title: Right tail of a measure
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
the right tail of $\mu$ at $x$ is the real number $\mu((x, \infty))$ when
$\mu((x, \infty)) < \infty$, and $0$ when $\mu((x, \infty)) = \infty$.

For a finite measure $\mu$ it is the mass of the open half-line $(x, \infty)$.

articles.title: The combined tail of a finite measure vanishes at infinity
articles.statement:
For every finite measure
$\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the combined tail $\mu((x, \infty)) + \mu((-\infty, -x))$, with both
masses taken as real numbers, tends to $0$ as $x \to \infty$.

articles.title: The left tail of a finite measure vanishes at infinity
articles.statement:
For every finite measure $\mu$
on $\mathbb{R}$, the left tail $\mu((-\infty, -x))$, taken as a real number, tends to $0$ as
$x \to \infty$.

articles.title: The right tail of a finite measure vanishes at infinity
articles.statement:
For every finite measure $\mu$
on $\mathbb{R}$, the right tail $\mu((x, \infty))$, taken as a real number, tends to $0$ as
$x \to \infty$.

articles.title: Convolution powers of a Gaussian are Gaussian
articles.statement:
The convolution power of a Gaussian is Gaussian with the mean and the
variance multiplied by `n`: the law of the sum of `n` i.i.d.
`N(μ, v)` variables is `N(nμ, nv)`.

articles.title: Dirac measure lies in its own domain of attraction
articles.statement:
The Dirac measure is in its own domain of attraction: with
`a n = 1` and `b n = (n - 1) a`, the normalized law of `S_n` is
`δ_a` for every `n`.

articles.title: Domain of attraction of a given index
articles.statement:
Indexed attraction requires a nondegenerate stable limit of that index.
The general normalized weak-limit relation alone does not assign an index.

articles.title: Stable law lies in its own domain of attraction
articles.statement:
A stable law is a normalized weak limit of its own convolution powers.
The positive-n inverse affine identity is exact; order zero uses normalizer one.

articles.title: Domain of attraction
articles.statement:
The probability measure `μ` is *in the domain of attraction* of `G`
if there exist sequences of normalizing constants `a n > 0` and
centering constants `b n` such that the law of `(S_n - b n) / a n`
(where `S_n` has law `μ^{*n}`) converges weakly to `G`, expressed here
as integration against arbitrary bounded continuous functions.

articles.title: Gaussian with nonzero variance is nondegenerate
articles.statement:
A Gaussian with nonzero variance is nondegenerate: it gives mass `0`
to every singleton, while `δ_a` gives mass `1` to `{a}`.

articles.title: Nondegenerate measure on the real line
articles.statement:
A measure `μ` on `ℝ` is *nondegenerate* if it is not a point mass
`δ_a` for any `a`.

articles.title: Dirac measures are stable of every index
articles.statement:
A Dirac law satisfies the fixed-dilation identity at every admissible index.
These are degenerate rescaling identities, with centering `na - n^(1/α)a`.

articles.title: Gaussian measures are stable of index 2
articles.statement:
Every real Gaussian measure is stable of index `2`: the sum of `n`
i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` variables is `N(nμ, nv)`, which is the pushforward of
`N(μ, v)` under `x ↦ √n · x + (n - √n) μ`.

articles.title: Stable distribution of a given index
articles.statement:
Indexed stability fixes the positive-n dilation to `n^(1/α)` and allows
arbitrary centering. Degenerate Dirac identities may satisfy several indices.

articles.title: Dirac measure is degenerate
articles.statement: A Dirac measure is degenerate, by definition.

articles.title: Nondegenerate Gaussian is not stable of index 1
articles.statement:
A nondegenerate Gaussian cannot have fixed stability index one. The n=4
convolution variance is `4v`, while every such affine dilation has variance `16v`.

articles.title: Antitone bounded functions are interval integrable
articles.statement: Antitone bounded functions are interval-integrable.

articles.title: Layer-cake formula for the first moment
articles.statement:
Layer-cake formula for the first moment on `(0, a]`: the integral of `y`
over `(0, a]` equals the integral of the right tail minus the endpoint
correction.

articles.title: Layer-cake formula for the truncated second moment
articles.statement:
Layer-cake formula for the truncated second moment, in terms of the upper
tail `tailGe`. The term `x ^ 2 * tailGt μ x` removes the contribution
from points with `|y| > x`, which lie outside the closed truncation interval.

articles.title: Non-strict absolute tail as combined tail plus endpoint atoms
articles.statement: The non-strict absolute tail adds both endpoint atoms to the canonical strict tail.

articles.title: Upper tail is asymptotic to the combined tail
articles.statement: The upper tail is asymptotically the combined tail.

articles.title: Closed upper tail of a measure
articles.statement: The upper tail `(μ {y | s ≤ |y|}).toReal`.

articles.title: Strict absolute tail equals the combined tail
articles.statement: At nonnegative thresholds the strict absolute tail is the canonical combined tail.

articles.title: Lower tail is asymptotic to the combined tail
articles.statement: The lower tail is asymptotically the combined tail.

articles.title: Strict upper tail of a measure
articles.statement: The lower tail `(μ {y | s < |y|}).toReal`.

articles.title: Corrected regularly-varying tail integral
articles.statement:
For a probability measure `μ`
on `ℝ` with regularly varying combined tail of index `-α`, `0 < α < 1`, and
tail balance `p`, the first-moment tail integral satisfies
`(∫ y in Ioc 0 (c * x), y ∂μ) / (x * combinedTail μ x) → p * α * c ^ (1 - α) / (1 - α)`.

articles.title: Truncated second moment asymptotic for regularly varying tails
articles.statement:
The corrected truncated-second-moment asymptotic: for a probability measure
on `ℝ` with regularly varying combined tail of index `-α`, `0 < α < 2`, the
ratio `(∫ y in Icc (-x) x, y ^ 2 ∂μ) / (x ^ 2 * combinedTail μ x)` tends to
`α / (2 - α)`.

Correction: `v1/Atlas/TheoryOfProbability/code/RegularVariation.lean` states
this with the constant `2 / (2 - α)`, which is wrong; the Pareto tail gives
`α / (2 - α)` (see the test file).

articles.title: Cramér rate function agrees with the extended conjugate
articles.statement: Under probability the conversion preserves the entire nonnegative conjugate.

articles.title: Cramér rate function of a constant law
articles.statement:
Constant laws retain zero at their center and top elsewhere,
including dimension zero.

articles.title: Convexity of the Cramér rate function
articles.statement: Convexity is transported from the actual canonical conjugate epigraph.

articles.title: Cramér rate function as a supremum when all moments are integrable
articles.statement: With all moments integrable, the canonical real expression represents every direction.

articles.title: Cramér rate function as a supremum
articles.statement: Supporting terms are obtained from the canonical conjugate, not a second transform.

articles.title: Cramér rate function as a real supremum under finite moments
articles.statement:
Physical finite-domain agreement: bounded real supporting values and integrable moments.
The finiteness premise belongs to this corollary, not the corrected definitions.

articles.title: Cramér rate function vanishes at the mean
articles.statement: The original integrable-vector and moment premises imply zero rate at the mean.

articles.title: Cramér rate function
articles.statement: The canonical extended conjugate, converted with top preserved.

articles.title: Fixed-direction Chernoff bound, rate form
articles.statement:
For a fixed `ξ` and
`s = inf_{x ∈ F} (⟪ξ, x⟫ - Λ(ξ))`, the `n`-th root of `μₙ(F)` has limsup at most
`exp(-s)`. Assume measurable i.i.d. coordinates under a probability measure,
measurable `F`, exponential integrability at `ξ`, and a bounded-below rate image
on `F`, with its real-valued `sInf` used for `s`.
Optimizing over admissible `ξ` gives the supremum of these fixed-direction rates;
the Legendre-rate Cramér upper bound requires further arguments.

articles.title: Fixed-direction Chernoff bound
articles.statement:
For i.i.d. random vectors in `ℝᵈ`,
the law `μₙ` of the empirical mean satisfies `μₙ(F) ≤ exp(-n * a)` whenever
`a` lower-bounds `⟪ξ, ·⟫ - Λ(ξ)` on measurable `F`. Assume a probability measure,
measurable coordinates and integrability of `exp ⟪ξ, X₀⟫` at this direction.

articles.title: Law of the empirical mean
articles.statement:
**Law of the empirical mean** `Aₙ = (1/n) ∑_{i<n} Xᵢ` for an `ℝᵈ`-valued sample.

Pushforward of `μ` under the map `ω ↦ (1/n) ∑_{i<n} Xᵢ(ω)`. Ported verbatim
from v1.

articles.title: Extended log moment of a constant vector
articles.statement: Extended log moments of constant vectors retain the exact inner product.

articles.title: Extended log moment agrees with the real one at integrable directions
articles.statement: Finite directions compose with the existing fixed-direction Chernoff API.

articles.title: Extended log moment is infinite at non-integrable directions
articles.statement: Measurability separates infinite moments from nonmeasurable totalized integrals.

articles.title: Extended log moment vanishes at zero
articles.statement: The zero direction has extended log moment zero under probability.

articles.title: Extended log moment generating function of a random vector
articles.statement: Extended log moment: nonintegrable measurable exponential moments give `⊤`.

articles.title: Cramér rate function is a convex rate function
articles.statement: The existing LDP convex-rate structure is available without global MGF finiteness.

articles.title: Fenchel–Young lower bound at integrable directions
articles.statement: The original real supporting term remains valid at integrable directions.

articles.title: Extended Fenchel–Young inequality for the Cramér rate function
articles.statement: Extended Fenchel–Young, valid for every measure and every direction.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the Legendre transform of the log moment
articles.statement: Probability makes the canonical conjugate nonnegative via the zero direction.

articles.title: Log moment generating function of a constant vector
articles.statement: The canonical real log moment of a constant vector.

articles.title: Log moment generating function vanishes at zero
articles.statement: The canonical real log moment is zero at the zero direction.

articles.title: Real-valued log-MGF expression
articles.statement:
**Real-valued log-MGF expression** `Λ(t) = log E[exp ⟪t, X⟫]`.

For a random vector `X : Ω → ℝᵈ`, this returns the logarithm of the moment
generating function evaluated at the dual variable `t ∈ ℝᵈ`, using the Euclidean
inner product. Under a probability measure it represents the cumulant generating
function at directions where the exponential is integrable. For a nonintegrable
exponential, the Bochner integral is `0` and `Real.log 0 = 0`, so this definition
returns `0`. The bounds below explicitly require exponential integrability.
Ported from v1.

articles.title: Lower semicontinuity of the Cramér rate function
articles.statement: Converted canonical conjugates are lower semicontinuous for arbitrary input data.

articles.title: Chernoff bound for the empirical mean of real-valued i.i.d. variables
articles.statement:
**Chernoff bound for the empirical mean of real-valued i.i.d. variables**,
in event form: if on the event `E` the empirical mean
`(1/n) ∑_{i<n} Xᵢ` satisfies the threshold inequality
`a ≤ t * (empirical mean) - log (mgf of X₁ at t)`, then
`μ(E) ≤ exp(-n * a)`.

Assume a probability measure, measurable independent identically distributed
coordinates, and integrability of `exp (t * X₀)`.

This is the one-dimensional core of the Cramér upper bound. The proof splits
on the sign of `t`: for `t > 0` it applies Mathlib's upper-tail Chernoff bound
to the sum `Sₙ`, and for `t < 0` the lower-tail Chernoff bound; in both cases
the exponential moment of the sum factors as `(mgf of X₁ at t)^n` by
independence and identical distribution.

articles.title: Large deviation bounds for arbitrary sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space with a
$\sigma$-algebra in which every open set is measurable, and let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be
measures on $X$ satisfying the large deviation principle with rate function
$I : X \to [0, \infty]$. Then for every set $\Gamma \subseteq X$, not necessarily measurable (for
non-measurable $\Gamma$, $\mu_n(\Gamma)$ is its outer measure), with interior $\Gamma^\circ$ and
closure $\overline{\Gamma}$, both
