$$-\inf_{x \in \Gamma^\circ} I(x) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(\Gamma)$$

and

$$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(\Gamma) \le -\inf_{x \in \overline{\Gamma}} I(x)$$

hold, computed in the extended reals with $\log 0 = -\infty$. In particular the bounds hold for
every Borel set $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Large deviation lower bound for arbitrary sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space with a
$\sigma$-algebra in which every open set is measurable, and let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be
measures on $X$ satisfying the large deviation principle with rate function
$I : X \to [0, \infty]$. Then for every set $\Gamma \subseteq X$, not necessarily measurable (for
non-measurable $\Gamma$, $\mu_n(\Gamma)$ is its outer measure), with interior $\Gamma^\circ$,

$$-\inf_{x \in \Gamma^\circ} I(x) \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(\Gamma),$$

computed in the extended reals with $\log 0 = -\infty$.

articles.title: Large deviation upper bound for arbitrary sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space with a
$\sigma$-algebra in which every open set is measurable, and let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be
measures on $X$ satisfying the large deviation principle with rate function
$I : X \to [0, \infty]$. Then for every set $\Gamma \subseteq X$, not necessarily measurable (for
non-measurable $\Gamma$, $\mu_n(\Gamma)$ is its outer measure), with closure $\overline{\Gamma}$,

$$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(\Gamma) \le -\inf_{x \in \overline{\Gamma}} I(x),$$

computed in the extended reals with $\log 0 = -\infty$.

articles.title: Log-scaled Dirac mass of a set avoiding the center
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a measurable space in which
every singleton is measurable, let $\delta_{x_0}$ be the Dirac measure at a point $x_0 \in X$, and
let $s \subseteq X$ be a set with $x_0 \notin s$. Then for every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$\frac{1}{n} \log \delta_{x_0}(s) = -\infty$ in the extended reals, with $\log 0 = -\infty$.

articles.title: Log-scaled Dirac mass of a set containing the center
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a measurable space, let
$\delta_{x_0}$ be the Dirac measure at a point $x_0 \in X$, and let $s \subseteq X$ be a set with
$x_0 \in s$. Then $\frac{1}{n} \log \delta_{x_0}(s) = 0$ in the extended reals for every natural
number $n$, the factor $1/n$ being read as $0$ when $n = 0$.

articles.title: The Dirac rate function is infinite away from its center
articles.statement:
For points $x \ne x_0$ of a set
$X$, the Dirac rate function at $x_0$ takes the value $\infty$ at $x$.

articles.title: The Dirac rate function vanishes at its center
articles.statement:
For every point $x_0$ of a set $X$, the
Dirac rate function at $x_0$ takes the value $0$ at $x_0$.

articles.title: Rate function of a Dirac mass
articles.statement:
For a point $x_0$ of a set $X$, the Dirac rate function
at $x_0$ is the function $X \to [0, \infty]$ that equals $0$ at $x_0$ and $\infty$ at every other
point.

articles.title: Infimum of the Dirac rate function over a set containing the center
articles.statement:
For a point $x_0$ of
a set $X$ and a subset $s \subseteq X$ with $x_0 \in s$, the infimum over $x \in s$ of the Dirac
rate function at $x_0$, evaluated at $x$, is $0$.

articles.title: Infimum of the Dirac rate function over a set avoiding the center
articles.statement:
For a point $x_0$ of a
set $X$ and a subset $s \subseteq X$ with $x_0 \notin s$, the infimum over $x \in s$ of the Dirac
rate function at $x_0$, evaluated at $x$, is $\infty$.

articles.title: Convex rate function
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real vector space carrying a topology (no compatibility
between the topology and the linear structure is assumed). A function $I : X \to [0, \infty]$ is a
convex rate function if it is a rate function and $I(ax + by) \le a I(x) + b I(y)$ for all
$x, y \in X$ and all real numbers $a, b \ge 0$ with $a + b = 1$.

articles.title: The absolute value is a good rate function
articles.statement:
The function $x \mapsto |x|$, viewed as a map
$\mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty]$, is a good rate function on $\mathbb{R}$.

It is continuous, hence lower semicontinuous, and its sub-level sets at finite levels are closed
intervals (or the singleton $\{0\}$ for a negative level), hence compact.

articles.title: Good rate function
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space. A function $I : X \to [0, \infty]$ is a
good rate function if it is a rate function and, for every real number $a \ge 0$, the sub-level
set $\{x \in X : I(x) \le a\}$ is compact.

Compactness is required only at finite levels: the sub-level set at level $\infty$ is all of $X$,
so requiring it as well would force $X$ itself to be compact.

articles.title: Good rate functions are rate functions
articles.statement:
Every good rate function on a topological space
is a rate function.

articles.title: Convex rate functions are rate functions
articles.statement:
Every convex rate function on a real vector space
with a topology is a rate function.

articles.title: Rate function
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space. A rate function on $X$ is a lower
semicontinuous function $I : X \to [0, \infty]$.

This is the basic regularity hypothesis used in the formulation of a large deviation principle.

articles.title: Large deviation principle for a Dirac mass
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a $T_1$ topological space equipped
with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and let $x_0 \in X$. The constant sequence of measures
$\mu_n = \delta_{x_0}$ satisfies the large deviation principle with the Dirac rate function of
$x_0$, which is $0$ at $x_0$ and $\infty$ elsewhere.

Indeed, the mass $1$ stays at $x_0$, so the exponential cost of a set is $0$ if it contains $x_0$
and $\infty$ otherwise.

articles.title: Large deviation principle from bounds on measurable sets
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space
with a $\sigma$-algebra containing every open set, let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence
of measures on $X$, and let $I$ be a rate function on $X$. Suppose that every measurable set
$\Gamma \subseteq X$, with interior $\Gamma^\circ$ and closure $\overline{\Gamma}$, satisfies

$$\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(\Gamma) \ge -\inf_{x \in \Gamma^\circ} I(x)$$

and

$$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(\Gamma) \le -\inf_{x \in \overline{\Gamma}} I(x),$$

where $\log 0 = -\infty$, an infimum over the empty set is $\infty$, and the limits are taken in
the extended reals. Then $(\mu_n)$ satisfies the large deviation principle with rate function $I$.

Open and closed sets are measurable and equal to their interior and closure respectively, so the
hypothesis contains the open-set and closed-set bounds. On a Borel space this is the textbook
Borel-set converse.

articles.title: Large deviation principle for a sequence of measures
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space with
a $\sigma$-algebra containing every open set, let $(\mu_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of
measures on $X$, and let $I : X \to [0, \infty]$. The sequence $(\mu_n)$ satisfies the large
deviation principle with rate function $I$ and speed $n$ if $I$ is a rate function, every open
set $U \subseteq X$ satisfies

$$\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(U) \ge -\inf_{x \in U} I(x),$$

and every closed set $F \subseteq X$ satisfies

$$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \mu_n(F) \le -\inf_{x \in F} I(x).$$

Here $\log 0 = -\infty$, an infimum over the empty set is $\infty$, and the limits are taken in
the extended reals.

articles.title: The epigraph of the Legendre transform is convex
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. Then the
set $\{(x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R} : \Lambda^*(x) \le t\}$ is convex.

articles.title: A finite Legendre transform is convex
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. If
$\Lambda^*(x)$ is a real number for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, then $\Lambda^*$, viewed as a
function $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, is convex on $\mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Fenchel–Young inequality for the Legendre transform
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. For all
$x, l \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we have $\langle l, x \rangle - \Lambda(l) \le \Lambda^*(x)$ in
$[-\infty, \infty]$.

articles.title: The Legendre transform is order-reversing
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2 : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$, with Legendre transforms
$\Lambda_1^*$ and $\Lambda_2^*$. If $\Lambda_1(y) \le \Lambda_2(y)$ for every
$y \in \mathbb{R}^d$, then $\Lambda_2^*(x) \le \Lambda_1^*(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Supremum formula for the Legendre transform
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$. For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the Legendre
transform $\Lambda^*$ of $\Lambda$ satisfies
$\Lambda^*(x) = \sup_{l \in \mathbb{R}^d} \big(\langle l, x \rangle - \Lambda(l)\big)$.

articles.title: The double Legendre transform lies below the function
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$ be a function that never takes the value
$-\infty$, with Legendre transform $\Lambda^*$. Then the Legendre transform $\Lambda^{**}$ of
$\Lambda^*$ satisfies $\Lambda^{**}(x) \le \Lambda(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

The proof bounds $\Lambda^{**}$ by the Fenchel biconjugate of $\Lambda$.

articles.title: The half squared norm is its own Legendre transform
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$q : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$ be $q(y) = \|y\|^2 / 2$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the
Euclidean norm. Its Legendre transform $q^*$ satisfies $q^*(x) = \|x\|^2 / 2$ for every
$x \in \mathbb{R}^d$; in particular every value of $q^*$ is finite.

articles.title: Legendre transform of the zero function away from the origin
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$
and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$ be the zero function. Its Legendre
transform $\Lambda^*$ satisfies $\Lambda^*(x) = +\infty$ for every nonzero $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: Legendre transform of the zero function at the origin
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$ be the zero function. Its Legendre transform
$\Lambda^*$ satisfies $\Lambda^*(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Legendre transform
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, give $\mathbb{R}^d$ its standard inner product,
and let $\Lambda : \mathbb{R}^d \to [-\infty, \infty]$. The Legendre transform of $\Lambda$ at
$x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the Fenchel conjugate of $\Lambda$ at the linear functional
$y \mapsto \langle x, y \rangle$, that is, the extended real number
$\Lambda^*(x) = \sup_{y \in \mathbb{R}^d} \big(\langle x, y \rangle - \Lambda(y)\big)$.

articles.title: Kolmogorov's maximal inequality for finitely-valued variables
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite
nonempty set and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For each $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ let $p_i$ be a probability
vector on $\alpha$, so $p_i(a) \ge 0$ and $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p_i(a) = 1$, and let
$X_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p_i(a) X_i(a) = 0$. Give each
$\omega \in \alpha^n$ the weight $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} p_i(\omega_i)$, so that the coordinates are
independent with laws $p_i$. Then for every real $\lambda > 0$, the total weight of the $\omega$
for which $\bigl|\sum_{j \le i} X_j(\omega_j)\bigr| \ge \lambda$ for some $i$ is at most
$\lambda^{-2} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sum_{a \in \alpha} p_i(a) X_i(a)^2$.

## Sources

- A. Kolmogoroff, "Über die Summen durch den Zufall bestimmter unabhängiger Größen", Math. Ann. 99 (1928), 309–319, DOI 10.1007/BF01459098.

articles.title: Mean bound for a truncated random variable
articles.statement: The absolute mean of canonical truncation is at most `|A|`.

articles.title: Truncation is bounded by the absolute cutoff
articles.statement: A canonical truncation is bounded by the absolute value of any cutoff.

articles.title: Truncation is bounded by a nonnegative cutoff
articles.statement: A canonical truncation is bounded by a nonnegative cutoff in absolute value.

articles.title: Truncations eventually agree with the variables
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be real-valued
functions on a probability space $(\Omega, P)$, let $A$ be a real number, and let
$Y_n = X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n| \le A\}}$ be the truncation of $X_n$ at $A$. If
$\sum_n P(|X_n| > A) < \infty$, then for almost every $\omega$ we have $X_n(\omega) = Y_n(\omega)$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

This follows from the first Borel–Cantelli lemma.

articles.title: Almost sure convergence of centered truncated sums
articles.statement:
If the truncated variables have summable variances, then almost surely
the partial sums of the centered truncations converge:
`∑ (Yᵢ - E[Yᵢ])` converges a.s.

articles.title: Eventually equal series inherit almost-everywhere convergence
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on
$\Omega$ and let $f_n, g_n : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ ($n \ge 0$) be functions such that for
$\mu$-almost every $\omega$ we have $f_n(\omega) = g_n(\omega)$ for all sufficiently large $n$. If
there is a function $S : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\sum_{i < n} f_i(\omega) \to S(\omega)$ as
$n \to \infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$, then there is a function $T : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$
with $\sum_{i < n} g_i(\omega) \to T(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$.

articles.title: Almost-sure convergence of L¹-bounded sums of independent centered variables
articles.statement:
Let
$Z_0, Z_1, \dots$ be independent integrable real random variables on a probability space with
$E[Z_n] = 0$ for every $n$, and let $S_n = \sum_{k \le n} Z_k$. If there is a constant $R \ge 0$
with $E|S_n| \le R$ for every $n$, then $S_n$ converges almost surely to a finite limit.

This is a key step toward the Kolmogorov three-series theorem: $(S_n)$ is a martingale for the
natural filtration, so the $L^1$-bounded martingale convergence theorem applies.

articles.title: Truncated sums converge almost surely
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be independent real random
variables on a probability space $(\Omega, P)$, let $A > 0$, and let
$Y_n = X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n| \le A\}}$ be the truncation of $X_n$ at $A$. If the series
$\sum_n E[Y_n]$ converges absolutely and $\sum_n \operatorname{Var}(Y_n) < \infty$, then there is
a function $S : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\sum_{i < n} Y_i(\omega) \to S(\omega)$ as
$n \to \infty$ for almost every $\omega$.

This combines the convergence of the centered truncated sums with the convergence of the series
of means.

articles.title: Truncation preserves almost-sure limits of bounded partial sums
articles.statement:
A uniformly bounded family keeps its almost-sure partial-sum limit under
canonical truncation, on the same measure.

articles.title: $L^1$ norm bounded by the square root of the second moment
articles.statement:
If `∫ ‖f‖² dμ ≤ C` for an `L²` function on a probability space, then
`‖f‖₁ ≤ √C`.

articles.title: Truncation preserves independence
articles.statement: Truncation preserves independence.

articles.title: Integrability of truncated random variables
articles.statement: Canonical truncation is integrable on a finite measure space.

articles.title: Expectation of a product of independent functions factors
articles.statement:
If `f` and `g` are independent, the expectation of a product of functions of
`f` and `g` factors.

articles.title: Fourth-moment bound for sums of bounded independent variables
articles.statement:
Fourth-moment induction for sums of independent centered bounded random
variables: `E[S⁴] ≤ 3 E[S²]² + B² E[S²]`, together with the variance-of-sum
identity and `E[S] = 0`.

articles.title: Kolmogorov's three-series theorem (sufficiency direction)
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be
independent real random variables on a probability space $(\Omega, P)$, fix $A > 0$, and write
$Y_n = X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n| \le A\}}$ for the truncations. If
$\sum_n P(|X_n| > A) < \infty$, the series $\sum_n E[Y_n]$ converges absolutely, and
$\sum_n \operatorname{Var}(Y_n) < \infty$, then there is a function $S : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$
with $\sum_{i < n} X_i(\omega) \to S(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$ for almost every $\omega$; that
is, $\sum_n X_n$ converges almost surely.

The classical theorem only requires the series $\sum_n E[Y_n]$ to converge; here it must converge
absolutely.

articles.title: Measurability of a truncated random variable
articles.statement: Canonical truncation needs measurability only of the selected variable.

articles.title: Truncation preserves measurability
articles.statement: The canonical truncation of a measurable random variable is measurable.

articles.title: Measurability of scalar truncation
articles.statement: The scalar specialization of canonical truncation is measurable.

articles.title: Truncated random variables lie in every Lp space
articles.statement: Canonical truncation is in every `Lᵖ` on a finite measure space.

articles.title: Divergent tail probabilities prevent almost-sure convergence of partial sums
articles.statement:
Let
$(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of independent measurable real random variables on a probability
space $(\Omega, \mu)$, and let $A > 0$. If $\sum_n \mu(\{\omega : |X_n(\omega)| > A\}) = \infty$,
then there is no function $S : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$,
the partial sums $\sum_{i < n} X_i(\omega)$ converge to $S(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Pair of coordinates from two independent copies
articles.statement: The pair of the `n`-th coordinates of two independent copies.

articles.title: The `Summable`-means necessity claim in v1 is false
articles.statement:
The
deterministic sequence `X k ω = (-1)^k / (k + 1)` on the one-point
probability space `(Unit, dirac ())` has converging partial sums, is
constant (hence measurable and independent), agrees with its truncations
at `A = 1`, and has all variances `0` — yet its means
`∫ truncatedRV X 1 k = (-1)^k / (k + 1)` are not `Summable`, since
`Summable.abs` would force summability of the harmonic series. This is
why the ported necessity theorem above states convergence of the mean
partial sums rather than `Summable` of the means. The statement records
convergence of both the original and the truncated partial sums: the
truncated form is the hypothesis of v1's (false) unproved lemma, and the original
form is what the corrected assembly theorem needs.

articles.title: Kolmogorov three-series theorem, necessity, first series
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a
sequence of independent measurable real random variables on a probability space
$(\Omega, \mu)$ whose partial sums converge almost surely: there is a function
$S : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\sum_{i < n} X_i(\omega) \to S(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$
for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$. Then for every $A > 0$ the tail probabilities are summable:
$\sum_n \mu(\{\omega : |X_n(\omega)| > A\}) < \infty$.

Proof: argue by contradiction via the second Borel–Cantelli lemma. If the tail probabilities
summed to $\infty$, the events $\{|X_n| > A\}$ would occur infinitely often with probability
one; but almost-sure convergence of the partial sums forces $X_n \to 0$ almost surely, hence
eventually $|X_n| \le A$.

articles.title: Three-series necessity, second half of the variance step
articles.statement:
For a
uniformly bounded independent sequence whose partial sums converge almost
surely, the variances are summable. Proved by symmetrization: the
symmetrized sums are centered, so Paley–Zygmund gives a uniform lower
bound on block-tail probabilities, contradicting convergence in
measure unless the variances are summable.

articles.title: Symmetrized random variable
articles.statement: The symmetrized variable `Z n (ω, ω') = Y n ω - Y n ω'`.

articles.title: Mean step of three-series necessity
articles.statement:
For a uniformly bounded
independent sequence with summable variances whose partial sums converge
almost surely, the partial sums of the means converge (to some limit).
Proved by centering and applying the canonical centered-sum convergence
theorem with an `L¹` bound from the total variance. The mean partial sums
are the difference of the two convergent series at a single sample point.

articles.title: Kolmogorov three-series necessity, series (2)–(3)
articles.statement:
If the partial
sums of an independent sequence `Xₙ` converge almost surely, then for
every `A > 0` the truncations `Yₙ = Xₙ · 1_{|Xₙ| ≤ A}` have convergent
mean partial sums and summable variances. This is the corrected form of
v1's `summable_mean_and_variance_of_ae_tendsto_ax`: v1 claimed the means
themselves are `Summable`, which is false (see
`summable_mean_necessity_false`); only convergence of the mean partial
sums holds. Series (1) uses the public theorem from
`ThreeSeriesTailProb`.

articles.title: Formula for the truncated random variable
articles.statement: The canonical truncation is the identity inside the cutoff and zero outside it.

articles.title: Canonical truncation factors through scalar truncation
articles.statement: Canonical truncation factors through its scalar specialization.

articles.title: Truncation fixes values within the cutoff
articles.statement: Truncation fixes points inside or on the cutoff.

articles.title: Truncation leaves a family bounded by the cutoff unchanged
articles.statement: A family bounded by the cutoff is unchanged by canonical truncation.

articles.title: Truncation vanishes outside the closed band
articles.statement: Truncation of a value strictly outside the closed band is zero.

articles.title: Canonical truncation preserves nonnegativity
articles.statement: Canonical truncation preserves nonnegativity.

articles.title: Truncation of a random variable
articles.statement:
For a sequence $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of real-valued functions
on $\Omega$, a threshold $A \in \mathbb{R}$ and an index $n$, the truncation of $X_n$ at $A$ is
$Y_n = X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n| \le A\}}$, that is, $Y_n(\omega) = X_n(\omega)$ when
$|X_n(\omega)| \le A$ and $Y_n(\omega) = 0$ otherwise.

This is the key construction in the Kolmogorov three-series theorem.

articles.title: Scalar truncation fixes values within the cutoff
articles.statement: Scalar truncation fixes values inside or on the cutoff.

articles.title: Scalar truncation vanishes beyond the cutoff
articles.statement: Scalar truncation kills values strictly outside the cutoff.

articles.title: Scalar truncation preserves nonnegativity
articles.statement: Scalar truncation preserves nonnegativity.

articles.title: Scalar truncation function
articles.statement: Scalar truncation is canonical truncation of the identity sequence.

articles.title: Variance bound for a truncated random variable
articles.statement: The variance of canonical truncation is at most `A²`.

articles.title: Law of the iterated logarithm, square-integrable form
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be independent,
identically distributed, measurable real random variables on a probability space with
$\mathbb{E}[X_0^2] < \infty$, $\mathbb{E}[X_0] = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_0) = 1$, and let
$S_n = X_0 + \dots + X_{n-1}$. Then almost surely
$\limsup_{n \to \infty} S_n / \sqrt{2 n \log \log n} = 1$ and
$\liminf_{n \to \infty} S_n / \sqrt{2 n \log \log n} = -1$.

Integrability of $X_0$ is not assumed separately, since it follows from square integrability on a
probability space.

articles.title: Law of the iterated logarithm
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be independent, identically distributed,
measurable real random variables on a probability space such that $X_0$ is integrable,
$\mathbb{E}[X_0^2] < \infty$, $\mathbb{E}[X_0] = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_0) = 1$, and let
$S_n = X_0 + \dots + X_{n-1}$. Then almost surely
$\limsup_{n \to \infty} S_n / \sqrt{2 n \log \log n} = 1$ and
$\liminf_{n \to \infty} S_n / \sqrt{2 n \log \log n} = -1$.

Proof: Hartman–Wintner truncation and exponential maximal bounds give the upper half; a CLT block
argument and the second Borel–Cantelli lemma give the lower half.

## Sources

- A. Y. Khinchin 1924, A. N. Kolmogorov 1929, P. Hartman and A. Wintner, On the law of the iterated logarithm, Amer. J. Math. 63 (1941) 169–176; textbook in Durrett, Probability Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Foundations of Modern Probability (Hartman-Wintner LIL). Lean i.i.d. mean-zero variance-one normalized `√(2 n log log n)` form.

articles.title: Almost sure convergence from shrinking tail bounds
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\Omega$, let $f_k : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $a \in \mathbb{R}$.
Suppose that for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$, we have
$|f_k(\omega) - a| < 1/(m+1)$ for all sufficiently large $k$. Then for $\mu$-almost every
$\omega$, $f_k(\omega) \to a$ as $k \to \infty$.

articles.title: Chebyshev bound along the subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\Omega$, let
$A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$ be pairwise independent measurable sets, let
$S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$, and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \infty$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$
let $\varphi(k)$ be the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the probability of the set of $\omega$ with
$|S_{\varphi(k)}(\omega)/\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] - 1| \ge \varepsilon$ is at most
$1/(\varepsilon^2 (k+1)^2)$.

These bounds are summable in $k$, which gives almost sure convergence along the subsequence.

articles.title: The σ-algebra generated by an indicator function
articles.statement:
For a set $s \subseteq \Omega$, the
σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by the indicator function $1_s : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ (the
preimages of Borel sets of $\mathbb{R}$) is contained in the σ-algebra generated by $s$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the expected partial sums
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\Omega$,
let $A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$ be measurable sets and let $S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$. Then
$n \mapsto \mathbb{E}[S_n]$ is nondecreasing.

This holds because $\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \sum_{i\lt n} \mu(A_i)$ and every summand is nonnegative.

articles.title: The expected partial sums along the subsequence are positive
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability
measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$, let $S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$, and
suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \infty$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\varphi(k)$ be the least $n$
with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$. Then $\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] > 0$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$.

Indeed $\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] \ge (k+1)^2 > 0$.

articles.title: Upper bound for the expected partial sums along the subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability
measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$ be measurable sets, let
$S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$, and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \infty$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$
let $\varphi(k)$ be the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$. Then
$\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] < (k+1)^2 + 1$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

This holds because $\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)-1}] < (k+1)^2$ and the expectation grows by at most
one per step.

articles.title: The expected partial sums grow by at most one per step
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$ be measurable sets and let
$S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[S_{n+1}] - \mathbb{E}[S_n] \le 1$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Indeed the difference equals $\mu(A_n) \le 1$.

articles.title: Ratios of consecutive subsequence expectations tend to one
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability
measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$ be measurable sets, let
$S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$, and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \infty$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$
let $\varphi(k)$ be the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$. Then
$\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k+1)}] / \mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] \to 1$ as $k \to \infty$.

This slow growth lets the proof of the pairwise-independent strong law pass from the subsequence
to the full sequence.

articles.title: Divergent total probability makes the expected partial sums diverge
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
probability measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots \subseteq \Omega$ be measurable sets with
$\sum_n \mu(A_n) = \infty$, and let $S_n = \sum_{i\lt n} 1_{A_i}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \infty$
as $n \to \infty$.

Here $\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \sum_{i\lt n} \mu(A_i)$.

articles.title: Bracketing by a strictly increasing sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be
strictly increasing and let $n \ge \varphi(0)$. Then there is $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$\varphi(k) \le n < \varphi(k+1)$.

This is used to sandwich a general index $n$ between two consecutive subsequence indices.

articles.title: Independent events have independent indicators
articles.statement:
If two sets $s$ and $t$ are independent
with respect to a probability measure $\mu$, then their real-valued indicator functions $1_s$ and
$1_t$ are independent random variables with respect to $\mu$.

articles.title: The square of an indicator is itself
articles.statement:
For every set $s \subseteq \Omega$, the real-valued
indicator function $1_s$ satisfies $1_s^2 = 1_s$.

articles.title: Expectation of a sum of indicators
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\Omega$ and let
$A_0, A_1, \dots$ be measurable sets. For every $n$, the partial sum
$S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$ has expectation $E[S_n] = \sum_{i < n} \mu(A_i)$.

articles.title: Indicators are square-integrable
articles.statement:
If $\mu$ is a probability measure and $s$ is a
measurable set, then the real-valued indicator function $1_s$ lies in $L^2(\mu)$.

articles.title: Partial sums of indicators are square-integrable
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure and
let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be measurable sets. For every $n$, the partial sum
$S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$ lies in $L^2(\mu)$.

articles.title: Pairwise-independent strong law for indicator sums
articles.statement:
Let $A_1, A_2, \dots$ be pairwise
independent events in a probability space with $\sum_n P(A_n) = \infty$, and write
$S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n 1_{A_i}$. Then almost surely $S_n / E[S_n] \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$, where
$E[S_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i)$.

## Sources

- Lecture 9.

articles.title: The partial sum as a sum of indicator functions
articles.statement:
For sets $A_0, A_1, \dots$ in $\Omega$ and
every $n$, the partial sum $S_n$, defined pointwise by $S_n(\omega) = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}(\omega)$,
equals, as a function on $\Omega$, the sum $\sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$ of the real-valued indicator
functions.

articles.title: Partial sums of indicators are nondecreasing
articles.statement:
For sets $A_0, A_1, \dots$ and every
$\omega \in \Omega$, the map $n \mapsto S_n(\omega)$, where $S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$, is
nondecreasing.

articles.title: Partial sums of indicators are nonnegative
articles.statement:
For sets $A_0, A_1, \dots$, every $n$ and every
$\omega \in \Omega$, the partial sum $S_n(\omega) = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}(\omega)$ satisfies
$S_n(\omega) \ge 0$.

articles.title: Partial sums of indicators
articles.statement:
For sets $A_0, A_1, \dots$ in $\Omega$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$ is the sum of the indicators of the first $n$ sets, viewed as a
real-valued function on $\Omega$.

articles.title: Indices of the quadratic subsequence are positive
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be subsets of $\Omega$, write $S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$,
and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \int S_n \, d\mu \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$. If
$\varphi(k)$ is the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$, then $\varphi(k) > 0$ for
every natural number $k$.

This holds because $\mathbb{E}[S_0] = 0 < (k+1)^2$.

articles.title: Lower bound on the expected count along the quadratic subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
probability measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be subsets of $\Omega$, write
$S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$, and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \int S_n \, d\mu \to \infty$
as $n \to \infty$. If $\varphi(k)$ is the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$, then
$\mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] \ge (k+1)^2$ for every natural number $k$.

articles.title: The quadratic subsequence is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be measurable subsets of $\Omega$, write
$S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$, and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \int S_n \, d\mu \to \infty$
as $n \to \infty$. If $\varphi(k)$ is the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$, then
$\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is strictly increasing.

articles.title: Quadratic subsequence for the pairwise-independent strong law
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
probability measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be subsets of $\Omega$, and write
$S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$. Assuming $\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \int S_n \, d\mu \to \infty$ as
$n \to \infty$, this is the sequence $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ for which
$\varphi(k)$ is the least $n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$.

Because the thresholds grow quadratically, the Chebyshev tail bounds for
$S_{\varphi(k)} / \mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}]$ are summable.

articles.title: Summable deviation probabilities along the quadratic subsequence
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
probability measure on $\Omega$, let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be pairwise independent measurable
subsets of $\Omega$, write $S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$, and suppose that
$\mathbb{E}[S_n] = \int S_n \, d\mu \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$. Let $\varphi(k)$ be the least
$n$ with $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge (k+1)^2$. Then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$, the sum over
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ of the probabilities
$\mu\{\omega : |S_{\varphi(k)}(\omega) / \mathbb{E}[S_{\varphi(k)}] - 1| \ge \varepsilon\}$
is finite.

By Chebyshev's inequality the $k$-th term is at most $1/(\varepsilon^2 (k+1)^2)$; this is the
Borel–Cantelli input along the subsequence.

articles.title: Variance of an indicator is at most its probability
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $\Omega$ and let $s \subseteq \Omega$ be measurable. Then the indicator function $1_s$
satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(1_s) \le \mu(s)$.

In fact $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(1_s) = \mu(s)(1 - \mu(s))$.

articles.title: Variance of a sum of pairwise independent indicators is at most its mean
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be
a probability measure on $\Omega$ and let $A_0, A_1, \dots$ be pairwise independent measurable
subsets of $\Omega$. Then for every $n$, the partial sum $S_n = \sum_{i < n} 1_{A_i}$ satisfies
$\operatorname{Var}(S_n) \le \mathbb{E}[S_n]$, where variance and expectation are taken
with respect to $\mu$.

This follows from $\operatorname{Var}(1_{A_i}) \le \mu(A_i)$ and the fact that pairwise
independence makes covariances vanish.

articles.title: Large deviations of mean-zero sums on the cube have vanishing measure
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be square integrable on $[0,1]$ with $\int_0^1 f = 0$ and
$\int_0^1 |f|^2 > 0$, and let $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive reals with
$a_n \to \infty$. For each $n$ let

$$F_n = \{ (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in [0,1]^n : |f(x_1) + \cdots + f(x_n)| \ge a_n \sqrt{n} \}.$$

Then $m_n(F_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, where $m_n$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Sources

- MA-ProofBench (L. Pu et al., arXiv:2606.13782), Level II (Measure and integration; Classical measure theory), problem `ma_proofbench_l2_06`.

articles.title: Variance of the sample mean of i.i.d. samples
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ be real-valued
random variables on a measure space $(\Omega, \mu)$ that are mutually independent and each have
the same distribution as $X_0$, and suppose $X_0$ is square-integrable. Then for every integer
$n \ge 1$, with variances taken with respect to $\mu$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} X_i\Big) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_0)}{n}.
$$

Square-integrability is required only of $X_0$; identical distribution transfers it to every
sample.

articles.title: Rank criterion
articles.statement:
**Rank criterion** (Cochran 1934): square matrices `A k` over a field that sum to
the identity have ranks adding up to the size iff they are idempotent and pairwise
annihilating.

articles.title: Group mean of observations
articles.statement: The mean of the observations `x i` with `grp i = g` (`0` for an empty group).

articles.title: Law of the Gaussian sample mean
articles.statement:
For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)` with `n ≥ 1`, the sample mean has the law
`N(μ, v / n)`.

articles.title: Cochran's theorem
articles.statement:
**Cochran's theorem**, independence part: if `Z` has independent standard normal coordinates
and symmetric matrices `A k` sum to the identity with ranks adding up to the dimension, the
quadratic forms `Zᵀ (A k) Z` are mutually independent.

articles.title: Independence of squared lengths of orthogonal Gaussian projections
articles.statement:
Under the standard Gaussian law, the squared lengths `‖P_{K k} Z‖²` of the projections onto
pairwise orthogonal subspaces are mutually independent.

articles.title: Independence of orthogonal projections of a standard Gaussian
articles.statement:
Under the standard Gaussian law, orthogonal projections onto pairwise orthogonal subspaces are
mutually independent.

articles.title: Gaussian one-way layout
articles.statement:
For i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` observations `xᵢ` labelled by groups
`grp i`, the vector of group means is independent of the vector of within-group residuals
`xᵢ - x̄_{grp i}`.

articles.title: Independence of the Gaussian sample mean and residuals
articles.statement:
For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)`, the sample mean is independent of the residual
vector `(Xᵢ - X̄)ᵢ`.

articles.title: Independence of the Gaussian sample mean and sum of squared deviations
articles.statement:
For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)`, the sample mean `X̄` is independent of the sum of
squared deviations `∑ (Xᵢ - X̄)² = (n - 1) S²`.

articles.title: One-way analysis of variance
articles.statement:
For i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` observations labelled by groups, the
between-group sum of squares `∑ᵢ (x̄_{grp i} - x̄)²` is independent of the within-group sum of
squares `∑ᵢ (xᵢ - x̄_{grp i})²`.

articles.title: Cochran's theorem
articles.statement:
**Cochran's theorem**, matrix form: if `Z` has independent standard normal coordinates and
`A` is a symmetric idempotent matrix of positive rank, the quadratic form `Zᵀ A Z` is
chi-square with `rank A` degrees of freedom.

articles.title: Sum of squares of independent standard normals is chi-square
articles.statement:
For independent standard normal coordinates, the sum of the squares of the coordinates in a
nonempty finite set `s` has the chi-square law with `|s|` degrees of freedom.

articles.title: Cochran's theorem
articles.statement:
**Cochran's theorem**, projection form: for the standard Gaussian law on a
finite-dimensional real inner product space `E` and a subspace `K` of positive dimension, the
squared norm of the orthogonal projection onto `K` is chi-square with `dim K` degrees of
freedom.

articles.title: Squared orthonormal coordinates of a standard Gaussian are chi-square
articles.statement:
Coordinates of the standard Gaussian law in an orthonormal basis `b`: the sum of the squared
coordinates `⟪b i, x⟫` over a nonempty set `s` of indices is chi-square with `|s|` degrees of
freedom.

articles.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, solved form
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of `frischWaughLovell_residual`, if
`⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W ≠ 0` then `t = ⟪z⊥, y⊥⟫_W / ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W`.

articles.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, residualized form
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of `frischWaughLovell`, if
also `y⊥ = y - A v` is the weighted residual of `y` on `A` (`Aᵀ W y⊥ = 0`), then
`t ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W = ⟪z⊥, y⊥⟫_W`: the coefficient of `z` in the full regression is the coefficient of
the regression of the residualized response on the residualized regressor.

articles.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell
articles.statement:
**Frisch–Waugh–Lovell** for weighted least squares with a symmetric weight matrix `W`: if
`(b, t)` solves the normal equations of the regression of `y` on `[A | z]` and `z⊥ = z - A u`
is the weighted residual of `z` on `A` (`Aᵀ W z⊥ = 0`), then `t ⟪z⊥, z⊥⟫_W = ⟪z⊥, y⟫_W`, where
`⟪x, y⟫_W = x ⬝ᵥ W y`.

articles.title: Gauss–Markov covariance minimality
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real $m \times n$ matrix such that
$X^\top X$ is invertible, and let $B = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top$. Then $BX = I_n$, and for every
real $n \times m$ matrix $A$ with $AX = I_n$ the matrix $AA^\top - BB^\top$ is positive
semidefinite.

In the linear model $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ whose noise has identity covariance, $By$ is the
least-squares estimator of $\beta$, the estimators $Ay$ with $AX = I_n$ are exactly the linear
unbiased ones, and $AA^\top$ is the covariance of $Ay$.

## Sources

- C. F. Gauss, *Theoria combinationis observationum erroribus minimis obnoxiae* (1823); A. C. Aitken, “On Least Squares and Linear Combination of Observations,” *Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh* 55 (1936), 42–48, DOI `10.1017/S0370164600014346`.

articles.title: Pairwise Markov property of Gaussian vectors
articles.statement:
If `V = (X₀, X₁, Y) ~ N(μ, S)` with `S`
positive definite, then `X₀` and `X₁` are conditionally independent given `Y` iff
`(S⁻¹)₀₁ = 0`. (The standard Borel sample space is the setting of Mathlib's conditional
independence.)

articles.title: Uniqueness of Dempster's MLE
articles.statement:
Under the hypotheses of
`gaussLogLik_le_of_inv_eq_on_graph`, a positive definite `K` supported on `G` with the same
objective value is `K̂`.

articles.title: Dempster's covariance-selection MLE
articles.statement:
**Dempster's covariance-selection MLE** (sufficiency): a positive definite `K̂` supported on
`G` whose inverse agrees with `S` on the diagonal and the edges maximizes `log det K - tr (S K)`
over positive definite `K` supported on `G`.

articles.title: Gaussian log-likelihood of a precision matrix
articles.statement: The Gaussian log-likelihood objective `log det K - tr (S K)` of a precision matrix `K`.

articles.title: The conditional covariance is the inverse of a precision block
articles.statement:
For positive definite `S`
on `ι ⊕ κ`, `S₁₁ - S₁₂ S₂₂⁻¹ S₂₁ = ((S⁻¹)₁₁)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Matrix supported on the edges of a graph
articles.statement: A matrix vanishes off the edges of `G`: `K i j = 0` for distinct non-adjacent `i, j`.

articles.title: Measurability of the conditioning block
articles.statement: The `κ`-block is a measurable function of the vector.

articles.title: Partial correlation from the precision matrix
articles.statement: The partial correlation from the precision matrix: `ρ₁₂·rest = -Ω₀₁ / √(Ω₀₀ Ω₁₁)`.

articles.title: Partial correlation from the conditional covariance
articles.statement:
The partial correlation of coordinates `0` and `1` given the `κ`-block, computed from the
conditional covariance `C = S₁₁ - S₁₂ S₂₂⁻¹ S₂₁`: `C₀₁ / √(C₀₀ C₁₁)`.

articles.title: Conditioning block of a vector
articles.statement: The `κ`-block (the conditioning coordinates) of a vector on `Fin 2 ⊕ κ`.

articles.title: Sample second-moment matrix
articles.statement: The sample second-moment matrix `m⁻¹ ∑ₛ xₛ xₛᵀ` of `m` observations in `ℝ^ι`.

articles.title: Sum of sample quadratic forms as a trace
articles.statement: The quadratic forms of a sample add up to `m · tr (S K)`.

articles.title: Log-density of the multivariate Gaussian
articles.statement:
Let $J$ be a finite set with $n$ elements, let
$\mu, x \in \mathbb{R}^J$, let $S$ be a positive definite real $J \times J$ matrix, and write
$\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, S)$ for the multivariate Gaussian density at $x$ with mean $\mu$ and
covariance $S$. Then $\log \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, S) = -\frac{n}{2} \log (2\pi) -
\frac{1}{2} \log \det S - \frac{1}{2} (x - \mu)^{\mathsf T} S^{-1} (x - \mu)$.

articles.title: The weighted mean is the Gaussian MLE of the mean
articles.statement:
Let $I$ and $J$ be finite sets, let
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$ such that $\sum_i w_i > 0$,
let $m$ be their weighted mean, and let $S$ be a positive definite real $J \times J$ matrix.
Write $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, S)$ for the multivariate Gaussian density at $x$ with mean $\mu$
and covariance $S$. Then for every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$,
$\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu, S) \le
\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid m, S)$.

articles.title: The weighted Gaussian MLE when the sample covariance is positive definite
articles.statement:
Let $I$ and
$J$ be finite sets, let $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$ such
that $\sum_i w_i > 0$, let $m$ be their weighted mean, and let $C$ be their weighted scatter
matrix about $m$ (the weighted sample covariance); assume $C$ is positive definite. Write
$\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, S)$ for the multivariate Gaussian density at $x$ with mean $\mu$ and
covariance $S$. Then for every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$ and every positive definite real
$J \times J$ matrix $S$,
$\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu, S) \le
\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid m, C)$.

articles.title: The weighted Gaussian MLE for points in general position
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a nonempty finite
set and $J$ a finite set, and let $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with positive
weights $w_i > 0$ that do not all lie in an affine hyperplane: for every nonzero
$v \in \mathbb{R}^J$ there are $i, j \in I$ with
$\langle v, x_i \rangle \ne \langle v, x_j \rangle$. Let $m$ be their weighted mean and $C$ their
weighted scatter matrix about $m$ (the weighted sample covariance), and write
$\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, S)$ for the multivariate Gaussian density at $x$ with mean $\mu$ and
covariance $S$. Then for every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$ and every positive definite real
$J \times J$ matrix $S$,
$\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu, S) \le
\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid m, C)$.

articles.title: The weighted Gaussian log-likelihood via the scatter matrix
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set and
$J$ a finite set with $n$ elements, let $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real
weights $w_i$ whose sum $W = \sum_{i \in I} w_i$ is nonzero, let $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$, let $S$
be a positive definite real $J \times J$ matrix, and let $C(\mu)$ be the weighted scatter matrix
of the $x_i$ about $\mu$. Write $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, S)$ for the multivariate Gaussian
density at $x$ with mean $\mu$ and covariance $S$. Then
$\sum_{i \in I} w_i \log \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu, S) = -\frac{W}{2} \big(n \log (2\pi) +
\log \det S + \operatorname{tr}(S^{-1} C(\mu))\big)$.

articles.title: Aitken's theorem
articles.statement:
The GLS estimator has minimal covariance among linear unbiased
estimators: for every `A` with `A X = 1`, `A V Aᵀ - B V Bᵀ` is positive semidefinite, where
`B = glsMatrix X V`.

articles.title: Covariance of the generalized least-squares estimator
articles.statement: The covariance of the GLS estimator: `B V Bᵀ = (Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Unbiasedness of the generalized least-squares estimator
articles.statement: The GLS estimator is unbiased: `B X = 1` when `Xᵀ V⁻¹ X` is invertible.

articles.title: Generalized least-squares matrix
articles.statement:
The generalized least-squares matrix `(Xᵀ V⁻¹ X)⁻¹ Xᵀ V⁻¹`; `glsMatrix X V *ᵥ y` is the GLS
estimate of `b` in `y = X b + e` with `Cov e = V`.

articles.title: Column-centered data matrix
articles.statement: The column-centered data matrix `X i j - x̄ⱼ`.

articles.title: Sample mean of a data matrix column
articles.statement:
The sample mean of column `j` of an `n × p` data matrix (rows are observations). For
`n = 0` it is the junk value `0`.

articles.title: Quadratic form expanded in the ordered eigenbasis
articles.statement: The quadratic form expanded in the ordered eigenbasis: `xᵀ S x = ∑ λᵢ ⟪vᵢ, x⟫²`.

articles.title: Courant–Fischer min–max, matrix form
articles.statement:
Every subspace of dimension `p - k` contains a
nonzero vector whose Rayleigh quotient is at least `λₖ`.

articles.title: Courant–Fischer max–min, matrix form
articles.statement:
Every subspace of dimension `k + 1` contains a
nonzero vector whose Rayleigh quotient is at most `λₖ`.

articles.title: Frobenius error of the truncated SVD
articles.statement:
The squared Frobenius error of the truncated SVD is the sum of the discarded squared
singular values.

articles.title: Eckart–Young, best-approximation form
articles.statement:
The truncated SVD is a best rank-`k` approximation
of `A` in the Frobenius norm: the least squared distance from `A` to a matrix of rank at most `k`
is `∑_{k ≤ i < n} σᵢ²`, attained by `truncSVD A k`.

articles.title: Lower bound on the Rayleigh quotient for orthogonal directions
articles.statement:
Dual of `rayleigh_le_of_orthogonal`: on nonzero directions orthogonal to the eigenvectors
after index `k`, the Rayleigh quotient is at least the `k`-th eigenvalue.

articles.title: Ordered eigenbasis vectors are eigenvectors
articles.statement: The `k`-th basis vector is an eigenvector for the `k`-th eigenvalue.

articles.title: Ordered orthonormal eigenbasis of a symmetric matrix
articles.statement:
An orthonormal eigenbasis of a real symmetric matrix, ordered to match
`orderedEigenvalues`; for a covariance matrix these are the principal axes.

articles.title: Ordered eigenvalues are decreasing
articles.statement: The ordered eigenvalues are decreasing.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix are nonnegative
articles.statement: The eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix are nonnegative.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix in decreasing order
articles.statement:
The eigenvalues `λ₀ ≥ λ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ λ_{p-1}` of a real symmetric `p × p` matrix, in decreasing
order (Mathlib's `LinearMap.IsSymmetric.eigenvalues` of `Matrix.toEuclideanLin S`).

articles.title: Rank of the truncated SVD is at most k
articles.statement: The truncated SVD has rank at most `k`.

articles.title: Hotelling's characterization of the principal axes
articles.statement:
On nonzero directions orthogonal
to the first `k` eigenvectors, the Rayleigh quotient is at most the `k`-th eigenvalue; the bound
is attained at the `k`-th eigenvector (`rayleigh_orderedEigenbasis`).

articles.title: Rayleigh quotient of an eigenvector is its eigenvalue
articles.statement: The Rayleigh quotient of the `k`-th eigenvector is the `k`-th eigenvalue.

articles.title: Rayleigh quotient of a matrix
articles.statement: The Rayleigh quotient `wᵀ S w / wᵀ w` of a real matrix (junk value `0` at `w = 0`).

articles.title: Right singular vectors of a matrix
articles.statement:
Right singular vectors of `A`: an orthonormal eigenbasis of `Aᵀ A`, ordered so that the
`i`-th vector has eigenvalue `σᵢ²` with `σ₀ ≥ σ₁ ≥ ⋯` the singular values.

articles.title: Entries of the sample covariance matrix
articles.statement:
Entries of the sample covariance matrix:
`Sⱼₖ = (n - 1)⁻¹ ∑ᵢ (Xᵢⱼ - x̄ⱼ)(Xᵢₖ - x̄ₖ)`.

articles.title: Sample covariance matrix is symmetric
articles.statement: The sample covariance matrix is symmetric.

articles.title: Sample covariance matrix is positive semidefinite
articles.statement: The sample covariance matrix is positive semidefinite (for every `n`).

articles.title: Unbiased sample covariance matrix
articles.statement:
The unbiased sample covariance matrix `(n - 1)⁻¹ (X - x̄)ᵀ (X - x̄)` of an `n × p` data
matrix. The divisor needs `2 ≤ n`; for `n = 1` the factor is the junk value `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0`
(and for `n = 0` the product is the zero matrix).

articles.title: Sample variance of scores is a quadratic form
articles.statement: The sample variance of the scores along `w` is the quadratic form `wᵀ S w`.

articles.title: Principal component scores
articles.statement: The principal-component scores `(X - x̄) w` of the observations along a direction `w`.

articles.title: Centered columns sum to zero
articles.statement: The centered columns sum to zero (for at least one observation).

articles.title: Ordered eigenvalues sum to the trace
articles.statement: The ordered eigenvalues sum to the trace.

articles.title: Principal component scores have sample mean zero
articles.statement: The scores along any direction have sample mean zero.

articles.title: Eckart–Young (Frobenius norm)
articles.statement:
Every matrix of rank at most `k` has squared Frobenius
distance from `A` at least the sum of the discarded squared singular values.

articles.title: Trace of the sample covariance is the total sample variance
articles.statement:
The trace of the sample covariance matrix is the total sample variance, the sum of the
column sample variances.

articles.title: Truncated singular value decomposition
articles.statement:
The rank-`k` truncated singular value decomposition `A Vₖ Vₖᵀ = ∑_{i<k} σᵢ uᵢ vᵢᵀ`,
where `Vₖ` collects the first `k` right singular vectors.

articles.title: Proportion of variance explained is at most one
articles.statement: The proportion of variance explained is at most one.

articles.title: More components explain more variance
articles.statement: Keeping more components explains more variance.

articles.title: Proportion of variance explained is nonnegative
articles.statement: The proportion of variance explained is nonnegative.

articles.title: All components explain all of the variance
articles.statement: All `p` components explain all of the variance, when the total variance is positive.

articles.title: Proportion of variance explained by principal components
articles.statement:
The proportion of total sample variance explained by the first `k` principal components:
`(λ₀ + ⋯ + λ_{k-1}) / tr S` for the sample covariance matrix `S`. The junk value `0` is
returned when the total variance `tr S` is `0` (constant data).

articles.title: Snedecor's `F` law
articles.statement:
**Snedecor's `F` law** (Casella–Berger, Definition 5.3.6): for independent `V₁ ~ χ²_{d₁}` and
`V₂ ~ χ²_{d₂}` with `d₁, d₂ ≥ 1`, `(V₁ / d₁) / (V₂ / d₂)` has density
`Γ((d₁ + d₂)/2) / (Γ(d₁/2) Γ(d₂/2)) · (d₁/d₂)^{d₁/2} x^{d₁/2 - 1} (1 + d₁ x / d₂)^{-(d₁+d₂)/2}`
on `x > 0`.

articles.title: Student's `t` law
articles.statement:
**Student's `t` law** (Casella–Berger, Definition 5.3.4): for independent `Z ~ N(0, 1)` and
`V ~ χ²_k` with `k ≥ 1`, `Z / √(V / k)` has density
`Γ((k + 1)/2) / (√(k π) Γ(k/2)) · (1 + t²/k)^{-(k+1)/2}`.

articles.title: One-sample `t` statistic
articles.statement:
For an i.i.d. sample `X₁, …, Xₙ ~ N(μ, v)` with `n ≥ 2` and
`v > 0`, `√n (X̄ - μ) / S` with `S² = ∑ (Xᵢ - X̄)² / (n - 1)` has the Student `t` law with
`n - 1` degrees of freedom.

articles.title: Hoeffding's central limit theorem
articles.statement:
**Hoeffding's central limit theorem** (1948, §7): for an i.i.d. sample from `μ` and a
symmetric square-integrable kernel `h` of degree `m`, `√n (U_n - θ)` converges in distribution
to `N(0, m² σ₁²)`, where `θ = E h` and `σ₁² = Var h₁`.

articles.title: Quadratic form of a weighted scatter matrix
articles.statement:
Let $I$ and $J$ be finite sets, let
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$,
and let $C$ be the weighted scatter matrix of the $x_i$ about $\mu$. Then for every
$u \in \mathbb{R}^J$,

$$
u^{\mathsf T} C u =
\Big(\sum_{i \in I} w_i\Big)^{-1} \sum_{i \in I} w_i \big(u \cdot (x_i - \mu)\big)^2,
$$

with the convention $0^{-1} = 0$.

articles.title: Weighted quadratic forms as traces against the scatter matrix
articles.statement:
Let $I$ and $J$ be finite
sets, let $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$ such that
$\sum_i w_i \ne 0$, let $A$ be a real $J \times J$ matrix, let $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$, and let $C$
be the weighted scatter matrix of the $x_i$ about $\mu$. Then

$$
\sum_{i \in I} w_i \, (x_i - \mu)^{\mathsf T} A \, (x_i - \mu) =
\Big(\sum_{i \in I} w_i\Big) \operatorname{tr}(A C).
$$

articles.title: The bias-variance split of a weighted quadratic form
articles.statement:
Let $I$ and $J$ be finite sets, let
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$ such that $\sum_i w_i \ne 0$,
let $m$ be their weighted mean, let $A$ be a symmetric real $J \times J$ matrix, and let
$\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$. Then

$$
\sum_{i \in I} w_i \, (x_i - \mu)^{\mathsf T} A \, (x_i - \mu) =
\sum_{i \in I} w_i \, (x_i - m)^{\mathsf T} A \, (x_i - m) +
\Big(\sum_{i \in I} w_i\Big) (m - \mu)^{\mathsf T} A \, (m - \mu).
$$

articles.title: Weighted residuals sum to zero
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set and $J$ any index set, let
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$ such that $\sum_i w_i \ne 0$,
and let $m$ be their weighted mean. Then $\sum_{i \in I} w_i (x_i - m) = 0$.

articles.title: Weighted mean
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set and $J$ an index set, and let
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$. Their weighted mean is the
point $\big(\sum_{i \in I} w_i\big)^{-1} \sum_{i \in I} w_i x_i$ of $\mathbb{R}^J$, that is
$\sum_i w_i x_i / \sum_i w_i$, with the convention $0^{-1} = 0$ when the weights sum to $0$.

articles.title: Weighted scatter matrices of points in general position are positive definite
articles.statement:
Let $I$
and $J$ be finite sets and let $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with positive weights
$w_i > 0$ that do not all lie in an affine hyperplane: for every nonzero $v \in \mathbb{R}^J$
there are $i, j \in I$ with $\langle v, x_i \rangle \ne \langle v, x_j \rangle$. Then for every
$\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$ the weighted scatter matrix of the $x_i$ about $\mu$ is positive definite.

articles.title: Weighted scatter matrix
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set and $J$ an index set, let
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^J$ ($i \in I$) be points with real weights $w_i$, and let
$\mu \in \mathbb{R}^J$. The weighted scatter matrix of the $x_i$ about $\mu$ is the real
$J \times J$ matrix

$$
C = \Big(\sum_{i \in I} w_i\Big)^{-1} \sum_{i \in I} w_i \, (x_i - \mu)(x_i - \mu)^{\mathsf T},
$$

with the convention $0^{-1} = 0$ when the weights sum to $0$. When $\mu$ is the weighted mean of
the $x_i$, it is the weighted sample covariance.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov equations for bounded measurable functions
articles.statement:
For a Markov chain `X` with transition kernel `κ`, the conditional
expectation of `f (X (m + n))` given the past up to time `m` is the
`κ ^ n`-integral of `f` evaluated at `X m`. For `n = 1` this is the
one-step function form; the general case follows by integrating the
canonical conditional-indicator formula over each past-measurable set.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov equations, conditional form
articles.statement:
Let $X = (X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
Markov chain with state space $S$, with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)$, with Markov
transition kernel $\kappa$, under a probability measure $\mu$. Then for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$
and every measurable $B \subseteq S$,

$$\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathbf{1}_B(X_{m+n}) \mid \mathcal{F}_m] = \kappa^n(X_m, B)$$

$\mu$-almost everywhere, where $\kappa^n$ is the $n$-fold composition of $\kappa$ (the identity
kernel for $n = 0$). For $n = 1$ this is the defining one-step Markov property.

articles.title: One-step Chapman–Kolmogorov equation for functions
articles.statement:
For a
bounded measurable `f`, the conditional expectation of `f (X (k+1))`
given `ℱ k` is the `κ`-integral of `f` evaluated at `X k`.

articles.title: Integrated Chapman–Kolmogorov equation for functions
articles.statement:
The
unconditional expectation of `f (X (m + n))` is the expectation of the
`κ ^ n`-integral of `f` evaluated at `X m`.

articles.title: Markov chain with respect to a filtration
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\Omega$, let
$(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on $\Omega$, and let $\kappa$ be a Markov
kernel from a measurable space $S$ to itself. A sequence of random variables
$X_n : \Omega \to S$ is a Markov chain with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ with transition kernel
$\kappa$ under $\mu$ if it is adapted to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
every measurable $B \subseteq S$,

$$\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathbf{1}_B(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = \kappa(X_n, B)$$

$\mu$-almost everywhere. This is the standard form
$P(X_{n+1} \in B \mid \mathcal{F}_n) = \kappa(X_n, B)$ of the Markov property.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov equations, forward (law) form
articles.statement:
Let $X = (X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be
a Markov chain with state space $S$, with respect to a filtration, with Markov transition kernel
$\kappa$, under a probability measure $\mu$, and let $\kappa^n$ be the $n$-fold composition of
$\kappa$ (the identity kernel for $n = 0$). Then for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ the law of
$X_{m+n}$ is the law $\nu_m$ of $X_m$ pushed forward through $\kappa^n$: for every measurable
$B \subseteq S$, $\mu(X_{m+n} \in B) = \int_S \kappa^n(x, B) \, d\nu_m(x)$.

articles.title: Canonical Markov law started from a point starts there almost surely
articles.statement:
The canonical Markov law with initial distribution `dirac i` starts at `i`
almost surely. Its initial marginal is supplied by the existing construction.

articles.title: Finite restrictions of the shifted path
articles.statement:
For all $n, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and every path
$\omega : \mathbb{N} \to S$, let $\theta_n \omega$ be the shifted path, $(\theta_n \omega)_k =
\omega_{n+k}$. The restriction of $\theta_n \omega$ to the times $0, \dots, b$ equals the
restriction of $\omega$ to the times $0, \dots, n + b$ with its entries at times $n, \dots, n + b$
kept and reindexed as $0, \dots, b$; that is, it is the tuple
$(\omega_n, \omega_{n+1}, \dots, \omega_{n+b})$.

articles.title: Integral of a shifted path functional
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard Borel space,
$\kappa$ a Markov kernel on $S$, and $Y : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$ a bounded function,
measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra. Fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a history
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_n)$ of states in $S$, and let $P_{n,x}$ be the Ionescu–Tulcea trajectory
measure on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ that equals $x$ at times $0, \dots, n$ and afterwards draws each
next state from $\kappa$ applied to the current state. Then

$$\int Y(\theta_n \omega) \, dP_{n,x}(\omega) = \int Y \, dP_{\delta_{x_n}},$$

where $(\theta_n \omega)_k = \omega_{n+k}$ is the time-$n$ shift and $P_{\delta_{x_n}}$ is the
law on path space of the Markov chain with transition kernel $\kappa$ and initial distribution
the Dirac measure at $x_n$.

The statement also takes a finite measure $\mu$ on $S$, which does not appear in it.

articles.title: Canonical Markov law satisfies the finite Markov chain specification
articles.statement:
The coordinate process under the existing canonical matrix-derived Markov law
satisfies the original finite-state Markov-chain specification on `Filtration.piLE`.

articles.title: Last-coordinate history
articles.statement:
For $a \in \mathbb{N}$ and a history $x = (x_0, \dots, x_a)$ of
states in $S$, indexed by $\{0, \dots, a\}$, the last-coordinate history of $x$ is the history
indexed by $\{0\}$ whose only entry is $x_a$.

articles.title: Markov chain construction theorem
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, let
$\kappa$ be a Markov kernel from $S$ to $S$ and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $S$. Then
there is a probability measure $P$ on the path space $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ such that, writing
$X_n(\omega) = \omega_n$ for the coordinates, the law of $X_0$ under $P$ is $\mu$, and for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ the regular conditional distribution of $X_{n+1}$ given $(X_0, \dots, X_n)$
under $P$ agrees with the kernel $(x_0, \dots, x_n) \mapsto \kappa(x_n, \cdot)$ for almost every
$(x_0, \dots, x_n)$ with respect to the law of $(X_0, \dots, X_n)$ under $P$.

That is, the coordinate process $(X_0, X_1, \dots)$ under $P$ is a Markov chain with initial
distribution $\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$.

articles.title: Markov property of the canonical Markov chain measure
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard
Borel space, let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel from $S$ to $S$, let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $S$, and let $P_\mu$ be the canonical Markov chain measure on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ with initial
distribution $\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$. Write $X_n(\omega) = \omega_n$. For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the regular conditional distribution of $X_{n+1}$ given $(X_0, \dots, X_n)$
under $P_\mu$ agrees with the lifted kernel $(x_0, \dots, x_n) \mapsto \kappa(x_n, \cdot)$ for
almost every $(x_0, \dots, x_n)$ with respect to the law of $(X_0, \dots, X_n)$ under $P_\mu$.

articles.title: Initial distribution of the canonical Markov chain measure
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a Markov
kernel from a measurable space $S$ to itself and let $\mu$ be a measure on $S$. Under the
canonical Markov chain measure $P_\mu$ on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ with initial measure $\mu$ and
transition kernel $\kappa$, the law of the initial coordinate is $\mu$: the pushforward of $P_\mu$
along $\omega \mapsto \omega_0$ equals $\mu$.

articles.title: Canonical Markov chain measure
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel from a measurable space
$S$ to itself and let $\mu$ be a measure on $S$. The canonical Markov chain measure $P_\mu$ is the
measure on the path space $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ given by the Ionescu–Tulcea theorem for the initial
measure $\mu$ and, at each time $n$, the kernel sending a history $(x_0, \dots, x_n)$ to
$\kappa(x_n, \cdot)$. When $\mu$ is a probability measure, $P_\mu$ is the law of the Markov chain
with initial distribution $\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$.

articles.title: Path measure from a point as a trajectory measure
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on
$S$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_n)$ a history of states in $S$. The law on path
space of the Markov chain with transition kernel $\kappa$ and initial distribution the Dirac
measure at $x_n$ equals the Ionescu–Tulcea trajectory measure on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ started at
time $0$ from the one-entry history $(x_n)$ (the last-coordinate history of $x$), in which each
next state is drawn from $\kappa$ applied to the current state.

articles.title: Markov chain path measure
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on $S$ and a Markov kernel $\kappa$ on
$S$, the path measure $P_\mu$ is the measure on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$, with the product
$\sigma$-algebra, obtained by integrating against $\mu(dx)$ the Ionescu–Tulcea trajectory
measure that starts at $x$ at time $0$ and draws each next state from $\kappa$ applied to the
current state. It is the Markov chain measure of $\kappa$ and $\mu$; when $\mu$ is a
probability measure it is the law on path space of the Markov chain with initial distribution
$\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$.

articles.title: Expectation under the chain started from a point
articles.statement:
For a Markov kernel $\kappa$ on $S$,
a function $Y : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$ of paths and a state $x \in S$, the expectation
$E_x Y$ is the integral of $Y$ against the Markov chain path measure with transition kernel
$\kappa$ and initial distribution the Dirac measure at $x$.

articles.title: Lifted transition kernel on histories
articles.statement:
For a kernel $\kappa$ on $S$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
this is the kernel from histories $(x_0, \dots, x_n)$ of states in $S$, indexed by
$\{0, \dots, n\}$, to $S$ that sends $(x_0, \dots, x_n)$ to $\kappa(x_n, \cdot)$. It is the
Markov lift kernel of $\kappa$ at $n$.

articles.title: Lifting a kernel to histories
articles.statement:
For a kernel $\kappa$ from a measurable space $S$ to itself
and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the lifted kernel from $S^{\{0, \dots, n\}}$ to $S$ sends a history
$(x_0, \dots, x_n)$ to $\kappa(x_n, \cdot)$: it reads off the last coordinate and applies $\kappa$.

This is the form of kernel used by the Ionescu–Tulcea trajectory construction.

articles.title: Measurability of the Markov expectation
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard Borel space,
$\kappa$ a Markov kernel on $S$, and $Y : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$ a bounded function,
measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra. Then the map $x \mapsto E_x Y$, sending a state
$x$ to the expectation of $Y$ under the Markov chain with transition kernel $\kappa$ started
from $x$, is measurable.

articles.title: Shifted finite-dimensional distributions
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on $S$ and
$a, b \in \mathbb{N}$. For a history $x = (x_0, \dots, x_a)$ of states in $S$, let $Q_x$ be the
law of the history $(X_0, \dots, X_{a+b})$ that equals $x$ at times $0, \dots, a$ and then draws
each next state from $\kappa$ applied to the current state (the Ionescu–Tulcea partial
trajectory from time $a$ to time $a + b$). Then the image of $Q_x$ under
$(X_0, \dots, X_{a+b}) \mapsto (X_a, \dots, X_{a+b})$, with the times reindexed as
$0, \dots, b$, equals the law of $(X_0, \dots, X_b)$ under the partial trajectory from time $0$
to time $b$ started from the one-entry history $(x_a)$. This holds as an identity of kernels
in $x$.

articles.title: One-step shift of the partial trajectory kernel
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on $S$
and $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$. For a history $z = (z_0, \dots, z_{a+b})$ of states in $S$, extend
$z$ by one step, drawing $z_{a+b+1}$ from $\kappa(z_{a+b}, \cdot)$, and then keep the entries
at times $a, \dots, a + b + 1$, reindexed as $0, \dots, b + 1$. The law of the result equals
the law obtained by first keeping the entries of $z$ at times $a, \dots, a + b$, reindexed as
$0, \dots, b$, and then extending that history by one step in the same way. This holds as an
identity of kernels in $z$.

articles.title: One-step shift of a Markov partial trajectory
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on a
measurable space $S$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $z = (z_0, \dots, z_{a+b})$ be a history
in $S^{\{0, \dots, a+b\}}$. Let $\mu_z$ be the one-step partial trajectory of the lifted kernel
of $\kappa$ from time $a + b$ to time $a + b + 1$ started at $z$, that is, the law of
$(z_0, \dots, z_{a+b}, X)$ where $X$ has law $\kappa(z_{a+b})$. Then the image of $\mu_z$ under
the map $(y_0, \dots, y_{a+b+1}) \mapsto (y_a, \dots, y_{a+b+1})$ that drops the first $a$
coordinates equals the one-step partial trajectory of the lifted kernel from time $b$ to time
$b + 1$ started at $(z_a, \dots, z_{a+b})$, that is, the law of $(z_a, \dots, z_{a+b}, X')$ where
$X'$ has law $\kappa(z_{a+b})$.

articles.title: The path filtration is contained in the product σ-algebra
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a measurable space.
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th σ-algebra of the path filtration on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$,
generated by the coordinate maps $\omega \mapsto \omega_i$ for $i \le n$, is contained in the
product σ-algebra on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$.

articles.title: Path filtration
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a measurable space. The path filtration on the path space
$S^{\mathbb{N}}$ is the filtration indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, relative to the product σ-algebra,
whose σ-algebra at time $n$ is the one generated by the coordinate maps $\omega \mapsto \omega_i$
for $i \le n$.

articles.title: Time shift on path space
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a set and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The time-$n$ shift on
the path space $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ sends a path $\omega$ to the path $k \mapsto \omega_{n+k}$.

articles.title: The shifted trajectory of a Markov chain restarts from its last state
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a
Markov kernel on a measurable space $S$, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_n) \in S^{\{0, \dots, n\}}$. Let $P_x$ be the trajectory measure on
$S^{\mathbb{N}}$ of the lifted kernel of $\kappa$ started at time $n$ from the history $x$, and
let $P_{x_n}$ be the trajectory measure of the lifted kernel started at time $0$ from the
one-point history $x_n$. Then the image of $P_x$ under the time-$n$ shift
$\omega \mapsto (k \mapsto \omega_{n+k})$ equals $P_{x_n}$.

articles.title: Powers of an ergodic chain are eventually all positive
articles.statement:
Once a power of an ergodic chain is all-positive, every later power is
all-positive: there is a threshold `w` past which every power is all-positive.

articles.title: Pairwise positive powers of an ergodic chain
articles.statement:
An ergodic chain has, for every pair of states, some positive power with
a positive `(i, j)`-entry. (This is the per-pair form; it is strictly weaker
than ergodicity, which asks for one power working for all pairs at once.)

articles.title: The convergence theorem
articles.statement:
**The convergence theorem** (Levin, Peres and Wilmer, Theorem 4.9): a primitive
(irreducible and aperiodic) stochastic matrix with stationary distribution `π` converges to `π`
geometrically fast in total variation, uniformly in the starting state.

articles.title: Identity Markov chain
articles.statement: The identity chain: `prob i j` is `1` on the diagonal and `0` elsewhere.

articles.title: Ergodicity is primitivity of the transition matrix
articles.statement:
Ergodicity is exactly primitivity of the transition matrix. This is the
bridge to Mathlib: `Matrix.IsPrimitive` is the same condition for a bare
matrix, while `IsErgodic` is the stochastic-matrix form, with nonnegativity
supplied by the `StochasticMatrix` structure.

articles.title: The uniform Markov chain is ergodic
articles.statement: The uniform chain is ergodic, with witness `n = 1`.

articles.title: Ergodic finite Markov chain
articles.statement:
A finite-state Markov chain (given by its stochastic transition matrix `P`) is
*ergodic* if some positive power `P^n` has all strictly positive entries.

articles.title: Additivity of recursive matrix powers
articles.statement: Powers add: `matPow (a + b)` is the matrix product of `matPow a` and `matPow b`.

articles.title: Recursive matrix power agrees with the matrix power
articles.statement: The recursively defined power `matPow` agrees with the ordinary matrix power.

articles.title: Powers of the identity chain are the identity matrix
articles.statement: Every power of the identity chain is the identity matrix.

articles.title: First recursive power of a stochastic matrix
articles.statement: One step of the power recursion: `matPow 1` is the matrix itself.

articles.title: Later powers of a positive stochastic matrix power stay positive
articles.statement:
If some power `w` of a stochastic matrix is all-positive, then every later
power `m ≥ w` is all-positive: write `m = (m - w) + w`, use `matPow_add`, and
note that row `i` of `matPow (m - w)` sums to `1`, so some entry of that row is
positive, and that entry times the positive `matPow w` entry gives a positive
summand.

articles.title: Recursive powers of a stochastic matrix power
articles.statement: Powers of a power: `(P.pow p).matPow n = P.matPow (p * n)`.

articles.title: Powers of a stochastic matrix are stochastic
articles.statement:
Every row of every power of a stochastic matrix sums to `1`: powers of a
stochastic matrix are stochastic.

articles.title: The identity Markov chain is not ergodic
articles.statement:
The identity chain is not ergodic (for `M ≥ 1`): every power has a zero
off-diagonal entry.

articles.title: Powers of an ergodic Markov chain are ergodic
articles.statement: Every positive power of an ergodic chain is ergodic.

articles.title: Power of a stochastic matrix
articles.statement: The `p`-th power of a stochastic matrix, as a stochastic matrix.

articles.title: Transition probabilities of the identity chain
articles.statement: The identity chain has the displayed transition probabilities.

articles.title: Transition probabilities of the uniform chain
articles.statement: The uniform chain has constant transition probabilities `1 / (M + 1)`.

articles.title: Stationary distribution of a primitive chain has full support
articles.statement: The stationary distribution of a primitive stochastic matrix has full support.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the stationary distribution of a primitive chain
articles.statement:
A primitive stochastic matrix has at most one stationary distribution. In fact `π'` may be
any stationary vector of total mass `1`, not necessarily nonnegative.

articles.title: Convergence of matrix powers to the stationary distribution
articles.statement:
For a primitive stochastic matrix with stationary distribution `π`, every row of `Pⁿ`
converges to `π`: `Pⁿ(x, y) → π(y)`.

articles.title: Underlying matrix of a stochastic matrix power
articles.statement: The underlying matrix of `P.pow p` is the `p`-th matrix power of `P`.

articles.title: Underlying matrix of a stochastic matrix
articles.statement: Underlying matrix of probabilities of a `StochasticMatrix`.

articles.title: Doeblin's argument
articles.statement:
**Doeblin's argument** (Levin, Peres and Wilmer, proof of Theorem 4.9): if the `r`-step
transition probabilities dominate `δ π`, then the total variation distance of `Pⁿ(x, ·)` from the
stationary distribution `π` is at most `(1 - δ) ^ ⌊n / r⌋`. The bound is informative when
`r > 0` and `0 < δ`; for `r = 0` (`n / 0 = 0`) or `δ ≤ 0` it reads `d_TV ≤ 1` or weaker.

articles.title: Uniform Markov chain on finitely many states
articles.statement: The uniform chain: every transition has probability `1 / (M + 1)`.

articles.title: Non-explosion
articles.statement:
**Non-explosion** (Norris 1997, §2.7, for a finite state space): almost surely
the jump times of the chain started at `i` tend to `∞`, so `X t` is a genuine state of the
jump chain for every `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Holding times of the shifted steps
articles.statement: The holding times of the shifted steps started at `Y n` are the holding times after `n`.

articles.title: Holding times of a continuous-time Markov chain
articles.statement:
The `n`-th **holding time** `S n = E n / q (Y n)`, where `q k = -Q k k`; it is `∞` when
`Y n` is absorbing (`q (Y n) = 0`). Negative clock values, a null event, give `S n = 0`.

articles.title: Strong Markov property at jump times
articles.statement:
**Strong Markov property at jump times** (Norris 1997, §2.6–2.7): let `A` be a
measurable set of histories of the first `n` steps such that `T n < ∞` whenever the history
lies in `A`; these histories determine `Y 0, …, Y n` and `S 0, …, S (n - 1)`. Then for every
state `k` and every measurable set `B` of paths, the path after `T n` is independent of the
event `{history ∈ A, Y n = k}` and distributed as the chain started at `k`.

articles.title: Restart law at a fixed time
articles.statement:
**Restart law at a fixed time** (cf. the Markov property, Norris 1997, §2.8), for events of
`X s` and of the path after `s` only: for the chain started at `i`, the probability that
`X s = k` and that the path after `s` lies in a measurable set `B` is `exp (s Q) i k` times the
