probability that the chain started at `k` lies in `B`. This is weaker than the Markov property
with respect to the natural filtration: arbitrary events of the path before `s` are not covered
(only through the finite-dimensional distributions, `ctmcInputMeasure_real_ctmcPath_fdd`).

articles.title: Kolmogorov
articles.statement:
**Kolmogorov** (Norris 1997, §2.8, Theorem 2.8.2 for a finite state space): the chain
built from the jump chain and the holding times has transition function `exp (t • Q)`:
`P_i(X t = j) = exp (t Q) i j` for every `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Finite-dimensional distributions
articles.statement:
**Finite-dimensional distributions** (Norris 1997, §2.8, Theorem 2.8.2 (c)): with
increments `s 0, …, s (n - 1) ≥ 0`, times `t k = s 0 + ⋯ + s k`, and states `j 0, …, j (n - 1)`,
`P_i(X (t k) = j k for all k) = ∏ₖ exp (s k Q) (j (k - 1)) (j k)`, where `j (-1) = i`.

articles.title: Law of the driving step sequence of a Markov chain
articles.statement: The law of the i.i.d. step sequence `ω : ℕ → (ι → ι) × ℝ` driving the chain.

articles.title: Jump chain of the shifted steps
articles.statement: The jump chain of the shifted steps started at `Y n` is the jump chain after `n`.

articles.title: Jump chain of a continuous-time Markov chain
articles.statement: The **jump chain** started at `i`: `Y 0 = i` and `Y (n + 1) = ξ n (Y n)`.

articles.title: Jump matrix is row-stochastic
articles.statement: The jump matrix of a rate matrix is row-stochastic.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the jump matrix
articles.statement: The entries of the jump matrix of a rate matrix are nonnegative.

articles.title: Jump matrix of a rate matrix
articles.statement:
The **jump matrix** `Π` of a matrix `Q` (Norris 1997, §2.6): for a state with exit rate
`q i = -Q i i ≠ 0`, `Π i j = Q i j / q i` for `j ≠ i` and `Π i i = 0`; a state with `q i = 0`
is absorbing, `Π i j = δ i j`.

articles.title: Row of the jump matrix as a probability mass function
articles.statement: Row `i` of the jump matrix of a rate matrix, as a probability mass function on `ι`.

articles.title: Additivity of jump times under shifting
articles.statement:
`T (n + m) = T n + T' m`, where `T'` are the jump times of the shifted steps started at
`Y n`.

articles.title: Jump times are nondecreasing
articles.statement: The jump times are nondecreasing.

articles.title: Jump times of a continuous-time Markov chain
articles.statement: The `n`-th **jump time** `T n = S 0 + ⋯ + S (n - 1)`, with `T 0 = 0`.

articles.title: First-jump decomposition
articles.statement:
**First-jump decomposition** of the path: before the first holding time the chain is at
`i`; afterwards it is the chain started at `ξ 0 i` driven by the shifted steps.

articles.title: Path value between consecutive jump times
articles.statement: If `T n ≤ t < T (n + 1)`, then `X t = Y n`.

articles.title: Path restarts at a jump time
articles.statement:
After a finite jump time `T n`, the path is the path started at `Y n` driven by the
shifted steps: `X (T n + s) = X' s` with `X'` built from `shift n ω` started at `Y n`.

articles.title: Path of a continuous-time Markov chain
articles.statement:
The **path** of the chain started at `i`: `X t = Y n` for the `n` with
`T n ≤ t < T (n + 1)`. If `t` is at or after the explosion time `sup T n` (a null event, by
`IsRateMatrix.ae_tendsto_ctmcJumpTime`), the value is an arbitrary state that does not depend
on `i`, `Q` or `ω`.

articles.title: Shift of the step sequence of a Markov chain
articles.statement: The shift of the step sequence by `n`: `(shift n ω) m = ω (n + m)`.

articles.title: Law of one step of the chain construction
articles.statement:
The law of one step `(ξ, E)` of the construction: `ξ : ι → ι` has independent coordinates
with `ξ i ∼ Π i`, and `E` is an independent exponential clock of rate `1`.

articles.title: Measurability of the holding times
articles.statement: The holding time `S n` is a measurable function of the steps.

articles.title: Measurability of the jump chain
articles.statement: The jump chain `Y n` is a measurable function of the steps.

articles.title: Measurability of the jump times
articles.statement: The jump time `T n` is a measurable function of the steps.

articles.title: Joint measurability of the chain path in time and steps
articles.statement: The path `(t, ω) ↦ X t` is jointly measurable in the time and the steps.

articles.title: Measurability of the chain state at a fixed time
articles.statement: The state `X t` is a measurable function of the steps.

articles.title: Rows of the jump matrix sum to one
articles.statement: The rows of the jump matrix of a rate matrix sum to `1`.

articles.title: Backward equations for the mean hitting time
articles.statement:
**Backward equations for the mean hitting time** (compare Norris 1997, §3.3): if
`m : ι → ℝ` is nonnegative and `(Q m) i = -1` for `i ∉ A`, then `E_i H_A ≤ m i` (so it is
finite), `E_i H_A = 0` on `A`, and the real vector `E_i H_A` solves the same backward
equations. With uniqueness of the solution, this identifies `E_i H_A`.

articles.title: First-jump decomposition of a hitting time
articles.statement:
From a state `i ∉ A`, the hitting time of
`A` is the first holding time plus the hitting time of the chain restarted after the first
jump.

articles.title: Hitting time from inside the target set is zero
articles.statement:
From a state `i ∈ A`, the hitting time of `A` is `0` as soon as the first holding time is
positive (which fails only on a null event, see `ctmcHoldingTime`).

articles.title: Backward equations for the product moment of two hitting times
articles.statement:
Let `mA`, `mB`, `f` be
nonnegative with `(Q mA) i = -1` off `A`, `(Q mB) i = -1` off `B` and
`(Q f) i = -(mA i + mB i)` off `A ∪ B`. Then `E_i (H_A H_B) ≤ f i` (so it is finite), it is `0`
on `A ∪ B`, and its real part `p` solves `(Q p) i = -(E_i H_A + E_i H_B)` off `A ∪ B`.

articles.title: Hitting time of a continuous-time Markov chain
articles.statement:
The **hitting time** `inf {t ≥ 0 | X t ∈ A}` of a set of states `A` by the chain
`X = ctmcPath Q i ω` started at `i`, valued in `ℝ≥0∞` (it is `∞` if `A` is never visited).

articles.title: Minimality of the mean hitting time
articles.statement:
**Minimality of the mean hitting time** (compare Norris 1997, §3.3): if every state off
`A` has a positive exit rate, every `m : ι → ℝ≥0∞` with `1 / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j m j ≤ m i` off `A`
dominates `E_i H_A`.

articles.title: Minimality of the product moment
articles.statement:
If `mA`, `mB` are supersolutions of the mean
equations of `A` and `B` (as in `lintegral_ctmcHittingTime_le`) and `F` satisfies
`(mA i + mB i) / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j F j ≤ F i` off `A ∪ B`, then `F` dominates `E_i (H_A H_B)`.

articles.title: Product moment of hitting times from inside their union is zero
articles.statement: From a state of `A ∪ B`, the product moment of the hitting times of `A` and `B` is `0`.

articles.title: Product moment of two hitting times, first-step equation
articles.statement:
From `i ∉ A ∪ B` with
`q i ≠ 0`, `E_i (H_A H_B) = (E_i H_A + E_i H_B) / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j E_j (H_A H_B)` in `ℝ≥0∞`.

articles.title: Mean hitting time from inside the target set is zero
articles.statement: From a state of `A`, the mean hitting time of `A` is `0`.

articles.title: Mean hitting time, first-step equation
articles.statement:
**Mean hitting time, first-step equation** (compare Norris 1997, §3.3): from `i ∉ A`
with `q i = -Q i i ≠ 0`, `E_i H_A = 1 / q i + ∑ⱼ Π i j E_j H_A` in `ℝ≥0∞`.

articles.title: Uniformization
articles.statement:
If `c` bounds every exit rate `-Q i i`, then `Q + c • 1` has
nonnegative entries (Jensen 1953).

articles.title: Diagonal of a rate matrix is minus the total jump rate
articles.statement: The diagonal entry of a rate matrix is minus the total jump rate out of the state.

articles.title: Diagonal entries of a rate matrix are nonpositive
articles.statement: The diagonal entries of a rate matrix are nonpositive.

articles.title: Existence of a uniformization constant for a rate matrix
articles.statement: Every rate matrix admits a uniformization constant `c ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Rate matrix
articles.statement:
A real square matrix `Q` is a **rate matrix** (a `Q`-matrix in Norris's terminology) if its
off-diagonal entries are nonnegative and each of its rows sums to `0` (Norris 1997, §2.1).

articles.title: Rate matrix annihilates the constant vector
articles.statement: A rate matrix annihilates the constant vector `1`.

articles.title: Detailed balance propagates to the transition function
articles.statement:
Detailed balance for `Q`
implies `π i P t i j = π j P t j i` for every `t` (Norris 1997, §3.7). For a probability
vector `π` and a rate matrix `Q` this is the reversibility of the chain started from `π`.

articles.title: Detailed balance
articles.statement:
The row vector `π` is in **detailed balance** with the matrix `Q`:
`π i * Q i j = π j * Q j i` for all `i j` (Norris 1997, §3.7). This is only the algebraic
equation: it holds for `π = 0` and every `Q`. For a probability vector `π` and a stochastic
matrix it is the reversibility of the chain started from `π`.

articles.title: Detailed balance implies invariance for the transition semigroup
articles.statement:
Detailed balance with a matrix whose rows sum to `0` (for instance a rate matrix) makes `π`
invariant for every `P t`.

articles.title: Invariance under the semigroup
articles.statement:
`π Q = 0` if and only if `π P t = π` for every real
`t` (Norris 1997, §3.5, finite state space).

articles.title: Detailed balance implies invariance for the generator
articles.statement:
Detailed balance with a matrix whose rows sum to `0` implies invariance `π Q = 0`
(Norris 1997, §3.7).

articles.title: Continuity of the sticky kernel in the persistence
articles.statement: The sticky kernel depends continuously on the persistence.

articles.title: Two-state ancestry covariance
articles.statement:
**Two-state ancestry covariance** (the local-ancestry chain of a two-way pulse
admixture). With ancestry proportions `π = (α, 1 - α)` and persistence `c = (1 - r) ^ n`
(no recombination between the two sites along the `n` meioses since admixture, recombination
fraction `r` per meiosis), the indicators `I_x = [X = 0]`, `I_y = [Y = 0]` of ancestry `0` at
the two sites have covariance `α (1 - α) (1 - r) ^ n`. The kernel form of the ancestry pair is
the modeling assumption here; this statement does not derive it from a genealogy.

articles.title: Covariance under the sticky kernel
articles.statement:
If `(X, Y)` has joint law `P(X = i, Y = j) =
π i K i j` (stationary start, one step of the kernel), then
`Cov(f X, g Y) = c Cov_π(f, g)`. The algebraic identity holds for all real `π`, `f`, `g`, `c`;
it is a covariance of a probability law when `π` is a probability vector and `0 ≤ c ≤ 1`.

articles.title: The sticky kernel is the equal-input transition function
articles.statement:
With `∑ π = 1`,
`exp (t • κ (𝟙 πᵀ - 1)) = K (e^{-κ t})` for all real `κ` and `t`.

articles.title: Entries of the equal-input matrix
articles.statement: Entrywise form of the equal-input matrix.

articles.title: Equal-input matrix is idempotent
articles.statement: With `∑ π = 1`, `𝟙 πᵀ` is idempotent.

articles.title: Equal-input generator (F81 model)
articles.statement:
The **equal-input generator** `κ • (𝟙 πᵀ - 1)` with rate `κ` (Felsenstein's F81 model on
an arbitrary finite state space): jumps at rate `κ` to a state drawn from `π`.

articles.title: Equal-input matrix
articles.statement: The **equal-input matrix** `𝟙 πᵀ`: every row equals `π`.

articles.title: Equal-input generator is a rate matrix
articles.statement: For `κ ≥ 0`, `π ≥ 0` and `∑ π = 1`, the equal-input generator is a rate matrix.

articles.title: Entries of the sticky kernel
articles.statement: Entrywise form of the sticky kernel.

articles.title: Semigroup law
articles.statement:
**Semigroup law** of the sticky kernel in time:
`K (e^{-κ s}) * K (e^{-κ t}) = K (e^{-κ (s + t)})` (with `∑ π = 1`).

articles.title: Sticky kernel is row-stochastic
articles.statement: For `0 ≤ c ≤ 1`, `π ≥ 0` and `∑ π = 1` the sticky kernel is row-stochastic.

articles.title: Composition
articles.statement: With `∑ π = 1`, `K c * K c' = K (c c')` for all real `c`, `c'`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the sticky kernel
articles.statement: For `0 ≤ c ≤ 1` and `π ≥ 0` the entries of the sticky kernel are nonnegative.

articles.title: Sticky kernel at persistence one is the identity
articles.statement: The sticky kernel at persistence `1` is the identity.

articles.title: Powers of the sticky kernel
articles.statement:
With `∑ π = 1`, `K c ^ n = K (c ^ n)`: `n` steps of the sticky kernel are one step with
persistence `c ^ n`.

articles.title: Reversibility
articles.statement: `π i K i j = π j K j i` (detailed balance), for all real `c`, `π`.

articles.title: Sticky kernel at persistence zero is the equal-input matrix
articles.statement: The sticky kernel at persistence `0` is `𝟙 πᵀ`.

articles.title: Sticky kernel
articles.statement:
The **sticky kernel** with persistence `c`: `c • 1 + (1 - c) • 𝟙 πᵀ`. Started from `i`,
it stays at `i` with probability `c` and otherwise redraws the state from `π`.

articles.title: Rows of the sticky kernel sum to one
articles.statement: With `∑ π = 1`, the rows of the sticky kernel sum to `1` (for every real `c`).

articles.title: Long-distance limit
Short-distance limit
articles.statement: `K (e^{-κ t}) → 1` as `t → 0`, for every real `κ`.

articles.title: Stationary vector of the sticky kernel
articles.statement: With `∑ π = 1`, `π` is a stationary vector of the sticky kernel: `π K = π`.

articles.title: Generator commutes with the transition function
articles.statement: The generator commutes with the transition function.

articles.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov equation for the transition semigroup
articles.statement: The **semigroup property** (Chapman–Kolmogorov equation): `P (s + t) = P s * P t`.

articles.title: Uniformization
articles.statement:
For every real `c`,
`exp (t • Q) = e^{-c t} • exp (t • (Q + c • 1))` (Jensen 1953).

articles.title: Transition function of a rate matrix is row-stochastic
articles.statement:
The transition function of a rate matrix is row-stochastic for `t ≥ 0` (Norris 1997,
Theorem 2.1.2).

articles.title: Transition function fixes the constant vector
articles.statement: If `Q` annihilates the constant vector `1`, then `P t` fixes it: `P t *ᵥ 1 = 1`.

articles.title: Exponential of a nonnegative matrix is nonnegative
articles.statement: If `A` has nonnegative entries, so does `exp (t • A)` for `t ≥ 0`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the transition function of a rate matrix
articles.statement:
The transition function of a rate matrix has nonnegative entries for `t ≥ 0`, by
uniformization.

articles.title: Rescaling the generator rescales time
articles.statement: Rescaling the generator rescales time: `exp (t • (a • Q)) = exp ((a * t) • Q)`.

articles.title: Transition function at time zero is the identity
articles.statement: At time `0` the transition function is the identity.

articles.title: Transition semigroup of a continuous-time Markov chain
articles.statement:
The transition function `P t = exp (t • Q)` of the finite continuous-time Markov chain
with generator `Q` (Norris 1997, Theorem 2.1.1).

articles.title: Kolmogorov backward equation
articles.statement: The **Kolmogorov backward equation** `P' t = Q * P t` (Norris 1997, Theorem 2.1.1).

articles.title: Kolmogorov forward equation
articles.statement: The **Kolmogorov forward equation** `P' t = P t * Q` (Norris 1997, Theorem 2.1.1).

articles.title: Rows of the transition function sum to one
articles.statement: The rows of the transition function of a rate matrix sum to `1`, for every real `t`.

articles.title: Adding the next step to a past event
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be maps from a measurable space
$\Omega$ to a measurable space $S$, and write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the σ-algebra on
$\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the product
σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. If $C$ is measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ and
$B \subseteq S$ is measurable, then $C \cap X_{k+1}^{-1}(B)$ is measurable with respect to
$\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_{k+1})$.

articles.title: The σ-algebras generated by a sequence increase
articles.statement:
Let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be maps from a
measurable space $\Omega$ to a measurable space $S$, and for each $k$ let $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$
be the σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with
the product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. Then
$\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k) \subseteq \sigma(X_0, \dots, X_{k+1})$ for every $k$.

articles.title: The Markov property for measurable functions
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a probability measure on a
measurable space $\Omega$, let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be measurable maps from $\Omega$ to a measurable
space $S$, and let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on $S$. Write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the
σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the
product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. Suppose that for every $k$, every measurable $B \subseteq S$ and
every $C$ measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$,
$\int_C \mathbf{1}_{X_{k+1}^{-1}(B)} \, dP = \int_C \kappa(X_k(\omega), B) \, dP(\omega)$.
Then for every $k$, every $C$ measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ and every
measurable $f : S \to [0, \infty]$,
$\int_C f(X_{k+1}(\omega)) \, dP(\omega) =
\int_C \int_S f(y) \, \kappa(X_k(\omega), dy) \, dP(\omega)$.

articles.title: Finite-dimensional distributions given the past
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a probability measure on a
measurable space $\Omega$, let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be measurable maps from $\Omega$ to a measurable
space $S$, and let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on $S$. Write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the
σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the
product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$, and $\mathrm{FDD}_n(\mu, \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n)$ for the
finite-dimensional distribution of a Markov chain with initial measure $\mu$ and transition
kernel $\kappa$. Suppose that for every $k$, every measurable $B \subseteq S$ and every $C$
measurable with respect to $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$,
$\int_C \mathbf{1}_{X_{k+1}^{-1}(B)} \, dP = \int_C \kappa(X_k(\omega), B) \, dP(\omega)$.
Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $j$, all measurable sets $A_0, \dots, A_n \subseteq S$ and
every measurable set $C \subseteq \Omega$ that is also measurable with respect to
$\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_j)$,

$$
P\Bigl(C \cap \bigcap_{i=0}^{n} X_{j+1+i}^{-1}(A_i)\Bigr) =
\int_C \mathrm{FDD}_n(\kappa(X_j(\omega)), \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n) \, dP(\omega).
$$

articles.title: Finite-dimensional distributions of a Markov chain
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a probability measure on a
measurable space $\Omega$, let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be measurable maps from $\Omega$ to a measurable
space $S$, and let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel on $S$. Write $\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$ for the
σ-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by $\omega \mapsto (X_0(\omega), \dots, X_k(\omega))$, with the
product σ-algebra on $S^{k+1}$. Suppose $X$ is a Markov chain with transition kernel $\kappa$:
for every $k$, every measurable $B \subseteq S$ and every $C$ measurable with respect to
$\sigma(X_0, \dots, X_k)$,
$\int_C \mathbf{1}_{X_{k+1}^{-1}(B)} \, dP = \int_C \kappa(X_k(\omega), B) \, dP(\omega)$.
Let $\mu = P \circ X_0^{-1}$ be the initial distribution. Then for every natural number $n$ and
all measurable sets $A_0, \dots, A_n \subseteq S$,

$$
P(X_i \in A_i \text{ for } 0 \le i \le n) = \int_{A_0} \mu(dx_0) \int_{A_1} \kappa(x_0, dx_1)
\cdots \int_{A_n} \kappa(x_{n-1}, dx_n),
$$

where the right-hand side is the finite-dimensional distribution
$\mathrm{FDD}_n(\mu, \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n)$ of a Markov chain with initial measure $\mu$ and
transition kernel $\kappa$.

articles.title: Measurability of the finite-dimensional distributions in the starting state
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$
be a Markov kernel on a measurable space $S$, let $n$ be a natural number and let
$A_0, \dots, A_n$ be measurable subsets of $S$. Write $\mathrm{FDD}_n(\mu, \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n)$
for the finite-dimensional distribution of a Markov chain with initial measure $\mu$ and
transition kernel $\kappa$. Then the map
$x \mapsto \mathrm{FDD}_n(\kappa(x), \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n)$ from $S$ to $[0, \infty]$ is
measurable.

This is the regularity needed to integrate the finite-dimensional distributions against a
starting distribution.

articles.title: Finite-dimensional distribution of a Markov chain
articles.statement:
For a measure $\mu$ on a measurable
space $S$, a kernel $\kappa$ from $S$ to $S$, a natural number $n$ and sets
$A_0, \dots, A_n \subseteq S$, the finite-dimensional distribution
$\mathrm{FDD}_n(\mu, \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_n) \in [0, \infty]$ is defined by recursion on $n$:
$\mathrm{FDD}_0(\mu, \kappa; A_0) = \mu(A_0)$ and
$\mathrm{FDD}_{n+1}(\mu, \kappa; A_0, \dots, A_{n+1}) =
\int_{A_0} \mathrm{FDD}_n(\kappa(x), \kappa; A_1, \dots, A_{n+1}) \, d\mu(x)$.
Unfolded, it is the iterated integral

$$
\int_{A_0} \mu(dx_0) \int_{A_1} \kappa(x_0, dx_1) \cdots \int_{A_n} \kappa(x_{n-1}, dx_n).
$$

When $\mu$ is a probability measure and $\kappa$ a Markov kernel, this is the probability that a
chain with initial distribution $\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$ visits $A_0, A_1, \dots, A_n$
at consecutive times.

articles.title: Restricting an integral to a preimage
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$,
let $X : \Omega \to S$ be a measurable map to a measurable space $S$, let $A \subseteq S$ be
measurable, let $C \subseteq \Omega$ be any set and let $f : S \to [0, \infty]$ be any function.
Then
$\int_{C \cap X^{-1}(A)} f(X(\omega)) \, dP(\omega) =
\int_C \mathbf{1}_A(X(\omega)) \, f(X(\omega)) \, dP(\omega)$.

articles.title: Bridge: finite-state Markov chains satisfy the general one-step Markov property
articles.statement:
**Bridge: finite-state Markov chains satisfy the general one-step Markov
property.** For a finite Markov chain, the conditional expectation of the
indicator of `X (n+1) ∈ B` given `ℱ n` is the kernel of `P` evaluated at
`X n`, almost surely. This is the one-step form of `v1`'s general
`IsMarkovChain.markov_prop` specialized to the matrix kernel. No measurability
hypothesis on `B` is needed: the indicator is defined for every set, and the
proof only sums over the finite state space.

articles.title: Transition kernel of a stochastic matrix evaluated on a set
articles.statement:
The kernel of a stochastic matrix evaluated at a finite set is the sum of the
transition probabilities into that set.

articles.title: Transition kernel of a stochastic matrix
articles.statement:
The transition kernel of a stochastic matrix: `finiteChainKernel P x` is the
probability measure on `Fin (M + 1)` putting mass `P.prob x j` on each state `j`.
This is the kernel form of the transition matrix.

articles.title: Finite-state Markov chain with a given transition matrix
articles.statement:
`IsFiniteMarkovChain X P ℱ μ` asserts that the sequence `X : ℕ → Ω → Fin (M+1)`
is a Markov chain with transition matrix `P`, adapted to the filtration `ℱ`,
under the measure `μ`. Concretely: each `X n` is `ℱ n`-measurable, and the conditional
probability that `X (n+1) = j` given `ℱ n` equals `P.prob (X n) j`, matching the
Markov property `P(X_{n+1} = j | X_n = i, ...) = P_{ij}`.
Ported verbatim from `v1/Atlas/TheoryOfProbability/code/FiniteMarkovChain.lean`;
`v1` writes the filtration as `DiscreteFiltration Ω m`, which is `Filtration ℕ m`.

articles.title: One-step forward equation
articles.statement:
The law of `X (n+1)` is the law of `X n`
transported by the transition kernel of `P`.

articles.title: Finite Markov chains satisfy the general Markov property
articles.statement:
Convert the finite singleton-probability specification to the canonical general
Markov-chain predicate under the probability-space hypotheses of `condExp_indicator`.

articles.title: Detailed balance for cycle weights
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the
states $\{0, \dots, M\}$ satisfying Kolmogorov's cycle condition, fix a reference state $i_0$,
and write $w(j)$ for the cycle weight of a state $j$ relative to $i_0$. Then for all states
$i, j$ we have $w(i) \cdot P(i, j) = w(j) \cdot P(j, i)$.

articles.title: Cycle weights along a positive transition
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on
the states $\{0, \dots, M\}$ satisfying Kolmogorov's cycle condition, fix a reference state
$i_0$, and write $w(j)$ for the cycle weight of a state $j$ relative to $i_0$. If $i, j$ are
states with $P(i, j) > 0$, then $w(i) \cdot P(i, j) / P(j, i) = w(j)$.

articles.title: Path independence of cycle weight
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the
states $\{0, \dots, M\}$ satisfying Kolmogorov's cycle condition, and let $i_0, j$ be states. If
two paths (finite lists of states) both start at $i_0$, end at $j$, and have positive product of
the transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$, then the products of the
ratios $P(x, y) / P(y, x)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ along the two paths are equal.

This is the key step that makes the cycle weight well-defined and ultimately produces a
reversible measure.

articles.title: Cycle weight
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the states
$\{0, \dots, M\}$ and fix a reference state $i_0$. The cycle weight of a state $j$ relative to
$i_0$ is the product of the ratios $P(x, y) / P(y, x)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ along a
path (a finite list of states) from $i_0$ to $j$ whose product of transition probabilities
$P(x, y)$ over consecutive states is positive, where a ratio with $P(y, x) = 0$ counts as $0$;
such a path exists by irreducibility, and one is fixed by choice.

For chains satisfying Kolmogorov's cycle condition this value does not depend on the chosen path,
and the weights give a reversible measure.

articles.title: Detailed balance implies stationarity
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the finite state
space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ and let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the same states. If
$\pi$ and $P$ satisfy the detailed balance equations $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all
states $i, j$, then $\pi$ is stationary for $P$: $\sum_i \pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j)$ for every
state $j$.

articles.title: Detailed balance
articles.statement:
A probability distribution $\pi$ and a stochastic matrix $P$ on the
finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ satisfy the detailed balance (reversibility) equations
when $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i$ and $j$.

articles.title: Detailed balance distributions of irreducible chains are positive
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an
irreducible stochastic matrix on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$. If a probability
distribution $\pi$ satisfies the detailed balance equations $\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$
for all states $i, j$, then $\pi(i) > 0$ for every state $i$.

articles.title: Probability distribution on a finite state space
articles.statement:
A probability distribution on the
finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ is a function $\pi$ from the states to $\mathbb{R}$
with $\pi(i) \ge 0$ for every state $i$ and $\sum_i \pi(i) = 1$.

articles.title: Paths from positive matrix powers
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the states
$\{0, \dots, M\}$. If $n > 0$ and the $(i, j)$ entry of the $n$-th matrix power $P^n$ is positive,
then there is a path from $i$ to $j$ (a finite list of states starting at $i$ and ending at $j$)
along which the product of the transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$
is positive.

articles.title: Irreducible chains have positive paths
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on the
states $\{0, \dots, M\}$. For any two states $i, j$ there is a path from $i$ to $j$ (a finite list
of states starting at $i$ and ending at $j$) along which the product of the transition
probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ is strictly positive.

articles.title: Irreducible stochastic matrix
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the finite state space
$\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ and write $P^n$ for its $n$-th matrix power. Then $P$ is irreducible if for
all states $i$ and $j$ there is an $n \ge 1$ with $(P^n)_{ij} > 0$; that is, every state can be
reached from every state, itself included, in a positive number of steps.

articles.title: Reversible stochastic matrix
articles.statement:
A stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state space
$\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ is reversible if there is a probability distribution $\pi$ on the states
that is stationary for $P$ and satisfies the detailed balance equations
$\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i, j$.

articles.title: Stationary distribution
articles.statement:
A probability distribution $\pi$ on the finite state space
$\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ is stationary for a stochastic matrix $P$ on the same states if
$\pi P = \pi$, that is, $\sum_i \pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j)$ for every state $j$.

articles.title: Kolmogorov's cycle condition
articles.statement:
A stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state space
$\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ satisfies Kolmogorov's cycle condition when (1) for all states $x, y$,
$P(x, y) > 0$ implies $P(y, x) > 0$; and (2) for every $n \ge 0$ and every loop of states
$x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n$ with $x_n = x_0$ and $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_{i+1}, x_i) > 0$, we have
$\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_i, x_{i+1}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_{i+1}, x_i)$.

articles.title: Kolmogorov's cycle theorem, necessity half
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix
on the finite state space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$. If $P$ is reversible, that is, some probability
distribution $\pi$ is stationary for $P$ and satisfies the detailed balance equations
$\pi(i) P(i, j) = \pi(j) P(j, i)$ for all states $i, j$, then $P$ satisfies Kolmogorov's cycle
condition: (1) for all states $x, y$, $P(x, y) > 0$ implies $P(y, x) > 0$; and (2) for every
$n \ge 0$ and every loop of states $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n$ with $x_n = x_0$ and
$\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_{i+1}, x_i) > 0$, we have
$\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_i, x_{i+1}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} P(x_{i+1}, x_i)$.

articles.title: Kolmogorov's cycle theorem, sufficiency
articles.statement:
For an irreducible finite
Markov chain satisfying the cycle condition, there exists a reversible
measure: a distribution satisfying the detailed balance equations (and
hence stationary).

articles.title: Joining positive paths
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the states $\{0, \dots, M\}$,
and let $l_1, l_2$ be nonempty paths (finite lists of states) such that the last state of $l_1$
is the first state of $l_2$. If the products of the transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over
consecutive states $x, y$ along $l_1$ and along $l_2$ are both positive, then so is the product
along the path that follows $l_1$ and then $l_2$ with its first state removed.

articles.title: Path products are nonnegative
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the states
$\{0, \dots, M\}$. For every path (finite list of states), the product of the forward transition
probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive states $x, y$ along the path is nonnegative.

articles.title: Positive path products have positive steps
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix on the states
$\{0, \dots, M\}$, and let $l$ be a path (a finite list of states) whose $i$-th state, counting
from $0$, is $l_i$. If the product of the transition probabilities $P(x, y)$ over consecutive
states $x, y$ along $l$ is positive, then $P(l_i, l_{i+1}) > 0$ for every $i$ such that $i + 1$
is less than the length of $l$.

articles.title: Forward path product
articles.statement:
For a stochastic matrix $P$ and a path of states
$x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$, the path product is the real number
$\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} P(x_i, x_{i+1})$, the product of the forward transition probabilities along
the path. For the empty path and for a path consisting of a single state it is $1$.

articles.title: Ratio product of joined paths
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix and let $x_0, \dots, x_k$
and $y_0, \dots, y_l$ be paths of states with $x_k = y_0$. Then the ratio product along the
joined path $x_0, \dots, x_k, y_1, \dots, y_l$ equals the ratio product along
$x_0, \dots, x_k$ times the ratio product along $y_0, \dots, y_l$.

articles.title: First step of the ratio product
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix, $n$ a natural number
and $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n+1}$ states. Then the ratio product along $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n+1}$
equals $\frac{P(c_0, c_1)}{P(c_1, c_0)}$ times the ratio product along $c_1, \dots, c_{n+1}$,
where a quotient with denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: The ratio product around a loop is one
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix satisfying
Kolmogorov's cycle condition, and let $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n$ be a path of states with
$n \ge 1$ and $x_0 = x_n$ such that $P(x_{i+1}, x_i) > 0$ for every $i < n$. Then the ratio
product along $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n$ equals $1$.

articles.title: The ratio product is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For a stochastic matrix $P$, the ratio product along
every path of states is nonnegative.

articles.title: The ratio product as a finite product
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix, $n$ a natural
number and $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_n$ states. Then the ratio product along $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_n$
equals $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{P(c_i, c_{i+1})}{P(c_{i+1}, c_i)}$, where a quotient with
denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Positive paths have positive ratio product
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix such that
$P(x, y) > 0$ implies $P(y, x) > 0$ for all states $x$ and $y$. If the forward path product
along a path of states is positive, then the ratio product along that path is positive.

articles.title: Ratio product after appending a state
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a stochastic matrix,
$x_0, \dots, x_k$ a path of states and $j$ a state. Then the ratio product along
$x_0, \dots, x_k, j$ equals the ratio product along $x_0, \dots, x_k$ times
$\frac{P(x_k, j)}{P(j, x_k)}$, where a quotient with denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Ratio product along a path
articles.statement:
For a stochastic matrix $P$ and a path of states
$x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$, the ratio product is the real number
$\prod_{i=0}^{k-1} \frac{P(x_i, x_{i+1})}{P(x_{i+1}, x_i)}$, where a quotient with
denominator $0$ is taken to be $0$. For the empty path and for a path consisting of a single
state it is $1$.

This is the quantity that defines the "cycle weight" used to construct a reversible measure
from Kolmogorov's cycle condition.

articles.title: Powers of a stochastic matrix are nonnegative
articles.statement: Every entry of every power of a stochastic matrix is nonnegative.

articles.title: Matrix powers of a stochastic matrix
articles.statement:
For a stochastic matrix $P$ on the finite state
space $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th matrix power $P^n$ is defined by
$P^0 = I$, the identity matrix, and $(P^{n+1})_{ij} = \sum_k P(i, k) (P^n)_{kj}$. The entry
$(P^n)_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ in exactly $n$ steps.

articles.title: Stochastic matrix
articles.statement:
For a natural number $M$, a stochastic matrix of size $M + 1$ is a
square matrix $P = (P_{ij})$ indexed by the states $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$, with real entries
$P_{ij} \ge 0$ for all states $i, j$, whose rows sum to $1$: $\sum_j P_{ij} = 1$ for every $i$.
It is the transition matrix of a Markov chain on these $M + 1$ states.

articles.title: A.e. equality from a.e. equality on the fibers of a natural-valued function
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$
be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $T : \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function whose
fibers $\{T = n\}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, are all measurable, and let $f, g : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$.
If for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $f = g$ almost everywhere with respect to the restriction
of $\mu$ to $\{T = n\}$, then $f = g$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

articles.title: A.e. equality from a.e. equality on the finite fibers
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a
measurable space $\Omega$, let $\tau : \Omega \to \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ satisfy
$\tau \ne \infty$ $\mu$-almost everywhere and have every fiber $\{\tau = n\}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
measurable, and let $f, g : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$. If for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we have
$f = g$ almost everywhere with respect to the restriction of $\mu$ to $\{\tau = n\}$, then
$f = g$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

articles.title: Markov property
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on
$S$, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel on $S$, and $P_\mu$ the path measure on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ of the
Markov chain with initial measure $\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$. Let
$Y : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded and measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra,
let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\theta_n$ be the shift $(\theta_n \omega)_k = \omega_{n+k}$, and let
$\mathcal{F}_n$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the coordinates $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_n$.
For $x \in S$, let $E_x[Y]$ be the integral of $Y$ against the path measure of the chain started
at $x$. Then for $P_\mu$-almost every $\omega$,

$$E_{P_\mu}[Y \circ \theta_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n](\omega) = E_{\omega_n}[Y].$$

In other words, conditioning on the trajectory up to time $n$ depends only on the state at
time $n$.

articles.title: Markov property, set-integral form
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\mu$ a
finite measure on $S$, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel on $S$, and $P_\mu$ the path measure on
$S^{\mathbb{N}}$ of the Markov chain with initial measure $\mu$ and transition kernel $\kappa$.
Let $Y : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded and measurable for the product
$\sigma$-algebra, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\theta_n$ be the shift
$(\theta_n \omega)_k = \omega_{n+k}$, and let $\mathcal{F}_n$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by
the coordinates $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_n$. For $x \in S$, let $E_x[Y]$ be the integral of $Y$
against the path measure of the chain started at $x$. Then for every set $A \in \mathcal{F}_n$,

$$\int_A Y(\theta_n \omega) \, dP_\mu(\omega) = \int_A E_{\omega_n}[Y] \, dP_\mu(\omega).$$

articles.title: The shift by a random time agrees with the fixed shift on its level set
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a
type, let $T : (\mathbb{N} \to S) \to \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let
$\omega : \mathbb{N} \to S$ be a path with $T(\omega) = n$. Then the path $\omega$ shifted by $T$,
namely $k \mapsto \omega(T(\omega) + k)$, equals the path $\omega$ shifted by $n$, namely
$k \mapsto \omega(n + k)$.

articles.title: Path shifted by a random time
articles.statement:
For a type $S$ and a function
$T : (\mathbb{N} \to S) \to \mathbb{N}$ (typically a stopping time), the shift by $T$ sends a path
$\omega : \mathbb{N} \to S$ to the path $k \mapsto \omega(T(\omega) + k)$.

articles.title: Strong Markov property for a.s.-finite stopping times
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty standard
Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $S$, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel on $S$, and $P_\mu$ the law
on the path space $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ of the Markov chain with initial distribution $\mu$ and
transition kernel $\kappa$. For $x \in S$ write $E_x$ for the expectation under the chain started
from $x$, and for a path $\omega$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ write $\theta_n \omega$ for the shifted
path $k \mapsto \omega(n + k)$. Let $T : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be a
stopping time for the path filtration, with $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}_T$, such that
$T \ne \infty$ $P_\mu$-almost surely, and let $Y_n : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$, for
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, be measurable functions with $|Y_n(\omega)| \le C$ for a single constant $C$
and all $n$ and $\omega$. Then the conditional expectation under $P_\mu$ given $\mathcal{F}_T$ of
$\omega \mapsto Y_{T(\omega)}(\theta_{T(\omega)} \omega)$ equals
$\omega \mapsto E_{\omega(T(\omega))}[Y_{T(\omega)}]$ $P_\mu$-almost surely.

On the null event $\{T = \infty\}$ both sides are evaluated at the same unspecified finite time,
which does not affect the almost-sure equality.

## Sources

- Theory of Probability, Lecture 31 (strong Markov property).

articles.title: Strong Markov property for everywhere-finite stopping times
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a nonempty
standard Borel space, $\mu$ a finite measure on $S$, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel on $S$, and $P_\mu$
the law on the path space $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ of the Markov chain with initial distribution $\mu$ and
transition kernel $\kappa$; for $x \in S$ write $E_x$ for the expectation under the chain started
from $x$. Let $T : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a stopping time for the path filtration, with
$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}_T$, and let $Y_n : S^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbb{R}$, for
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, be measurable functions with $|Y_n(\omega)| \le C$ for a single constant $C$
and all $n$ and $\omega$. Write $\theta_T \omega$ for the path $\omega$ shifted by $T$, namely
$k \mapsto \omega(T(\omega) + k)$. Then the conditional expectation under $P_\mu$ given
$\mathcal{F}_T$ of $\omega \mapsto Y_{T(\omega)}(\theta_T \omega)$ equals
$\omega \mapsto E_{\omega(T(\omega))}[Y_{T(\omega)}]$ $P_\mu$-almost surely.

This is the special case of the strong Markov property for a.s.-finite stopping times in which
the time is finite everywhere.

articles.title: Removing one coordinate from a finite vector
articles.statement: Remove one coordinate from a finite vector.

articles.title: Representation of positive unital operators by Markov kernels
articles.statement:
A positive unital linear map from `C(E, ℝ)` to itself is represented by a Markov kernel.
Continuity of the operator is unnecessary: each output already belongs to `C(E, ℝ)`.

articles.title: Positive-operator-to-Markov-kernel bridge
articles.statement:
On a compact metrizable Borel space,
a positive continuous linear operator on `C(E, ℝ)` that fixes `1` is represented by a Markov
kernel. The integral identity holds for every continuous function and every starting state.

articles.title: Kolmogorov extension for Markov semigroup laws
articles.statement: Kolmogorov extension applied to the proved finite Markov laws.

articles.title: Composition rule for finite-chain kernels
articles.statement:
Moving the starting time forward and then evolving to the first requested
time gives the same finite chain as evolving there directly.

articles.title: Deleting one time from a finite Markov chain kernel
articles.statement:
Deleting one requested time from an ordered finite Markov chain composes
the two adjacent transition kernels.

articles.title: Deleting the first time from a finite Markov chain kernel
articles.statement:
Deleting the first requested time composes the initial transition with
the transition to the next requested time.

articles.title: Restricting a finite Markov kernel along an increasing reindexing
articles.statement:
Restrict an ordered finite Markov law along any strictly increasing map
of coordinate sets.

articles.title: Finite-dimensional kernel of a Markov semigroup at ordered times
articles.statement:
The law, as a kernel in its starting point, at finitely many ordered
times.  `s` is the time of the input state and `t` lists the requested
absolute times.

articles.title: Restricting a finite Markov law along an increasing reindexing
articles.statement: Measure form of `finiteChainKernel_map_strictMono`.

articles.title: Finite-dimensional law of a Markov semigroup from a starting point
articles.statement: The ordered finite-dimensional law started from `x` at time `s`.

articles.title: Markov law at a finite set of times
articles.statement:
The canonical law at an arbitrary finite set of nonnegative times.

The generic construction does not assume `K 0 = Kernel.id`.  Consequently,
when zero is requested its marginal is `K 0 x`; callers that need a
deterministic initial value prove the identity law for their kernel.

articles.title: Kernel of a positive operator represents it on continuous functions
articles.statement: The chosen kernel represents `T` on every real-valued continuous function.

articles.title: Path measure is the projective limit of the finite Markov laws
articles.statement: The canonical path measure has exactly the constructed finite laws.

articles.title: Finite Markov laws form a projective family
articles.statement:
The finite laws obtained by sorting requested times form a projective
family; projectivity is a consequence of Chapman--Kolmogorov, not a premise.

articles.title: Markov kernels are determined by integrals of continuous functions
articles.statement:
Two Markov kernels on a compact metrizable Borel space are equal when they integrate every
real-valued continuous function equally at every starting state.

articles.title: Ordered finite projections of the Markov path measure
articles.statement:
The coordinates in increasing finset order have exactly the corresponding
iterated-kernel law.

articles.title: Finite projections of the Markov path measure
articles.statement:
Every finite coordinate projection of the canonical path measure is its
explicit iterated-kernel law.

articles.title: Operator composition corresponds to kernel composition
articles.statement:
Operator composition is represented by canonical kernel composition. The order is reversed:
`T.comp U` acts as `f ↦ T (U f)`, so the represented kernel first uses `K_T` and then `K_U`.

articles.title: Identity operator kernel is pointwise Dirac
articles.statement: Pointwise form of the identity theorem: every transition measure is Dirac.

articles.title: Identity operator gives the identity kernel
articles.statement: The kernel represented by the identity operator is Mathlib's identity kernel.

articles.title: Markov kernel of a positive unital operator
articles.statement:
The canonical chosen Markov kernel representing `T`. Its characterization theorem is
`integral_markovKernelOfPositiveOperator`; clients should use that theorem rather than unfold this
definition.

articles.title: Reindexing an ordered vector by a finite set
articles.statement: Reindex an ordered vector by the increasing enumeration of a finset.

articles.title: Increasing reindexing of a subset within a finite set
articles.statement:
The increasing reindexing of the elements of `J` among those of a
larger finset `I`.

articles.title: Path-space measure of a Markov semigroup
articles.statement:
The canonical path-space measure selected from Kolmogorov extension.

As for `finiteLaw`, no identity-at-zero hypothesis is built into this generic
object: its time-zero marginal is `K 0 x` unless the caller proves
`K 0 = Kernel.id`.

articles.title: Cutoff for a family of distance profiles
articles.statement:
A family of real numbers $d_n(t)$, indexed by
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and times $t \in \mathbb{N}$, exhibits cutoff if there are real numbers $t_n$
with $t_n \to \infty$ such that for every $\eta$ with $0 < \eta < 1$, as $n \to \infty$,
$d_n(\lceil (1+\eta) t_n \rceil) \to 0$ and $d_n(\lfloor (1-\eta) t_n \rfloor) \to 1$. Here the
ceiling and floor are taken in $\mathbb{N}$, so a negative argument gives $0$.

articles.title: Being $1/4$-mixed at a given time
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set, $P$ a real $S \times S$
matrix and $\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}$. Then $P$ is mixed at time $t \in \mathbb{N}$ with respect to
$\pi$ if for every $x \in S$ the total variation distance
$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{y \in S} |P^t(x, y) - \pi(y)|$ between the row $x$ of the matrix power $P^t$
and $\pi$ is at most $1/4$.

The mixing time is the least $t$ at which $P$ is mixed.

articles.title: Number of monochromatic edges
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a colouring $\sigma$ of its vertices with colours in
$\{0, \dots, q-1\}$, this is the number of edges $uv$ of $G$ with $\sigma_u = \sigma_v$, as a real
number, each edge counted once.

articles.title: Sign of a Boolean spin
articles.statement:
The sign of a Boolean spin is the real number $+1$ if the spin
is true and $-1$ if it is false.

articles.title: Coordinate step on the discrete torus
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ of the discrete torus
$\mathbb{Z}_n^d$ and a coordinate $k \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, the neighbour $x + e_k$ is obtained
from $x$ by replacing its $k$-th coordinate $x_k$ by $(x_k + 1) \bmod n$ and leaving the other
coordinates unchanged.

articles.title: Discrete torus
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, the vertices of the discrete torus
$\mathbb{Z}_n^d$ are the functions from $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, the
$d$-tuples of residues modulo $n$.

articles.title: Total variation distance of functions on a finite set
articles.statement:
For real-valued functions $\mu$
and $\nu$ on a finite set $S$, their total variation distance is
$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{y \in S} |\mu(y) - \nu(y)|$.

articles.title: Total variation distance of a matrix row from a function
articles.statement:
For a real $S \times S$ matrix
$Q$ indexed by a finite set $S$, a function $\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in S$, this is the
total variation distance $\frac{1}{2} \sum_{y \in S} |Q(x, y) - \pi(y)|$ of the row $x$ of $Q$
from $\pi$.

articles.title: Backwards martingale convergence theorem, almost sure convergence
articles.statement:
Let
$(\Omega, \mathcal F, \mu)$ be a probability space, let
$\mathcal F_0 \supseteq \mathcal F_1 \supseteq \cdots$ be a decreasing sequence of sub-σ-algebras
of $\mathcal F$, and let $\mathcal F_\infty = \bigcap_n \mathcal F_n$. If the real-valued process
$(M_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is a backwards martingale with respect to $(\mathcal F_n)$ and $\mu$, then
$M_n \to \mathbb E[M_0 \mid \mathcal F_\infty]$ as $n \to \infty$, $\mu$-almost everywhere.

articles.title: Backwards martingale convergence theorem in L¹
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mathcal F, \mu)$ be a
probability space, let $\mathcal F_0 \supseteq \mathcal F_1 \supseteq \cdots$ be a decreasing
sequence of sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal F$, and let $\mathcal F_\infty = \bigcap_n \mathcal F_n$.
If the real-valued process $(M_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is a backwards martingale with respect to
$(\mathcal F_n)$ and $\mu$, then the $L^1(\mu)$ norm
$\lVert M_n - \mathbb E[M_0 \mid \mathcal F_\infty] \rVert_1$ tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Identifying the a.e. limit of conditional expectations
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on a
measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, let $(\mathcal{G}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be any
sequence of sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal{F}$ (not assumed monotone), and let
$g : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable. Write $\mu[g \mid \mathcal{G}]$ for the conditional
expectation of $g$ given a sub-σ-algebra $\mathcal{G}$ with respect to $\mu$, and
$\mathcal{G}_\infty = \bigcap_n \mathcal{G}_n$. Suppose $h : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is
integrable, strongly measurable with respect to $\mathcal{G}_\infty$, and
$\mu[g \mid \mathcal{G}_n](\omega) \to h(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$ for $\mu$-almost every
$\omega$. Then $h = \mu[g \mid \mathcal{G}_\infty]$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

articles.title: Conditioning a backwards martingale on the next level
articles.statement: Conditioning a term on the next, smaller level gives the next term a.e.

articles.title: Terms of a backwards martingale are integrable
articles.statement: Every term is integrable by its canonical conditional-expectation representation.

articles.title: Conditional expectations form a backwards martingale
articles.statement:
Conditional expectations of arbitrary g form a canonical backwards martingale
along decreasing sub-sigma-algebras. The nonintegrable-g convention is retained.

articles.title: Backwards martingale
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal F)$
and let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of σ-algebras on $\Omega$. A sequence of
functions $M_n : \Omega \to \mathbb R$ is a backwards martingale with respect to $(\mathcal F_n)$
and $\mu$ if $M_0$ is $\mu$-integrable and, for every $n$, $M_n = \mathbb E[M_0 \mid \mathcal F_n]$
$\mu$-almost everywhere.

Here $\mathbb E[M_0 \mid \mathcal F_n]$ is the conditional expectation with respect to $\mu$ when
$\mathcal F_n \subseteq \mathcal F$ and the restriction of $\mu$ to $\mathcal F_n$ is σ-finite,
and is $0$ by convention otherwise. The definition is used when $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a decreasing
sequence of sub-σ-algebras, but it does not require this.

articles.title: Lévy's downward theorem, almost sure convergence
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mathcal F, \mu)$ be a
probability space, let $\mathcal F_0 \supseteq \mathcal F_1 \supseteq \cdots$ be a decreasing
sequence of sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal F$, and let $\mathcal F_\infty = \bigcap_n \mathcal F_n$.
For every function $g : \Omega \to \mathbb R$, the conditional expectations
$\mathbb E[g \mid \mathcal F_n]$ converge to $\mathbb E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty]$ as
$n \to \infty$, $\mu$-almost everywhere.

No integrability hypothesis is needed: for a non-integrable $g$ every conditional expectation is
$0$ by convention, and the statement is trivial.

articles.title: Lévy's downward theorem in L¹
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mathcal F, \mu)$ be a probability space,
let $\mathcal F_0 \supseteq \mathcal F_1 \supseteq \cdots$ be a decreasing sequence of
sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal F$, and let $\mathcal F_\infty = \bigcap_n \mathcal F_n$. For every
integrable function $g : \Omega \to \mathbb R$, the $L^1(\mu)$ norm
$\lVert \mathbb E[g \mid \mathcal F_n] - \mathbb E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty] \rVert_1$ tends to $0$
as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Conditional expectations along a filtration are strongly adapted
articles.statement:
Conditional-expectation representatives are strongly adapted separately
from their canonical backwards-martingale membership. No integrability of g is needed.

articles.title: Tail sigma-algebra of a constant filtration
articles.statement: A constant decreasing filtration has its constant value as tail algebra.

articles.title: Tail sigma-algebra lies in every level of the filtration
articles.statement: The tail sigma-algebra lies in every level of the decreasing filtration.

articles.title: Tail sigma-algebra lies in the ambient sigma-algebra
articles.statement: The tail sigma-algebra lies in the ambient sigma-algebra.

articles.title: Tail sigma-algebra of a decreasing filtration
articles.statement: The tail sigma-algebra of a decreasing filtration, the intersection of its levels.

articles.title: Almost-everywhere convergent conditional expectations converge in L¹
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a finite
measure on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, let $(\mathcal{G}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be
a sequence of sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal{F}$, let $g : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable,
and write $\mu[g \mid \mathcal{G}_n]$ for the conditional expectation of $g$ given
$\mathcal{G}_n$ with respect to $\mu$. If $h : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is integrable and
$\mu[g \mid \mathcal{G}_n] \to h$ $\mu$-almost everywhere as $n \to \infty$, then
$\int_\Omega |\mu[g \mid \mathcal{G}_n] - h| \, d\mu \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

This is Vitali's theorem applied to the uniformly integrable family of conditional expectations of
a single integrable function.

articles.title: Backwards martingales are uniformly integrable
articles.statement:
Canonical backwards membership is uniformly integrable in L1 on a finite measure.
The ambient bounds suffice; representative adaptedness and antitonicity are unnecessary.

articles.title: Convex nondecreasing functions preserve submartingales
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure,
let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration, and let $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued submartingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$. Let
$\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex and nondecreasing, and suppose $\varphi(X_n)$ is
integrable for every $n$. Then $(\varphi(X_n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a submartingale with respect
to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$.

Monotonicity is needed: a convex function of a submartingale need not be a submartingale. For
example, take $\varphi(x) = (x - 4)^2$ and a submartingale with $X_i = 2$ and $X_j = 3$ almost
surely for some $i < j$; then $\varphi(X_i) = 4 > 1 = \varphi(X_j)$.

articles.title: Convex functions of martingales are submartingales
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure,
let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration, and let $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$. Let
$\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex, and suppose $\varphi(X_n)$ is integrable for every
$n$. Then $(\varphi(X_n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a submartingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$
and $\mu$.

## Sources

- Lecture 26/27, martingale observations.

articles.title: Concave functions of martingales are supermartingales
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure,
let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration, and let $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$. Let
$\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be concave, and suppose $\varphi(X_n)$ is integrable for
every $n$. Then $(\varphi(X_n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a supermartingale with respect to
$(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$.

articles.title: Doob's L² maximal inequality, infinite horizon
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure, let
$(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration
$(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$ such that every $f_n$ is in $L^2(\mu)$ and $f_0 = 0$ almost
everywhere, and let $A_n$ be its predictable quadratic variation. Then
$\int \sup_n |f_n|^2 \, d\mu \le 4 \int \sup_n \max(A_n, 0) \, d\mu$, where both integrals are
of $[0, \infty]$-valued functions and may be infinite.

Since each $A_n$ is nonnegative almost everywhere, the right side is $4\,\mathbb{E}[A_\infty]$
with $A_\infty = \sup_n A_n$.

articles.title: Doob's L² maximal inequality in terms of the predictable quadratic variation, finite horizon
articles.statement:
**Doob's L² maximal inequality in terms of the predictable quadratic
variation, finite horizon.** Let $\mu$ be a probability measure and let $(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$
be a real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ such that
every $f_k$ is in $L^2(\mu)$ and $f_0 = 0$ almost everywhere, and let $A_n$ be its predictable
quadratic variation. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$\int (\max_{k \le n} |f_k|)^2 \, d\mu \le 4 \int A_n \, d\mu$.

articles.title: Doob's L² maximal inequality, finite horizon
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure and let
$(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration
$(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ such that every $f_k$ is in $L^2(\mu)$. Then for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\int (\max_{k \le n} |f_k|)^2 \, d\mu \le 4 \int f_n^2 \, d\mu$.

articles.title: Expectation of the predictable quadratic variation
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
and let $(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration
$(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ such that every $f_k$ is in $L^2(\mu)$, and let $A_n$ be its
predictable quadratic variation. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$\int A_n \, d\mu = \int f_n^2 \, d\mu - \int f_0^2 \, d\mu$.

The proof telescopes, using the orthogonality of martingale increments.

articles.title: Predictable quadratic variation
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\Omega$, let
$(\mathcal{F}_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration and let $(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued process. The predictable quadratic variation of $f$ with respect to
$(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ is the process defined pointwise by
$A_n(\omega) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{E}_\mu[(f_{k+1} - f_k)^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_k](\omega)$,
so $A_0 = 0$. For a square-integrable martingale this is the predictable part of $f^2$ in Doob's
decomposition.

articles.title: One-period fundamental theorem of asset pricing
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set of
states and $A$ a finite set of assets, and let $g(a, \omega) \in \mathbb{R}$ be the gain of
asset $a$ in state $\omega$. Call a portfolio $h \colon A \to \mathbb{R}$ an arbitrage if its
gain $\sum_{a \in A} h(a)\, g(a, \omega)$ is nonnegative in every state $\omega$ and positive
in some state. There is no arbitrage if and only if there is a function
$q \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with $q(\omega) > 0$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$ and
$\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} q(\omega) = 1$ such that
$\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} q(\omega)\, g(a, \omega) = 0$ for every asset $a \in A$, that is, a
strictly positive probability on the states under which every asset has zero expected gain.

## Sources

- J. M. Harrison and D. M. Kreps, J. Econom. Theory 20 (1979), DOI 10.1016/0022-0531(79)90043-7. It follows from `one_period_fundamental_theorem_asset_pricing_general`; the unused `[DecidableEq Ω]` and `[DecidableEq A]` keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Fundamental theorem of asset pricing for a finite one-period market
articles.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a
nonempty finite set of states and $A$ a finite set of assets, and let $g(a, \omega) \in \mathbb{R}$
be the gain of asset $a$ in state $\omega$. Call a portfolio $h \colon A \to \mathbb{R}$ an
arbitrage if its gain $\sum_{a \in A} h(a)\, g(a, \omega)$ is nonnegative in every state
$\omega$ and positive in some state. There is no arbitrage if and only if there is a function
$q \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with $q(\omega) > 0$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$ and
$\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} q(\omega) = 1$ such that
$\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} q(\omega)\, g(a, \omega) = 0$ for every asset $a \in A$.

articles.title: Square-integrable martingale convergence
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ on a probability space,
with $E[X_n^2] < \infty$ for every $n$, and let $(A_n)$ be its predictable quadratic variation.
Then for almost every $\omega$: if $A_n(\omega)$ converges to a real limit as $n \to \infty$,
then $X_n(\omega)$ converges to a real limit as well.

In particular, $X_n$ converges almost surely on the event $\{\sup_n A_n < \infty\}$, since
$A_n$ is almost surely non-decreasing in $n$.

articles.title: Supermartingale almost-sure convergence theorem
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued
supermartingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ on a probability space
$(\Omega, \mu)$, and let $C$ be a real number with $\int X_n^- \, d\mu \le C$ for every $n$, where
$X_n^-$ is the negative part of $X_n$. Then there is an integrable function
$X_\infty : \Omega \to \mathbb R$ such that $X_n(\omega) \to X_\infty(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$
for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$.

This follows from the submartingale theorem applied to $-X$, since $(-X_n)^+ = X_n^-$.

articles.title: Martingale almost-sure convergence theorem
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued
martingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ on a probability space
$(\Omega, \mu)$, and let $C$ be a real number with $\int X_n^+ \, d\mu \le C$ for every $n$, where
$X_n^+$ is the positive part of $X_n$. Then there is an integrable function
$X_\infty : \Omega \to \mathbb R$ such that $X_n(\omega) \to X_\infty(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$
for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$.

This is the submartingale theorem, since every martingale is a submartingale.

articles.title: Submartingale almost-sure convergence theorem
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued
submartingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ on a probability space
$(\Omega, \mu)$, and let $C$ be a real number with $\int X_n^+ \, d\mu \le C$ for every $n$, where
$X_n^+$ is the positive part of $X_n$. Then there is an integrable function
$X_\infty : \Omega \to \mathbb R$ such that $X_n(\omega) \to X_\infty(\omega)$ as $n \to \infty$
for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$.

articles.title: Expectations increase along a submartingale
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued
submartingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ on a probability space
$(\Omega, \mu)$. Then $\int X_i \, d\mu \le \int X_j \, d\mu$ for all natural numbers $i \le j$.

articles.title: L¹ bound for a submartingale with bounded positive parts
articles.statement:
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a
real-valued submartingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ on a probability
space $(\Omega, \mu)$, and let $C$ be a real number with $\int X_n^+ \, d\mu \le C$ for every $n$,
where $X_n^+$ is the positive part of $X_n$. Then for every $n$,
$\int |X_n| \, d\mu \le 2C - \int X_0 \, d\mu$.

The proof uses the identity $|x| = 2x^+ - x$ together with the monotonicity of
$n \mapsto \int X_n \, d\mu$.

articles.title: The $L^p$ martingale convergence theorem
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mu)$ be a probability space
with a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, write
$\mathcal{F}_\infty = \bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_n$, let $1 < p < \infty$, and let
$(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$
whose $L^p$ norms are uniformly bounded: there is a constant $R \ge 0$ with
$\|f_n\|_{L^p(\mu)} \le R$ for every $n$. Let $f_\infty$ be the limit process of $(f_n)$, that
is, a chosen $\mathcal{F}_\infty$-measurable function to which $f_n$ converges almost everywhere
if such a function exists, and $0$ otherwise. Then $f_n \to f_\infty$ almost surely, and
$\|f_n - f_\infty\|_{L^p(\mu)} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Equivalent conditions for uniform integrability of a martingale
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mu)$ be a
probability space with a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, and let
$(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$.
The following are equivalent:
1. $(X_n)$ is uniformly integrable.
2. There is an integrable $X_\infty$ such that $X_n \to X_\infty$ almost surely and
   $\int |X_n - X_\infty| \, d\mu \to 0$.
3. There is an integrable $X_\infty$ such that $\int |X_n - X_\infty| \, d\mu \to 0$.
4. There is an integrable $X_\infty$ such that $X_n = \mathbb{E}[X_\infty \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$
   almost surely for every $n$.

articles.title: Equivalent conditions for uniform integrability of a submartingale
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mu)$ be
a probability space with a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, and let
$(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued submartingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and
$\mu$. The following are equivalent:
1. $(X_n)$ is uniformly integrable.
2. There is an integrable $X_\infty$ such that $X_n \to X_\infty$ almost surely and
   $\int |X_n - X_\infty| \, d\mu \to 0$.
3. There is an integrable $X_\infty$ such that $\int |X_n - X_\infty| \, d\mu \to 0$.

articles.title: Bounded optional stopping, conditional form, supermartingale dual
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
measure on a measurable space $\Omega$, let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration
such that $\mu$ is σ-finite on every $\mathcal{F}_n$, and let $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued supermartingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$. Let $L$ and $M$ be
stopping times with values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ such that
$L(\omega) \le M(\omega) \le N$ for every $\omega$, for some $N \in \mathbb{N}$, and suppose
that $\mu$ is σ-finite on the σ-algebra $\mathcal{F}_L$ of events $A$ with
$A \cap \{L \le n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$ for every $n$. Write $f_L(\omega) = f_{L(\omega)}(\omega)$
and $f_M(\omega) = f_{M(\omega)}(\omega)$ for the stopped values. Then
$\mathbb{E}_\mu[f_M \mid \mathcal{F}_L] \le f_L$ holds $\mu$-almost everywhere.

This follows from the submartingale version applied to $-f$.

articles.title: Optional stopping for supermartingales at two bounded stopping times
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
measure on $\Omega$ and $(\mathcal G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ a filtration such that the restriction of $\mu$
to each $\mathcal G_n$ is σ-finite, and let $(f_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued supermartingale
with respect to $(\mathcal G_n)$ and $\mu$. Let $\tau$ and $\pi$ be stopping times for
$(\mathcal G_n)$ with values in $\mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $N$ be a natural number such
that $\tau(\omega) \le \pi(\omega) \le N$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. Then
$\int f_\pi \, d\mu \le \int f_\tau \, d\mu$, where $f_\tau(\omega) = f_{\tau(\omega)}(\omega)$.

This is the dual of the submartingale form of bounded optional stopping, obtained by applying
it to $-f$.

articles.title: Optional stopping for martingales at a bounded stopping time
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on
$\Omega$ and $(\mathcal G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ a filtration such that the restriction of $\mu$ to each
$\mathcal G_n$ is σ-finite, and let $(f_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to
$(\mathcal G_n)$ and $\mu$. Let $\tau$ be a stopping time for $(\mathcal G_n)$ with values in
$\mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $N$ be a natural number such that $\tau(\omega) \le N$ for
every $\omega \in \Omega$. Then $\int f_\tau \, d\mu = \int f_0 \, d\mu$, where
$f_\tau(\omega) = f_{\tau(\omega)}(\omega)$.

articles.title: Optional stopping for martingales at two bounded stopping times
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure
on $\Omega$ and $(\mathcal G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ a filtration such that the restriction of $\mu$ to each
$\mathcal G_n$ is σ-finite, and let $(f_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to
$(\mathcal G_n)$ and $\mu$. Let $\tau$ and $\pi$ be stopping times for $(\mathcal G_n)$ with
values in $\mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $N$ be a natural number such that
$\tau(\omega) \le \pi(\omega) \le N$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. Then
$\int f_\tau \, d\mu = \int f_\pi \, d\mu$, where $f_\tau(\omega) = f_{\tau(\omega)}(\omega)$.

articles.title: Optional stopping for supermartingales at a bounded stopping time
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure
on $\Omega$ and $(\mathcal G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ a filtration such that the restriction of $\mu$ to each
$\mathcal G_n$ is σ-finite, and let $(f_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a real-valued supermartingale with
respect to $(\mathcal G_n)$ and $\mu$. Let $\tau$ be a stopping time for $(\mathcal G_n)$ with
values in $\mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $N$ be a natural number such that
$\tau(\omega) \le N$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. Then $\int f_\tau \, d\mu \le \int f_0 \, d\mu$,
where $f_\tau(\omega) = f_{\tau(\omega)}(\omega)$.

articles.title: The stopped filtration generates the stopping-time σ-algebra
articles.statement:
Let
$(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on a measurable space $\Omega$ and let $\tau$
be a stopping time for it with values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. For each $n$, let
$\mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$ be the σ-algebra of the stopping time $\tau \wedge n$, the $n$-th
σ-algebra of the stopped filtration, and let $\mathcal{F}_\tau$ be the σ-algebra of $\tau$. Then
$\bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n} = \mathcal{F}_\tau$.

The inclusion $\le$ is monotonicity. For $\ge$, a set $s \in \mathcal{F}_\tau$ splits into its
finite-time part $s \cap \{\tau < \infty\} = \bigcup_n (s \cap \{\tau \le n\})$ and its
infinite-time part $s \cap \{\tau = \infty\}$, and both are measurable for the supremum.

articles.title: General optional stopping for uniformly integrable martingales
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
probability measure, let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration and let
$(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ that is
uniformly integrable. Let $f_\infty$ be the limit process of $f$ (its almost-everywhere limit, by
the martingale convergence theorem). Then for every stopping time $\tau$ with values in
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, the value $f_\tau$ of $f$ at $\tau$ (at points where
$\tau = \infty$ it is $\lim_n f_n$) satisfies
$\int f_0 \, d\mu = \int f_\tau \, d\mu = \int f_\infty \, d\mu$.

articles.title: Expectation form of conditional optional stopping for uniformly integrable submartingales
articles.statement:
**Expectation form of conditional optional stopping for uniformly
integrable submartingales.** For stopping times `L ≤ M` (possibly
infinite), `∫ f_L ≤ ∫ f_M`.

articles.title: General optional stopping, expectation inequality
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure,
let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration and let $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a
real-valued submartingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ that is uniformly integrable. Let
$f_\infty$ be the limit process of $f$ (its almost-everywhere limit, by the martingale
convergence theorem). Then for every stopping time $\tau$ with values in
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, the value $f_\tau$ of $f$ at $\tau$ (at points where
$\tau = \infty$ it is $\lim_n f_n$) satisfies
$\int f_0 \, d\mu \le \int f_\tau \, d\mu \le \int f_\infty \, d\mu$.

articles.title: The event that the stopping time is infinite is measurable for the stopped filtration
articles.statement:
Let
$(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on a measurable space $\Omega$ and let $\tau$
be a stopping time for it with values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. For each $n$, let
$\mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$ be the σ-algebra of the stopping time $\tau \wedge n$. Then the set
$\{\omega : \tau(\omega) = \infty\}$ is measurable with respect to
$\bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$.

articles.title: Infinite-time parts of limit-σ-algebra sets are measurable for the stopped filtration
articles.statement:
Let
$(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on a measurable space $\Omega$ and let $\tau$
be a stopping time for it with values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. For each $n$, let
$\mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$ be the σ-algebra of the stopping time $\tau \wedge n$. If a set
$s \subseteq \Omega$ is measurable with respect to $\bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_n$, then
$s \cap \{\tau = \infty\}$ is measurable with respect to $\bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$.

The proof is induction on the σ-algebra generated by the π-system of sets measurable at some
finite time. For $s \in \mathcal{F}_k$ and $m \ge k$, the sets
$(s \cap \{\tau > m\}) \cup \{\tau \le m\}$ lie in $\mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge m}$, and their
intersection over $m \ge k$, intersected with $\{\tau = \infty\}$, is $s \cap \{\tau = \infty\}$.

articles.title: Levels of the stopped filtration
articles.statement:
Let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration
on a measurable space $\Omega$ and let $\tau$ be a stopping time for it with values in
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th σ-algebra of the stopped
filtration is $\mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$, the σ-algebra of the stopping time $\tau \wedge n$.

articles.title: Stopped filtration
articles.statement:
Let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on a
measurable space $\Omega$ and let $\tau$ be a stopping time for it with values in
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. The stopped filtration is the filtration
$n \mapsto \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$, where $\mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$ is the σ-algebra of
the stopping time $\tau \wedge n$.

articles.title: Stopped value as conditional expectation of the limit
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure
on $\Omega$, let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration, and let
$(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$
that is uniformly integrable in $L^1(\mu)$. Let $f_\infty$ be its limit process, a function
measurable with respect to $\bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_n$ to which $f_n$ converges $\mu$-almost
everywhere. Then for every stopping time $\tau$ with values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, the
value $f_\tau$ of $f$ at $\tau$ (with $f_\tau(\omega) = \lim_n f_n(\omega)$ where
$\tau(\omega) = \infty$) satisfies $f_\tau = \mu[f_\infty \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$ $\mu$-almost
everywhere, where $\mu[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$ is conditional expectation given the
σ-algebra $\mathcal{F}_\tau$ of $\tau$.

For each $n$, bounded optional sampling gives
$f_{\tau \wedge n} = \mu[f_\infty \mid \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}]$ almost everywhere, and
Lévy's upward theorem for the filtration $n \mapsto \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}$ identifies the
almost-everywhere limit of these conditional expectations with
$\mu[f_\infty \mid \bigvee_n \mathcal{F}_{\tau \wedge n}] = \mu[f_\infty \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$.

articles.title: Conditional optional stopping with UI of the stopped process
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability
measure on $\Omega$, let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration, and let
$(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and $\mu$.
Let $L \le M$ be stopping times with values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, and suppose the
stopped process $(f_{M \wedge n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable in $L^1(\mu)$. Then
$f_L = \mu[f_M \mid \mathcal{F}_L]$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Here $f_L$ and $f_M$ are the values
of $f$ at the possibly infinite times $L$ and $M$, with $f_L(\omega) = \lim_n f_n(\omega)$ where
$L(\omega) = \infty$ and likewise for $M$, and $\mu[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_L]$ is conditional
expectation given the σ-algebra $\mathcal{F}_L$ of $L$.

If $f$ itself is uniformly integrable, then so is the stopped process $(f_{M \wedge n})$, so the
conclusion holds in that case as well.

articles.title: Conditional optional stopping for uniformly integrable submartingales
articles.statement:
**Conditional optional stopping for uniformly integrable
submartingales.** For stopping times `L ≤ M` (possibly infinite),
`f_L ≤ᵐ μ[f_M | ℱ_L]`.

articles.title: Stopping at a later time does not change the stopped value
articles.statement:
Let $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence of real-valued functions on $\Omega$ and let
$L, M : \Omega \to \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ satisfy $L(\omega) \le M(\omega)$ for every
$\omega$. Then the value at $L$ of the stopped process $n \mapsto f_{M \wedge n}$ equals the value
$f_L$ of $f$ at $L$ at every point of $\Omega$. Here the value of a sequence $(g_n)$ at a point
$\omega$ where the time is infinite is $\lim_n g_n(\omega)$ when this limit exists, and otherwise
a fixed default value that depends only on the sequence $(g_n(\omega))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$.

On $\{L = \infty\}$ the inequality forces $M = \infty$, so there the stopped process is $f$
itself.

articles.title: Value of a process at a possibly infinite time
articles.statement:
For a real-valued process
$(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ on $\Omega$ and a map $\tau : \Omega \to \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$,
the value $f_\tau$ of $f$ at $\tau$ is the function on $\Omega$ given by
$f_\tau(\omega) = f_{\tau(\omega)}(\omega)$ when $\tau(\omega) < \infty$ and
$f_\tau(\omega) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(\omega)$ when $\tau(\omega) = \infty$, where the limit
